en: The Sūtra on the Practice of the Way (Daoxing Banruo Jing), Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Practice of the Way (Daoxing Pin). The First Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā: The Practice of the Way.
The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha, accompanied by an incalculable great assembly of bhikṣus, including his disciples Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others;
and an infinite number of mahāsattva bodhisattvas, including Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, and others.
On the fifteenth day of the month, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"Today there is a great assembly of bodhisattvas; for the sake of these bodhisattvas, the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, and it is in this that bodhisattvas should train and achieve perfection."
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"Now, will Subhūti explain the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas by using his own power?"
"Is it by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that you speak?
Subhūti, knowing what Śāriputra was thinking, addressed him, saying:
"Whatever Dharma the disciples of the Buddha have spoken or accomplished, all is sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power."

Why is this? All the teachings spoken by the Buddha and all that is studied within those teachings possess realization and accord with the Dharma; they instruct one another in succession and bring one another to fulfillment, for within the Dharma there is never any mutual contention.
"Why is this? Because when the Dharma is taught at the proper time, there are no sons or daughters of good family who do not rejoice and find delight in practicing it.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha has commissioned me to explain the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas, and it is from within this that bodhisattvas should train and achieve perfection.

The Buddha has commissioned me to speak of the bodhisattva; yet, when there is a name for a bodhisattva, one becomes attached to that name of a bodhisattva. If there were no name, by what means could one designate a bodhisattva within the Dharma? One does not perceive any dharma that is a bodhisattva; the designation of a bodhisattva-dharma is utterly non-existent. One neither perceives a bodhisattva nor perceives the locus of such a being. How then could there be a bodhisattva who should be taught the *prajñāpāramitā*, or one who would thus speak of the *prajñāpāramitā*?”

Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva’s mind shall not be indolent; they shall not be afraid, nor timid, nor hesitant, nor fearful. The bodhisattva should reflect, "I shall train in this way," and should reflect, "I shall abide in this way."
One should practice with this reflection: when entering the center, one should not think, "This is a bodhisattva.
Why? Because there is both mind and no-mind.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti,
“What is meant by ‘having a mind’ and ‘being without a mind’? Subhūti replied:
“The mind neither exists nor does it not exist; it cannot be apprehended, nor can its location be known.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti, “In what sense does the mind neither exist nor not exist, and why can it neither be apprehended nor its location known?”
"In this way, it neither exists nor does it not exist; it neither has a mind that exists nor does it have a mind that does not exist?
Subhūti replied, "It neither has a mind that exists nor does it have a mind that does not exist."
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, Subhūti!
One who studies for the sake of the Buddha and studies as a Buddha does not speak of the wisdom of the empty body; rather, they speak of the supreme, foremost wisdom of the empty body."
From this, the bodhisattva has already attained *avaivartika* [non-retrogression]; having mastered the characters, he shall never again lose the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus, when a bodhisattva dwells within the *prajñāpāramitā*, if he wishes to study the dharma of the arhat, he should hear the *prajñāpāramitā*, and he should study, uphold, and guard it;
if he wishes to study the dharma of the pratyekabuddha, he should hear the *prajñāpāramitā*, and he should study, uphold, and guard it.
Those who wish to study the Dharma of a bodhisattva should hear the Prajñāpāramitā; they should study it, uphold it, and guard it.
Why is this? Because the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound, and a bodhisattva should study it accordingly.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have reflected deeply and find that the mind of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; its location cannot be known, nor can it be seen as being anywhere. This prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva likewise cannot be fully described, nor can the word 'bodhisattva' be fully explained. A bodhisattva has no fixed place of abiding; they are utterly unapprehendable. They do not emerge from anywhere, they do not enter anywhere, they do not abide anywhere, and they do not cease anywhere."

Why is this? Because the name "Bodhisattva" is utterly unobtainable; there is no such thing as abiding, nor such a thing as stopping. When this Prajñāpāramitā is thus taught, the Bodhisattva hears it and his mind does not grow weary, nor does he find it difficult, nor is he terrified or afraid. Having entered into the state of *avaivartika*, he fully understands it and can never again fall back.
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide within form; they should not abide within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? To dwell within form is to practice consciousness; to dwell within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is to practice consciousness.
One should not practice consciousness; were one to dwell therein, it would constitute a failure to follow the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because practicing with consciousness is not practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*;
one who does not practice cannot attain *sarvajñatā*.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"How should a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) so as to attain the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at form; they do not grasp at sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Not grasping at form is to be without form; not grasping at sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is to be without consciousness."
The Prajñāpāramitā is not received.
Why is it not received?
Because, like a reflection, it has nothing to be grasped and nothing to be attained; therefore, it is not received.

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at any dharmas of letters; therefore, this samādhi is without limit and without center, such that it cannot be attained by any arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is not received. Why is this?
A bodhisattva should not maintain conceptual notions when viewing *sarvajñatā*.
If one views it with conceptual notions, it is a lack of understanding; such a person is like other practitioners who do not believe in *sarvajñatā*.
Why is this? It is because they conversely claim to possess a self;
even if other practitioners of the Way come to believe in the Buddha, once they have believed in the Buddha, they instead take their minor path and enter into the Buddha-way.

Having entered the Buddha-way, one does not grasp at form; one does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Having not grasped them, one has not yet awakened, nor has one yet attained completion. One does not perceive wisdom, nor does one perceive wisdom within, nor does one perceive wisdom without, nor does one perceive wisdom elsewhere. One does not perceive wisdom within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one perceive wisdom without feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one perceive wisdom elsewhere. One is not liberated elsewhere; rather, through the accomplishment of training, one attains the full knowledge of a Buddha and is liberated from within the Dharma—this is called the equality of all phenomena, Nirvāṇa.

Bodhisattvas, do not act in this way; do not view dharmas internally or externally. Alas! They are equal to the *prajñāpāramitā*; all are without that which is received and without that from which they arise. Who, then, attains any dharma?
There is nothing to be grasped, nothing to be gathered, and no perception of nirvāṇa.

For this reason, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā does not accept form, nor does it accept feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; yet it does not enter parinirvāṇa midway. It fully possesses the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; therefore, it is called the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā.
When a bodhisattva has entered into the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should regard it in this way:
"What is this perfection of wisdom?
In what place within the perfection of wisdom can any dharma be found or known? For nowhere can any such thing be apprehended or cognized.

Therefore, a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* should form this thought: upon hearing this, they should not be indolent, nor should they shrink back, nor be afraid, nor terrified, nor find it difficult; they should know that such a bodhisattva is not separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, and the bodhisattva should understand it in this way.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"By what means does a bodhisattva understand the prajñāpāramitā?

Form is detached from its original form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached from their original consciousness; the prajñāpāramitā is detached from its original prajñāpāramitā."
Subhūti said, “It is so. Śāriputra said:
“Excellent, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva were to emerge from this, they would thereby personally attain sarvajñatā. Subhūti said:
"It is so. When a bodhisattva emerges from this, they immediately attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). Why is this?
Because *sarvajñatā* is nowhere born; since it is thus nowhere born, the bodhisattva swiftly approaches Buddhahood."
"When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, there is nothing that obstructs them within omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Śāriputra said, "Excellent!"
The Bodhisattva, with diligent effort, spoke these words: "Suppose one practices with regard to form; suppose one generates a practice regarding form;

suppose one contemplates a practice regarding form; suppose one brings about the cessation of a practice regarding form; suppose one brings about the emptiness of a practice regarding form. Suppose one establishes a desire for attainment through a practice regarding consciousness; suppose one practices with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; suppose one generates a practice regarding consciousness; suppose one contemplates a practice regarding consciousness; suppose one brings about the cessation of a practice regarding consciousness; suppose one brings about the emptiness of a practice regarding consciousness."
"In this way, a bodhisattva who practices with inverted perceptions and acts as such a practitioner does not guard the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor does he practice the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"If one wishes to practice, a bodhisattva should protect their practice and must not follow after it.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"How should a bodhisattva practice the prajñāpāramitā?"
Subhūti said:
"One does not practice with regard to form, nor does one give rise to the practice of form, nor contemplate the practice of form, nor extinguish the practice of form, nor empty the practice of form;

one does not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one give rise to the practice of consciousness, nor contemplate the practice of consciousness, nor extinguish the practice of consciousness, nor empty the practice of consciousness."

One does not practice with regard to form, nor does one practice with the perception of form, nor does one practice with the arising of form, nor does one practice with the observation of form; one does not practice with the cessation of consciousness, nor does one practice with the emptiness of consciousness.
There is neither seeing nor practice, neither seeing-practice, nor practice-seeing; there is likewise no practice, and no practice of cessation.
This is what constitutes the absence of views. Why is this?

Because all dharmas come from nowhere and are sustained by nothing; the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not accept any characterizing marks of words. Therefore, this samādhi is without limit and without center, such that it cannot be reached or known by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who follow this samādhi will swiftly attain Buddhahood. By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, Subhūti spoke these words;

all the bodhisattvas attained the title of *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), having attained Buddhahood during the time of past Buddhas. Following this samādhi, they do not perceive a samādhi, nor is there any conceptualization of a samādhi; they do not construct a samādhi, nor do they cognize a samādhi through mindfulness, nor do they conceptualize sitting in a samādhi, nor do they say, "This is my samādhi. Those who have followed this Dharma are without doubt.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"What is the samādhi that follows along?
Once a bodhisattva has attained the name 'avaivartika' (non-retrogressive) and was able to become a Buddha in the presence of past Buddhas, can one perceive the locus of that samādhi?"
Subhūti said: “It cannot be seen, Śāriputra!”
“Good son, he neither knows nor understands.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“For what reason does he neither know nor understand?”
Subhūti said: “One neither attains samādhi, nor is there any samādhi, nor does one attain its name.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti!

As I have taught, this wisdom of the empty body constitutes the practice of the Bodhisattvas in accordance with the instruction of the Prajñāpāramitā. When Bodhisattvas train in this manner, they are training in the Prajñāpāramitā.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods!
When a bodhisattva trains in this manner, he is training in the prajñāpāramitā.”
Śāriputra asked the Buddha,
“By training in this way, what dharma does one study?
The Buddha said:
"In this way, a bodhisattva trains in the dharma of non-training. Why is this?
Because no dharma can be attained; do not be as deluded as children who train."
Śāriputra asked,
"Who is able to attain this Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"There is nothing to be attained; therefore, one attains the dharma of non-attainment.

Do not be as foolish as those who study like children, thinking that because there are words, they cannot attain [the truth], and thus desire to learn and enter into the dharma. They are merely doubly foolish, neither knowing nor understanding, and failing to comprehend the dharma."
Why is this? To study characters is to be attached to form (*rūpa*); because one seeks to attain this, one does not understand the Dharma, and what one contemplates is likewise unattainable.

Because of such lack of understanding and lack of faith, one does not abide within the Dharma, but instead falsely claims the existence of a self (*ātman*). Therefore, one is as deluded as a child learning [the alphabet].
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Does a bodhisattva who trains in this way train or not?
The Buddha said:
"To train in this way is not to train; the Buddha does not train in this way, yet it is by training that the Buddha becomes a Buddha.
Subhūti said, "O God among Gods!"
"If there were someone who asked such a question— 'Is this illusion one who, by training in the Buddha-dharma,
attains Buddhahood?'— or if someone were to ask this, how should you instruct them? The Buddha said:
"I shall therefore ask you a question; answer it as you see fit.
What do you think, Subhūti: is illusion different from form?
Is illusion different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
Subhūti replied to the Buddha, saying:
"Thus it is, O God among Gods!
Illusion is no different from form; form is illusion, and illusion is form. Illusion is no different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, how is it that what is conceived as equal does not follow the dharma by designating a bodhisattva through the five aggregates?
Subhūti replied:
“Thus it is, O God among Gods!
A bodhisattva who trains with the desire to become a Buddha is merely training in illusion. Why is this?

The illusionist should maintain that all these things are like this: they are maintained as being like the illusion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Form is like form, and the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and the five aggregates are like illusions. Illusion is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; such are the words and letters for the six sense-fields and the five aggregates.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“If there are newly initiated bodhisattvas who hear these words, will they not become terrified?
The Buddha said:
"Suppose a newly initiated bodhisattva encounters and follows an evil teacher; they will feel fear and dread.
But if they encounter and follow a virtuous teacher, they will feel neither fear nor dread."
Subhūti said: "What constitutes a bad teacher for a bodhisattva, and how should one recognize such a person?
The Buddha said:

"If that person does not respect the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, they will teach others to abandon and distance themselves from the bodhicitta, instead teaching various miscellaneous sūtras; they take pleasure in the mind-set of those miscellaneous sūtras and further teach other scriptures, such as the dharmas of the paths of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas. They teach these matters and encourage them to recite them, describing for them the works and causes of Māra that ruin and destroy Bodhisattvas. They speak in various ways of the hardships and sufferings of saṃsāra, saying:
'The path of the Bodhisattva cannot be attained.'"
"Therefore, he is a bad teacher for a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What constitutes a good teacher for a bodhisattva, and by what conduct can one recognize them?"
The Buddha said:

“That person honors the Mahāprajñāpāramitā and gradually instructs others to study and master its teachings; they speak of the works of Māra so that [others] may recognize them and guard against Māra. For this reason, such a person is a good teacher for a bodhisattva.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods!
For what reason is one called a bodhisattva?”
"For what reason is he called by the correct title 'Bodhisattva'?
The Buddha said:

"Because he has studied and fully understood all the teachings of the various sūtras, and because he has thoroughly comprehended all the teachings of the various sūtras, for this reason he is titled a Bodhisattva."
Subhūti said: "One who fully understands and comprehends all dharmas of the sūtras is therefore called a bodhisattva.
For what reason, moreover, is one called a mahāsattva?"
The Buddha said:
"A Mahāsattva is the most honored among those above and below heaven; for this reason, he is named Mahāsattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, too, would like to hear why one is called a Mahāsattva.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"If you wish to hear it, the Buddha shall explain it for you."

A Mahāsattva fully perceives and fully understands all beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions; they thoroughly comprehend and know everything that exists within the ten directions—knowing the lifespans of people, knowing whether there is evil or no evil, pleasure or no pleasure, and whether there is resolve or no resolve—they thoroughly comprehend and know all these things—and seeing them, they preach the Dharma for them. Because they are thus without attachment, they are named Mahāsattvas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I ask concerning the 'Mahāsattva'—by what name is he called a Mahāsattva?
If this Bodhisattva’s mind has no equal, if there is none who can attain his mind, and if it is a mind that cannot be reached by any Arhat or Pratyekabuddha."
The Buddha’s mind is thus: his mind has no attachments; his mind neither issues forth nor enters within.
Since the Buddha’s mind neither issues forth nor enters within, it is a mind free from attachment; for this reason, he is further called a Mahāsattva, the supreme being with whom none can equal.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
"For what reason is the bodhisattva’s mind unattached?
Subhūti replied:
"Because the mind has no arising, it is therefore without attachment.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason is a bodhisattva called one who has donned the great armor (mahāsaṃnāhasaṃnaddha) and one who has set out in the Great Vehicle (mahāyānasamprasthita)?"
“The Buddha has spoken thus; for what reason, then, is it called the Great Armor (*mahā-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) and the Mahāyāna-abhisamaya?
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what cause is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to be armored with the great armor?”
"How does one know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor?
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects in his mind as follows:"

"I shall deliver incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* people, causing them all to enter *parinirvāṇa*; thus, having all entered *parinirvāṇa*, there is not a single person among these dharmas who does not enter *parinirvāṇa*."
Why is this? Because they are fundamentally non-existent.
It is like a magician who, in a vast open space, conjures two great cities and fills them with conjured people, then cuts off the heads of all those conjured people.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would anyone ever die from being wounded or injured? Subhūti replied, "No."
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva delivers incalculable, asaṃkhyeya beings, causing them all to enter parinirvāṇa, there is not a single person among them who does not enter parinirvāṇa.
If, upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva is neither terrified nor afraid, and does not abandon the path to seek other ways, knowing this is what constitutes the Great Armor (mahāsaṃnāha-saṃnaddha).
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“As I have heard from the Buddha and as I recall the matters therein, it is not for the sake of donning the great armor (mahā-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha).”

Why is this? For one who acts in such a manner, there is no act of attaining *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), nor is there anything to be offered; since there is no person who acts, for what kind of person would one don the great armor (*mahāsaṃnāhasaṃnaddha*)?
"Form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Subhūti:
"Form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation."
"What do you mean? Subhūti replied:
"Form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation."
Pukkusāti said: "What is meant by form being without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation?
What is meant by feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness being without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation?"
Subhūti said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "Form is like an illusion;

it is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. They are without limit; they are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation."

For example, space is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; it has nothing produced, and is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. For this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dons the great armor (*mahāsaṃnāhasaṃnaddha*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason is one called 'one who has set out in the Mahāyāna' (mahāyāna-samprasthita)? What is this Mahāyāna?"
From what should one abide within the Great Vehicle?
From what does one emerge from the Great Vehicle?
Who is it that accomplishes the Great Vehicle?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Mahāyāna, Mahāyāna—there is no ‘correct’ in it, and its limits cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"I wish to know from where this *vaipulya* arises.
It arises from three places and abides within *sarvajñatā*; yet there is nothing that arises from within it, nor is there anything that will ever arise from it."
"For what reason?
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"Even if they were already born, as for those who are about to emerge in the future: if there are two dharmas that are unobtainable, and if one does not obtain them from anything, from what dharma could they possibly emerge?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The Mahāyāna, among the heavens above and the humans below, truly transcends all and has no equal. The Vehicle is equal to space; just as space covers incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings, so too does the Mahāyāna cover incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings. For this reason it is called the Mahāyāna, the Great Vehicle."

One does not see its coming, nor does one see its going; one does not see its place of abiding, nor does one see it as having a center or an edge. One neither hears nor sees it therein, nor is there anything seen at all, nor is it seen in the three locations; such is the nature of syllables.
"O God among Gods!
It is for this reason that it is called the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti! For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Subhūti, has the Buddha commissioned you to speak on the *prajñāpāramitā*, and even to explain the matters concerning the Mahāyāna?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In speaking the *prajñāpāramitā*, does Subhūti incur no fault?”
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"If one speaks of the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not go beyond it; one finds its very center."

Subhūti said: “A bodhisattva does not think about that state, nor does he think about this state, nor does he have a thought of no-center. Form is also without limit, and the bodhisattva is also without limit. Form and the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended and cannot be attained; all bodhisattvas cannot be attained and cannot be apprehended. What, then, is the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva?”
From what source should it be taught?
Since a bodhisattva is entirely unfindable and cannot be known as having a location, from what place should the Prajñāpāramitā be taught?
Why do Bodhisattvas further address one another as "Bodhisattva"?
Why is the perception of the "God among Gods" (Devātideva) merely according to the literal name? What is the nature of this intention (*citta*)?
Intention has no location; intention has no form. Intention is fundamentally a dharma of form.
What is form? Form cannot be perceived, nor does it have a body; what "form" could there be therein?

As for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—consciousness cannot be perceived, and the bodhisattva likewise cannot be perceived. The bodhisattva’s consciousness is not known to exist anywhere, nor can it be seen; all bodhisattvas are fundamentally without location and fundamentally cannot be seen. What, then, is the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva?

Thus it is said that a bodhisattva is entirely unfindable and cannot be perceived; nor can one know their whereabouts, for they are utterly non-existent. From what dharma, then, could one speak of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Therefore, he is designated by the name "Bodhisattva.
In this way, there is no conceptualization of a name, nor is there any conceptualization of the name itself; what then is the object of the mind?
Who is it that names the mind?
When the mind reaches its source, the source gives rise to the mind; the mind is formless.
For what reason is there consciousness?
It cannot be grasped, and even when reaching its source, there is nothing to be grasped; for what reason, then, would there be consciousness?

Such is the form of dharmas; even this form has no fundamental basis. If there is no fundamental basis, then who could have created these dharmas? They likewise have no basis; since the basis itself has no basis, from what could one speak of them?

The Prajñāpāramitā has no other location, nor does it have an origin; likewise, the dharmas of a bodhisattva are unobtainable. When a practicing bodhisattva hears this and is neither terrified, nor afraid, nor daunted, they are then practicing the Prajñāpāramitā and practicing the dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā.
When one reflects deeply in this manner, at that time one does not enter into form (*rūpa*).

Why is this? Because form has no place of arising, it is non-form; if it were thus non-form, it would be formlessness (*arūpa*), which likewise has no arising. From within this, nothing can be apprehended, yet the designation "form" is used.

Within the Dharma, there is fundamentally nothing; there is no "is. When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they contemplate the dharmas and enter deeply into them; at that time, they likewise do not enter into sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Why is this? Because consciousness has no place of arising, as it is not consciousness; it neither emerges from within consciousness nor enters into consciousness, for among all phenomena, one realizes that nothing exists.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"As I have heard the matters within the Dharma taught by Subhūti, such a bodhisattva is without arising."
If a bodhisattva is one who has no arising, for what reason does the suchness of a bodhisattva undergo the hardships of practicing the bodhisattva path?
If it is for the sake of the people of the world in the ten directions, how can they endure such hardship?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"I do not cause the bodhisattva to endure these humble sufferings either.
One who practices the path of a bodhisattva thinks to himself: "
"I do not record this as a humble ascetic practice.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva’s mind should not give rise to such thoughts as these:
"I shall endure with patience and humility, never harboring such thoughts.

One should not entertain such thoughts; rather, for the sake of immeasurable and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* beings, one should desire to bring them peace and security, regarding them as a father, regarding them as a mother, regarding them as a son, and regarding them as no different from one's own body, always maintaining a mind of loving-kindness toward them.

A bodhisattva should maintain the mind in this way: that all bodhisattvas are neither seen nor known to have a location; regarding internal and external phenomena in this manner, one should form such a thought and practice accordingly.
When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they do not practice patience, humility, or austerity.
Śāriputra, if it is as has been said, the bodhisattva does not perceive arising; the bodhisattva is one for whom there is no arising.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If it is the case that the bodhisattva is unarisen, then omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is also unarisen.
Subhūti replied:
"In this way, Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) has no place of birth.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva speaks in such a manner, the bodhisattva does not perceive a birth; thus, the bodhisattva is one who has no place of birth."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If it is the case that the bodhisattva is unproduced, then omniscience (sarvajñatā) is also unproduced.
Subhūti replied:
"In this way, Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is without origination.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If Sarvajñā is without origination, then the attainment of all dhyānas is likewise without origination."
Subhūti said: "In this way, one fully attains dhyāna, yet there is nothing produced.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"In this regard, the bodhisattva is unarisen; the bodhisattva is unarisen, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is also unarisen.
The dharma of omniscience is unarisen, and the complete attainment of the perfection of dhyāna is also unarisen.
The dharma of the complete attainment of dhyāna is also unarisen; this is the bodhisattva who has nothing to attain, and it is omniscience that has nothing to be attained."

Subhūti said: "One does not attain non-arising by means of a non-arisen dharma; nor does one attain it by means of an arisen dharma; nor is there the attainment of non-arising by means of that which is neither-arisen-nor-non-arisen."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If there is no non-existence and nothing produced, yet one attains the dharma of non-production, it is for this reason that one attains the dharma of non-production."
Subhūti said: "If that which is unarisen were to arise, and yet there were no such thing as the unarisen, then one would attain [realization] through the unarisen.
Śāriputra addressed Subhūti:
"Even if, Subhūti, there were no 'unborn' and no 'non-unborn,' for that reason it would be the 'unborn.
Subhūti is unborn. Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"There is nothing produced, and there is joy in hearing that nothing is produced. Śāriputra,
this joy in the unproduced is therefore true joy."
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"To hear that which is unarisen is what constitutes hearing.
Śāriputra then addressed Subhūti:
Having heard these words, Subhūti said to Śāriputra: “There is no speaking of that which is not spoken;

this is what is meant by ‘speaking of the non-speakable. This is what is meant by ‘delighting in the non-delightable. For this reason it is called speaking, and for this reason it is called delighting.”
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, Subhūti!
You are the most honored among those who dwell in the Dharma."
"Why is this? It is because the Venerable Subhūti answers according to whatever is asked.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"The Dharma taught by the disciples of the Buddha is not known even in the ten directions; when those who are transformed come, they understand according to what is asked.
Why is this? Even the methods of the ten directions do not know where they arise."
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, Subhūti!
From what dharma do you deliver bodhisattvas?"
Subhūti said: "They are born from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

When this Dharma is being taught or read, if a bodhisattva believes it without doubt, that bodhisattva should know this: there is no increase for one who follows this Dharma, and no decrease for one who does not follow it."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"Following this Dharma does not cause it to increase, nor does not following this Dharma cause it to decrease. One teaches all people according to the Dharma; by following the Dharma, one does not lose any person, causing them all to become bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
"Why is this? Because all people study the Dharma, yet that Dharma remains as it was, both in its worldly and its transcendental aspects. Subhūti said:
“Excellent, Śāriputra!
The Dharma you have understood is no different from what you have said. Why is this?
One should contemplate the human body with earnest mindfulness; one should understand it thus: the human body is empty in various ways, and its mindfulness is likewise empty in various ways.
One should understand that this human body is difficult to fully comprehend, and that which is contemplated is likewise difficult to fully comprehend.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva should train in this way;
they should practice in this way.
**Chapter Two: On Difficult Questions** At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra arrived together with forty thousand devaputras, accompanying one another to join the assembly.
The Four Great Kings arrived together with twenty thousand devaputras from the heavens, accompanying one another to join the assembly.
The Brahmakāyika devas arrived together with ten thousand devaputras, accompanying one another to join the assembly.
The Brahmāpāriṣadya devas and five thousand sons of gods followed one another to join the assembly and sat together.

These sons of gods possessed merit from their past lives; their radiance was magnificent, and sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and his might, the light of these sons of gods shone through with penetrating clarity.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable Subhūti!
This great assembly of many tens of millions of devaputras wishes to hear Subhūti preach the Prajñāpāramitā."
"How does a bodhisattva abide in the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Kauśika!"
“Those many tens of millions of devaputras who delight in this, listen as I shall speak.
Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the Buddha’s might, Subhūti extensively expounded the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the devaputras:
“Which devaputras have not yet practiced the bodhisattva path? Those who have not yet practiced it must now all practice it.”
Having attained the path of the srotāpanna, one can no longer attain the path of the bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because the path of birth and death has been closed off.

Even if these individuals practice the bodhisattva path, I rejoice on their behalf; I shall never sever the dharmas of merit, for I cause them to seek the Middle Way of the Honored One of the Dharma, truly desiring to lead them upward to Buddhahood.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Subhūti! It is wonderful that you thus encourage and delight the bodhisattvas in their training."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“Subhūti ought to repay his debt of gratitude; he must not fail to repay it. Why is this?”

In the past, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas caused their disciples to expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas; the Tathāgata himself also studied therein at that time. By means of such teachings, he brought himself to the state of Buddhahood. For this reason, one should repay the Buddha’s kindness.

I, too, shall likewise preach this Prajñāpāramitā; bodhisattvas shall likewise receive the bodhisattva-dharma. I shall further exhort and delight them; having received it all and been exhorted and delighted by all, bodhisattvas will swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika! Listen to what you have asked.
How does a bodhisattva abide within the *prajñāpāramitā*? A bodhisattva who maintains the dharma of emptitude abides within the *prajñāpāramitā*."

Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the great armor and set out in the Mahāyāna should not dwell within form; he should not dwell within sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He should not dwell within the stage of a srotāpanna; he should not dwell within the stage of a sakṛdāgāmin; he should not dwell within the stage of an anāgāmin; he should not dwell within the stage of an arhat; he should not dwell within the stage of a pratyekabuddha; and he should not dwell within the stage of a buddha.

One should not dwell in the notion that form exists or does not exist; one should not dwell in the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness exist or do not exist. One should not dwell in the notion that there is a stream-enterer or no stream-enterer; one should not dwell in the notion that there is a once-returner or no once-returner; one should not dwell in the notion that there is a non-returner or no non-returner; one should not dwell in the notion that there is an arhat or no arhat; one should not dwell in the notion that there is a pratyekabuddha or no pratyekabuddha; one should not dwell in the notion that there is a buddha or no buddha.

One should not dwell in the thought that form is impermanent; one should not dwell in the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent. One should not dwell in the thought that form is suffering or pleasure; one should not dwell in the thought that form is beautiful or ugly. One should not dwell in the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering or pleasure; one should not dwell in the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are beautiful or ugly. One should not dwell in the thought that form is "mine" or "not mine"; one should not dwell in the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are "mine" or "not mine. One should not dwell in the thought that the fruit of stream-entry is an unshakable attainment; once the fruit of stream-entry has been attained, one should not dwell therein.
Why is this? Because one who follows the path of the srotāpanna passes beyond after seven deaths and seven births; therefore, one should not dwell within the path of the srotāpanna.
One should not dwell within the path of the sakṛdāgāmin because its accomplishment is unshakable; once the path of the sakṛdāgāmin has been accomplished, one should not dwell within it.
Why is this? Because one who follows the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin dies once and is reborn once before passing away; therefore, one should not dwell within the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
One should not dwell within the path of the Anāgāmin because it is accomplished through immovability; once the path of the Anāgāmin has been accomplished, one should not dwell within it.
Why is this? Once the path of the Anāgāmin has been accomplished, one attains parinirvāṇa in the heavens; therefore, one should not dwell within the path of the Anāgāmin.
One should not dwell in the immovable accomplishment of the path of an arhat, nor should one dwell in it once the path of an arhat has been accomplished. Why is this?

Once the path of the Arhat has been accomplished, one is entirely exhausted of this world and has no further place of abiding; one attains parinirvāṇa within nirvāṇa. Therefore, one should not dwell within the path of the Arhat.
One should not dwell in the realization of the Pratyekabuddha path, for it is unshakable. Why is this?

Once the Pratyekabuddha path has been accomplished, one surpasses the stage of the Arhat but cannot reach the Buddha path; thus, one enters parinirvāṇa midway. For this reason, one should not dwell in the realization of the Pratyekabuddha path.
One should not abide within the Buddha-way.

Why? Because one performs meritorious deeds for the sake of incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* beings; with these incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* beings, I shall cause them all to enter *parinirvāṇa*. Since one abides correctly within the Buddha-way for this purpose, one should not abide within it.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"How should the Buddha abide?
Subhūti, knowing what Śāriputra was thinking, then asked Śāriputra:
"How does the Buddha dwell? Where does he abide?
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"The Buddha has no abode. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has a mind that dwells nowhere; it does not abide in a place of movement, nor does it abide in a place free from movement."
Subhūti said: "So it is, so it is!
A bodhisattva should train in this way:
just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha abides—yet even that abiding is non-abiding—one should abide in this manner, training in non-abiding."
At that time, the sons of the gods had this thought in their minds:
"The thoughts of the yakṣas may still be known; whether the yakṣas are great or small, what they say can all be understood. But what the Venerable Subhūti says cannot be understood at all."
Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, said to them:
"These words are difficult to comprehend, impossible to hear, and impossible to know."
The sons of the gods further thought to themselves:
"These words must be understood; now the Venerable Subhūti has entered deeply and knows profoundly.
Subhūti, again knowing what was in the minds of the sons of the gods, spoke to them, saying:
"Having attained the realization of the path of *srotāpanna*, if one dwells therein and does not delight in departing from it;
having attained the realization of the path of *sakṛdāgāmin*, if one dwells therein and does not delight in departing from it;
having attained the realization of the path of *anāgāmin*, if one dwells therein and does not delight in departing from it;"
Having attained the realization of the path of Arhatship, if one dwells therein, it is because one does not delight in departing from it;
having attained the realization of the path of Pratyekabuddhahood, if one dwells therein, it is because one does not delight in departing from it;
and having attained the realization of the path of Buddhahood, if one dwells therein, it is because one does not delight in departing from it.
The sons of the gods further thought to themselves:
"Since the Venerable Subhūti speaks in such a manner, where else might we seek a Dharma teacher who speaks as the Venerable Subhūti does?"
Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, said to them:
"The Dharma-preacher is like an illusion; those who wish to hear the Dharma from me likewise hear nothing and realize nothing."
The sons of the gods again had this thought in their minds:
"How can it be that dharmas act in this way, and that people hear them in this way?
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, spoke to them, saying:
"Is an illusion like a person, and a person like an illusion?
I declare that the paths of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha are all like illusions; even the path of a Buddha, I declare, is likewise like an illusion."
The devaputras said to Subhūti,
“Is even the path of the Buddha likewise called an illusion?
Subhūti replied:
"Even Nirvāṇa is likewise like an illusion.
The devaputras asked Subhūti:
"Is even Nirvāṇa, as well as the Nirvāṇa and the one who attains Nirvāṇa, likewise like an illusion?"
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"Even if there were a dharma that transcended nirvāṇa, it too would be like an illusion. Why is this?"
“An illusory person, nirvāṇa, and space are like that—possessing nothing.
Śāriputra, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, and Mahākātyāyana asked Subhūti:
“What is the characteristic of the prajñāpāramitā?”
"From what dharma do they emerge?
Subhūti replied, "From this very dharma do the *avaivartika* bodhisattvas emerge; this is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"In this way, when these disciples hear the Dharma, they will all fully attain and quickly become arhats.
Subhūti said: "The exposition of characteristics within the Prajñāpāramitā is such that nothing at all emerges from the Dharma."

Why is this? Because within the Dharma there is nothing that exists, nothing that can be heard, and nothing that can be attained. Thus, for a bhikṣu who accords with the Dharma, there is no Dharma to hear and no Dharma to attain; from within this Dharma, there is nothing to be grasped.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"The Venerable Subhūti has rained down the treasure of the Dharma; I should now take some flowers and scatter them over the Venerable Subhūti."
Śakra Devānām Indra then manifested flowers and scattered them over Subhūti.
Subhūti understood this in his mind and said:

"These flowers did not emerge from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; I have seen these flowers before. These flowers that have been produced and scattered upon me are merely manifestations; they are transformations."

These flowers are transformation-flowers; they do not emerge from trees. These flowers produced by Śakra Devānām Indra, which he used to scatter over me, emerged from the Tree of the Mind, and were not born from trees.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"These flowers have no place from which they arise,
O Venerable Subhūti!"
"It does not emerge from the wish-fulfilling tree.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika has said:..."
"These flowers have no place from which they arise, nor do they emerge from the mind-tree.
"Are they, then, not flowers? Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“Venerable Subhūti, knowing well that there is neither increase nor decrease in what is spoken, he teaches the Dharma in this way.
Just as the Venerable Subhūti has instructed, so should a bodhisattva train.”
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika! These words are not otherwise;

a bodhisattva should train in this way to enter into the Dharma. When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they do not train in the path of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha; rather, they train in the Buddha-path, they train in the path of sarvajñatā.”

One who trains in this manner trains in incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* volumes of sūtras; they do not train in the production of form, nor do they train in the production of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. They do not train in the reception of other dharmas, nor do they train in receiving, nor do they train in losing. Training in non-loss is training for *sarvajñatā*; it is the emergence of *sarvajñatā*.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“To train in this training is neither to accept nor to reject; it is to train for the sake of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) and to emerge from sarvajñatā.”
Subhūti said: "So it is, Śāriputra!
Training in this manner neither accepts nor rejects; training in this way is the training for sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and it is for the sake of emerging from sarvajñatā."
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Śāriputra:
"How should a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
Śāriputra replied:
"One should ask the Venerable Subhūti.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"By virtue of what majestic power and grace should one train and understand?"
Subhūti said: "Kauśika,
you should learn and understand this by relying on the grace of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power."
As for the question, "How does a bodhisattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?"—

one should not practice within form (*rūpa*), nor should one practice apart from form; one should not practice within feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor should one practice apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Why is this? The Prajñāpāramitā is neither feeling, perception, mental formations, nor consciousness; yet the Prajñāpāramitā is not separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"The Mahāpāramitā is without limit and without bottom; what, then, is this pāramitā?
Subhūti replied:

“Kauśika! The mahāpāramitā is the boundless pāramitā, the bottomless pāramitā. The mahāpāramitā is utterly unobtainable; the boundless pāramitā is utterly invisible; the bottomless pāramitā is utterly unfathomable. It is neither bottomless nor not bottomless; it is neither bottomless nor not not bottomless. The pāramitās are equal in being neither bottomless nor not bottomless; the pāramitās are bottomless and yet not not bottomless. Furthermore, they have neither middle nor extremes, and they have no beginning or end. They are utterly immeasurable and utterly unknowable.”
Kauśika! From the bottom of the Dharma, the bottom of the pāramitās is bottomless, and furthermore, it is not even non-bottomless.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

The Dharma has neither bottom nor beginning; it has no center or periphery, and there is no time when it is exhausted. Seeking a bottom, one finds no bottom, yet there is also no "perfection of having no bottom."
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"How is this so, Venerable Subhūti?"
"For what reason are sentient beings bottomless and the pāramitās bottomless?
Subhūti said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"This matter is entirely incalculable; even if one were to calculate it by doubling and doubling again, sentient beings are bottomless and the pāramitās are bottomless."
Śakra Devānām Indra asked:
"For what reason is that person bottomless, and why are the perfections (pāramitās) bottomless?
Subhūti replied:
"Kauśika, what do you think? Within what dharma is there such a teaching that people are born from?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:

"There is no dharma that teaches in this way, nor is there any dharma that abides as such a teaching. Even if there were one who emerged, it would be merely a name; even if there were one who remained, it would be merely a name; it is only by means of names and words that they are attached to speech."
Any place where one dwells is merely a name; it is utterly non-existent, being nothing more than words used to designate and express.
A person is likewise a person; from beginning to end, they are empty and non-existent.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika, what do you think? Can a person be perceived?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"One cannot perceive a person.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika!..."
What is the nature of this mental attention?
What is the limit of such persons?

Suppose even a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to live for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and exhaustively deliver sentient beings, with those delivered in turn delivering others—would there ever be a time when those thus born would be completely exhausted?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"There is no time of interruption. Why is this?"
“Sentient beings have no end.
Subhūti said: “Sentient beings have no bottom;
the Prajñāpāramitā has no bottom. A bodhisattva who trains should understand it thus and know it thus; such is the practice of the dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The *Daoxing Banruo Boluomi Jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), Scroll One;
The *Daoxing Banruo Jing*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Yuezhi Country during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter Three: On Merit The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Three:

On Merit At that time, the gods of the Cāturmahārājika heaven, the Brahmā gods, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, the Īśvara gods, and the Nirmāṇarati gods simultaneously three times proclaimed these words of praise for the Dharma:
"The Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti is profoundly deep; the Tathāgatas are all born from it."

Those who hear it, or who recite, chant, read, and practice it, we shall regard with reverence as if they were Tathāgatas; we shall regard with reverence those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said to the devas and humans: "So it is, so it is!
In the past, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I attained the Prajñāpāramitā, and I was then granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, who said:"

"Hereafter, when you shall become a guide among men, you will fully attain the wisdom of a Buddha. After incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni, the most honored among all that is above and below heaven; you shall bring stability to the world and possess the utmost clarity of the Dharma, and thus be called a Buddha."
Then the devas and humans simultaneously addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, God among Gods!
By practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, you have personally attained omniscience (sarvajñatā)."
At that time, the Buddha was seated in the midst of the assembly among the devas. He addressed the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās:
"Now let the fourfold assembly bear witness; the gods of the desire realm, the Brahmā gods, and the Ābhāsvara gods shall all testify."
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

“If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who study the Prajñāpāramitā, who uphold it, and who recite it, then Māra or the gods of Māra will ultimately be unable to find an opportunity against those sons and daughters of good family.”
Kauśika! Whether they be humans or non-humans, no one shall ever be able to find an opportunity to harm these sons and daughters of good family. Kauśika!
Good sons and good daughters shall not meet with untimely death. Kauśika!

Among the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, those who practice the Buddha-way but have not yet attained the Prajñāpāramitā—those who have not yet studied it or recited it—all such devas will go to where these good sons and good daughters dwell.

Kauśika! A son of good family or a daughter of good family who studies, upholds, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā will have no fear, no terror, and no dread, whether they are in a secluded place or in a remote, hidden spot.
The Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying,
“We ourselves shall together protect these good men and good women who study the Prajñāpāramitā, who uphold it, and who recite it.”
The Brahmā Sanatkumāra and the various devas of the Brahma heavens addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“We ourselves shall collectively protect these good men and good women who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā.”
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I myself shall protect these sons and daughters of good family who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā.”
Śakra Devānām-indra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"It is difficult to encounter those who study the Prajñāpāramitā; when good men and good women have minds that are unshakable, those who receive this Prajñāpāramitā are thereby receiving all six pāramitās."
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Kauśika!
One who receives the Prajñāpāramitā receives all six pāramitās."
Furthermore, Kauśika!
Listen, Kauśika, you sons and daughters of good family who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā. Kauśika!
"I say that my words are excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; you should listen attentively to what I have to say.
Śakra Devānām Indra listened to the Buddha and received his instruction.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām-Indra:

"In my Dharma, there are those who would harass, those who would harm, and those who would disturb; those who wish to harass, wish to harm, or wish to disturb will gradually give rise to evil intentions, but before they can reach their goal, they will perish midway.
Those who wish to harass, wish to harm, or wish to disturb will find that whatever they subsequently do ultimately fails."

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, whenever those who bring them evil approach them, they will be subdued and turn back before they even arrive; subsequently, their desires shall never be fulfilled.
Kauśika! When good sons and good daughters perform their deeds and all see them for themselves—those who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā—it is, Kauśika, as if:

There is a medicinal herb called *mṛdvī*. Once, a hungry snake was wandering about in search of food when it encountered an insect on its path. As the snake was about to devour the insect, the fragrance of the *mṛdvī* herb reached the insect's location; upon smelling the scent of the herb, the snake immediately retreated.
Why is this? Because the power of the medicine repels it, the snake’s venom immediately subsides; such is the way the power of the medicine suppresses it. Kausika!

Noble sons and noble daughters who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā—should anyone wish to harm them, they shall naturally perish, repelled by the majestic spiritual power of the Prajñāpāramitā and suppressed by the might of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:

"Should there be those who plot against them, wherever they come from, they shall be severed and destroyed right there and never succeed. The Four Heavenly Kings will all protect these good men and good women who enter and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā; whatever they do will be sovereign, whatever they say will be like nectar, their speech will not be frivolous, anger will not arise, and self-conceit will not arise—the Four Heavenly Kings will protect them all."

These sons and daughters of good family who study, uphold, and recite the *prajñāpāramitā* speak without deviation; their speech is like nectar, their words are not frivolous, malice does not arise, and self-conceit does not develop.
Why is this? Because by practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not harbor self-directed anger, does not harbor self-conceit, and does not harbor self-approval.
These sons and daughters of good family will naturally give rise to this thought:
"If any conflict arises, I shall always physically distance myself from it."
Displeased by this matter, he felt ashamed in his own presence and thought to himself:
"These wicked people must not be approached.
He thought to himself:
"I seek the path of the Buddha; I must not follow words of anger, but must quickly cause myself to attain a virtuous mind.
Good sons and good daughters, whatever they do, they shall all personally see those who study, uphold, and recite the excellent Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā can transcend all evil states; its actions are performed with sovereign mastery, and there is none equal to it.”
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family studies, upholds, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā, they shall never feel fear or dread even when passing through the midst of extreme perils; even if they enter an army, they will not be struck by weapons."
The Buddha said:
"What I have spoken is without deviation. Kauśika!"

As the Buddha has said that no one can cause harm, when good sons and good daughters at such a time recite, uphold, or mind the Prajñāpāramitā, even if death should arrive, or if they should die therein, or if enemies should seek to harm them therein—it shall be exactly as the Buddha spoke and not otherwise. These good sons and good daughters will never suffer an untimely death therein; even if there are those who shoot at them or those who brandish weapons toward them while they are therein, their bodies will never be struck.
Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā is the supreme, great incantation, the most powerful incantation among men.

Those sons and daughters of good family who study this incantation do not think of evil for themselves, nor do they think of evil toward others; they have no such thoughts at all. They are truly heroes among men, attaining Buddhahood by their own power, and protecting the people and all crawling and flying creatures. Those who study this incantation will swiftly achieve the Way of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Once the Prajñāpāramitā has been written down, even if one is unable to study it or recite it, one should maintain its physical scroll; neither humans nor spirits will be able to cause harm to such a person, though the karmic offenses of past lives cannot be invoked [to prevent their ripening]."
It is like this, Kauśika!
At the place where one has first attained Buddhahood, even if there were people coming from all four directions,
or spirits, or birds and beasts, none would be able to cause them harm.
Whether it be ghosts and spirits or birds and beasts, should they wish to come and harass people or wish to come and harm them, they will ultimately be unable to succeed. Why is this?

Because it is the place where the Buddha attained the Way; it is protected by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. The Buddhas of the past, future, and present—the Gods among Gods—are all honored as the most venerable among men, and all have attained Buddhahood therein.
Those who are about to set forth again to seek the Buddha-way shall all attain the Buddha-way therein.
If there are those who enter this place, they will have no fear, no dread, and no apprehension; such is the Prajñāpāramitā.

Wherever the Prajñāpāramitā resides, all devas, humans, asuras, spirits, and nāgas shall pay homage, show reverence, and protect it; for this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is protected by its own majestic spiritual power.
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,

if there were one who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, or one who upholds its scrolls, and takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it with offerings— namely, famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags— or if, after the Parinirvāṇa, one erects a stūpa for the Buddha’s relics and takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it with offerings— namely, famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags— which of these would produce greater merit?"
The Buddha said:
"I ask you this on purpose, Kauśika!"
"Reveal to me, Kauśika, according to your inclination:
How is it that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha achieves omniscience (sarvajñatā), and this body appears? From what dharma did the Tathāgata train and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Śakra Devānām-indra replied to the Buddha:
“The Tathāgata learned from training in the Prajñāpāramitā and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"It is not by means of bodily relics that one attains Buddhahood; rather, it is from within omniscience (sarvajñatā) that a Tathāgata emerges, for the Tathāgata has issued forth from within the Prajñāpāramitā."
Thus it is, Kauśika!
The body of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) arises from within the prajñāpāramitā;
the body of sarvajñatā of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is born from that body of sarvajñatā.
I manifest the body of a Buddha; it is from sarvajñā (all-knowledge) that I attain the body of a Buddha, and from sarvajñā that my relics arise after my parinirvāṇa, to be honored as before.

If, Kauśika, there are good sons or good daughters who write down the Prajñāpāramitā, study, uphold, recite, and practice it, and who take refuge in it, pay homage to it, and serve and make offerings to it— with fine flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags— then they are making an offering to Sarvajña (the All-Knowing One).
In this way, Kauśika!
having transcribed the Prajñāpāramitā and made such offerings to the scroll, the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family from within that Dharma is incomparable.
"Why is this? Because one who possesses *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) has already performed the offering.
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are those people of Jambudvīpa who do not make offerings to or serve the Prajñāpāramitā truly unaware of its sublimity?"
"The merit of one who makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā is supreme and beyond compare.
One should take up and offer worship to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“Kauśika, how many people among those in Jambudvīpa believe in the Buddha, believe in the Dharma, and believe in the Saṃgha of bhikṣus?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The people of Jambudvīpa are few; those who have faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus are but very few. Furthermore, those who practice for the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, or Pratyekabuddha, up to those who practice the path to Buddhahood, are likewise very few."
The Buddha said,
"So it is, Kauśika! There are but very few people."
There are many who seek the Buddha-way and practice in pursuit of the Buddha-way; yet, by the time they finally become Buddhas, there are very few indeed.
Thus, among incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* people who initially set out seeking the Buddha-way, only one or two emerge from among them to abide in the stage of *avaivartika*.
"In this way, Kauśika!
These sons and daughters of good family who practice seeking the path of the Buddha will likewise attain Buddhahood after the assembly.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good sons and good daughters who study the Prajñāpāramitā, those who uphold the sūtra and those who recite the sūtra, should be saluted, served, and revered.”
Why is this? Because those who understand the matters within the Prajñāpāramitā are few.

All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, as well as all the Bodhisattvas of the past who practiced the Buddha-way, all achieved their mastery by training in the Prajñāpāramitā; I, too, at that time, trained together among them.
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall receive this Prajñāpāramitā. Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, takes up his relics and erects a stūpa made of the seven precious substances to make offerings to them—throughout their entire life, taking refuge in them, paying homage, and serving them with celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incense, celestial silken banners, celestial canopies, and celestial pennants.
"In this way, Kauśika, what do you think? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to make such an offering, would their merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "It would be very great, indeed very great!"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as when a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out the *Prajñāpāramitā*, takes up this scroll, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves and makes offerings to it—namely, with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags and pennants—they will obtain much more merit."
The Buddha said:
“Set aside this stūpa, Kaucika!

Furthermore, suppose there were stupas made of the seven treasures filling the entirety of Jambudvīpa, and some son or daughter of good family were to take refuge in them, pay homage, serve, and make offerings for as long as their life lasts—using celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incenses, celestial silken fabrics, celestial canopies, and celestial banners.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would the merit of these good sons and good daughters be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as great as the merit obtained by a son of good family or a daughter of good family who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes up the scroll, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves and makes offerings to it—namely, with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags.”
The Buddha said:
"Set aside the affairs performed in Jambudvīpa, Kauśika!

Suppose there were stupas made of the seven treasures filling the four continents, and some son or daughter of good family were to take refuge in them, pay homage, serve, and make offerings throughout their entire life—using celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incenses, celestial silks, celestial canopies, and celestial banners—would not their merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Very much, very much,
O Heaven among Heavens!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as when a son or daughter of good family writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes up the scroll, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves and makes offerings to it—with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags—thereby gaining much more merit."
The Buddha said,
"Setting aside the stupas for the four continents, Kausika!

Suppose there were one world-system, and furthermore another world-system, and likewise a thousand such world-systems, all four sides of which were filled with stūpas made of the seven treasures. If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for as long as they lived, took refuge in them, prostrated, served, and made offerings—using celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incense, celestial silken cloth, celestial canopies, and celestial banners.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

"It is not as meritorious for this son of good family or daughter of good family to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, to hold its volume, to take refuge in it, to pay homage to it, and to serve and make offerings to it—with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags—as the latter would obtain much more merit."
The Buddha said:
"Set aside the thousand worlds, Kauśika!

In this way, throughout the two thousand worlds of the middle chiliocosm, the four directions were entirely filled with stupas made of the seven treasures. If there were sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as they lived, took refuge, paid homage, served, and made offerings—offering celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incense, celestial silks, celestial canopies, and celestial banners.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

“Yet it is not as much as the merit gained by a son or daughter of good family who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes up its scrolls, and reverently honors, serves, and makes offerings to them—with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower parasols, and flags.”
The Buddha said:
"Setting aside these two thousand worlds for a moment, Kauśika!

Suppose that throughout the three thousandfold world system, the four directions were entirely filled with stupas made of the seven treasures; and suppose there were sons of good family or daughters of good family who, for as long as they lived, took refuge in them, paid homage, served, and made offerings—offering celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incenses, celestial silken fabrics, celestial canopies, and celestial banners.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would the merit of these sons and daughters of good family be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for those sons and daughters of good family to write down the Prajñāpāramitā, to hold its scrolls, to take refuge in it, to pay homage to it, and to serve and make offerings to it—with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags—as the latter would obtain much more merit."
The Buddha said:
"Setting aside these seven-jeweled stūpas throughout the three thousandfold world-system,
Kauśika!..."

If all the *sattvas* within the three thousand great world-systems were to attain human birth, and having clearly become humans, each were to construct a stupa made of the seven treasures; and if these people were to provide offerings throughout their entire lives, using various musical instruments, flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, hundreds of kinds of fragrances, silken banners, parasols, and flags—furthermore, using celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incenses, celestial silks, celestial parasols, and celestial flags—if all such *sattvas*, as well as all the *sattvas* within the three thousand great world-systems, were to erect these stupas of the seven treasures and offer them all such musical performances.
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would the merit and blessings of that not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Those who make such offerings, their merit and virtue will be exceedingly great, exceedingly great,
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as much as the merit gained by a son or daughter of good family who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, carries its scrolls, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it with offerings—namely, famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is utterly peaceful and secure, O God among Gods!”

To take refuge, pay homage, serve, and make offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—the Gods among Gods, the All-Knowing Ones—is itself to pay homage, serve, take refuge in, and fully offer to the ultimate.
The Buddha said:

"Setting aside these seven-jeweled stūpas within the three thousand great world-systems, suppose that in as many buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges River, every single *sattva* were to erect seven-jeweled stūpas for each, making offerings to them all for one *kalpa*, and then for another *kalpa*, using celestial flowers, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial blended incense, celestial silks, celestial canopies, and celestial banners, and offering all the various musical performances of the heavens above and the earth below."
"In this way, Kauśika!
Would the merit and blessings of that not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as much as the merit obtained by a son or daughter of good family who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, takes up the scroll, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it with offerings—namely, famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags."
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "It is so, Kauśika!

It is not as if a son or daughter of good family were to obtain from this Dharma a merit that is exceedingly great—beyond further calculation, beyond further discussion, beyond further praise, beyond further measurement, and beyond further limit."
Why is this? Because from within the Prajñāpāramitā emerge the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and Sarvajñās.
Thus it is, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, carries its scrolls, takes refuge in it, pays homage to it, and serves and makes offerings to it—namely, with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
It is due to the power of merit, due to the power of blessings, due to the power of merit from previous lives, and due to the power of the Buddha’s blessings.
The Buddha said:

"If all sentient beings (*sattva*) in Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of a hundred times the Ganges were each to erect stupas made of the seven treasures, they would not even enter into calculation; a thousandfold more would not enter into calculation; a hundred-thousandfold more would not enter into calculation; ten-trillion-fold more would not enter into calculation; and an incalculable number of times more would not even enter into the calculation of making offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*."
At that time, forty thousand devas and humans came together with Śakra Devānām Indra to the great assembly. The devas said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Venerable One, you should take up the Prajñāpāramitā; you should recite the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
“You should study it, Kauśika!
You should uphold the sūtra scroll and you should recite it.”
