Why is this? It is because the asuras conceived this thought in their minds:
"We wish to engage in battle with the Trāyastriṃśa devas."
The Asuras immediately raised their armies and ascended to heaven.
At that time, Kauśika!
if one recites and contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā, the hosts of Asura soldiers will immediately retreat.
Śakra Devānām Indra then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is a most supreme incantation, O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is a most honored incantation; the Prajñāpāramitā is an incantation without equal."
The Buddha said, "So it is, Kauśika!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme incantation; the Prajñāpāramitā is the most venerable incantation; there is no incantation equal to the Prajñāpāramitā."
Kauśika! Those who uphold this incantation—past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—all attained Buddhahood by means of this very incantation;
those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are yet to come in the future shall all likewise attain Buddhahood by studying this incantation.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions currently existing have all brought forth this prayer and thereby attained Buddhahood themselves. Kauśika!

Because of this prayer, the merit of the Ten Precepts emerges and illuminates the world; the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the [ten] powers illuminate the world. From within the Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives birth to the merit of the Ten Precepts, which pervades the entire world; the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the [ten] powers all illuminate the world.

Now, before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha had appeared in the world, the Bodhisattva fully illuminated the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
"Just as, Kauśika, when the moon is at its fullness,
it emerges from the sky and illuminates the constellations; even so, Kauśika!"
The fullness of the merit of the Bodhisattva’s practice is likewise.

Before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, the Bodhisattva acted as a light-bringer; one should know that all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas emerge from skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If there are good men or good women who uphold, study, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, they will be fully endowed with supreme virtue."
Śakra Devānām Indra asked the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods!
What is meant by being fully endowed with supreme virtue?”
The Buddha said:
"That person shall never die from poison, nor drown in water, nor die by being struck by weapons.

If at any time an official rebellion arises, or if one is unjustly oppressed by officials, they should recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā while sitting or walking; then the officials will ultimately be unable to cause them harm."
Why is this? Because they are protected by the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, if there should be any other matter, one should recite and keep the Prajñāpāramitā in mind and go to that place—whether to the presence of a king, a crown prince, or a high minister—and then engage them in pleasant conversation, discourse with them, and share in joyful laughter.

Why is this? Because by practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, they maintain mindfulness of the good and contemplate the good; they cause all people, down to the smallest crawling insects, to become virtuous. Maintaining an impartial mind of compassion and pity, for this reason, whenever people see them, they all rise to their feet.
"In this way, Kauśika!
If there were anyone seeking an opportunity [to harm], they would be unable to cause injury.

At that time, there was a certain follower of another path who, seeing from afar the great assembly of the Buddha, advanced slowly with the intent to disrupt the gathering. As he drew near to where the Buddha was, Śakra Devānām Indra had this thought:
"How may I, for the remainder of my life, remain constantly by the Buddha's side to receive and recite the Prajñāpāramitā?
Heretics wish to disturb me and sever this Dharma."

Śakra Devānām-indra, having heard the Prajñāpāramitā from the Buddha, immediately received and recited it; those heterodox practitioners then circumambulated the Buddha from afar, keeping him to their right, and departed by way of that path.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"How can I cause these followers of other paths to depart by way of that side road?
As soon as Śāriputra had this thought, the Buddha knew it immediately.

The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “When Śakra Devānām-indra recollects the *prajñāpāramitā*, these followers of heterodox paths depart. Because these followers of heterodox paths come with no good intentions, but rather come entirely with evil intentions, Māra the Wicked then thinks:

‘The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is seated together with his fourfold assembly; the gods of the Desire Realm, the Brahmā gods, and all the celestial beings have likewise gathered therein. There are no followers of heterodox paths, but only an assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have received their predictions, who shall become leaders among men and attain Buddhahood for themselves. I must go to corrupt and disrupt them.’”
Māra the Wicked mounted a single-axle chariot drawn by four horses and proceeded slowly forward until he reached the Buddha’s dwelling. Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:

"Māra the Wicked has come to the Buddha’s dwelling riding a chariot drawn by four horses; yet this chariot and its horses of Māra the Wicked are no different from those of King Bimbisāra, nor do they resemble the four-horse chariot of King Prasenajit."
"It is not of the Śākya clan, for the four-horse chariot is unlike [ours];
it is not fallen from the Śāri lineage, for the four-horse chariot is unlike [ours];
this is the work of the evil Māra."
"Day and night, the evil Māra constantly seeks an opportunity against the Buddha and perpetually disturbs the people of the world.
Śakra Devānām Indra always made this vow:
"I shall always keep the Prajñāpāramitā in mind; I shall constantly bear it in mind, uphold it, and recite it to completion."
As Śakra Devānām Indra recited the Prajñāpāramitā in his mind, desiring to reach its ultimate conclusion, Māra the Evil One returned by way of his path.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa and Kāyika heavens, holding celestial flowers, flew through the air and stood there; they then scattered them over the Buddha and over the four directions, saying:
"The Prajñāpāramitā has been cut off for a very long time; now the people of Jambudvīpa have finally heard it and finally seen it."
He then took various kinds of celestial flowers and scattered them over the Buddha from all four sides.
The Buddha said:
"Those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā and those who maintain the Prajñāpāramitā shall not be taken advantage of by Māra or his retinue."
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The merit and blessings of such people are not small, for they have heard the Prajñāpāramitā; how much more so for those who learn, uphold, recite, and contemplate it! Having learned, upheld, and recited it, and having taken up its study in this way, dwelling by means of this Dharma—if such a person had previously seen a Buddha and heard the Prajñāpāramitā, how much more so for one who learns, upholds, and recites it, and having learned, upheld, and recited it, practices according to the matters therein and dwells fully in this Dharma? Such a person has thereby made an offering to the Tathāgata."
Why is this? Because it is from this that sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) practices the prajñāpāramitā.
For example, O God among Gods!
Those who wish to obtain the greatest of jewels should seek them from the great ocean;
those who wish to obtain the treasure of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) that constitutes a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, should seek it from within the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said: "It is so;
from within this emerges the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Sarvajñā."
Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“There is no one who speaks of the dānapāramitā, nor does anyone speak of the śīlapāramitā, nor the kṣāntipāramitā, nor the vīryapāramitā, nor the dhyānapāramitā; nor is there anyone who speaks of these names, but only those who speak together of the prajñāpāramitā.”
"For what reason?
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme among the five pāramitās.
How so, Ānanda? If one does not practice giving, by what cause could it become the dānapāramitā of sarvajñatā?”
If one does not practice non-action, on what basis can it be the *śīla-pāramitā*?
If one does not practice non-action in patience, on what basis can it be the *kṣānti-pāramitā*?
If one does not practice non-action in diligence, on what basis can it be the *vīrya-pāramitā*?
If one does not cultivate a single-minded focus, by what means could there be the dhyāna-pāramitā?
If one does not cultivate wisdom, by what means could there be the prajñā-pāramitā of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)?
Ānanda said: “So it is, O God among Gods!
If one does not practice giving, it is not the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) for the sake of omniscience (sarvajñatā).”
If one does not practice morality, it is not the perfection of morality (śīla-pāramitā);
if one does not practice patience, it is not the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
if one does not practice diligence, it is not the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
If one does not practice single-mindedness, it is not the dhyāna-pāramitā;
if one does not practice wisdom, it is not the prajñā-pāramitā of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), but rather what is not the prajñā-pāramitā.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Ānanda. Among the five pāramitās, the prajñāpāramitā is the most honored.
It is like the vast earth: if seeds are scattered upon it, they all sprout simultaneously and grow into great trunks.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is the earth; the five *pāramitās* are the seeds that grow from within it. That which is *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is perfected through the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"In this way, Ānanda,
among the five pāramitās, the prajñāpāramitā is supremely great and sovereign in its teaching.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has not yet finished describing the merits of those sons and daughters of good family who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā. How so?”
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"I do not say that the merit of the practitioner has not yet reached its completion; rather, I speak of the son of good family or daughter of good family who writes down the Prajñāpāramitā, maintains the scroll, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it with offerings—namely, famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags and pennants. It is this merit of offering that I am speaking of."
Śakra Devānām-Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I myself shall protect and look after those sons and daughters of good family who write out the Prajñāpāramitā, who hold its scrolls, and who take refuge in it, pay homage to it, and serve and make offerings to it—with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags. I shall protect the merit of these offerings."
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Good sons and good daughters who recite the Prajñāpāramitā—when several thousand devas go to the place of the Dharma teacher to listen to the Dharma, they do not understand it within the Dharma."

Just as the devas and humans were about to question the Dharma Master, a celestial deity spoke to them; because they had cultivated compassion within the Dharma, those individuals immediately understood for themselves. That which the devas could not comprehend was spontaneously understood by them, and these sons and daughters of good family came to personally perceive and know all the merits they had performed.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

When a son or daughter of good family writes out the Prajñāpāramitā and teaches it among the fourfold assembly of disciples, their mind shall be entirely free from any difficulty; even if there are those with physical forms or those who wish to test them, they shall never be afraid."
"Why is this? Because they are protected by the Prajñāpāramitā, those who wish to test them through physical means will simply depart of their own accord.
The Buddha said:
“I do not perceive anyone who should practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do I perceive the *prajñāpāramitā* itself.
When a son or daughter of good family is subdued by the *prajñāpāramitā*, no one dares to treat them with contempt; their mind is neither terrified, nor fearful, nor does it experience any dread.”
Good sons and good daughters will clearly perceive for themselves all the merits they have performed.
Furthermore, Kauśika, these good sons and good daughters will be held in high esteem by their parents;

they will be pitied by śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way; and whether they be friends, brothers, or kinsmen from their maternal or paternal families, all will honor, respect, and love them. Should anyone at times speak ill of them, they will resolve the matter by upholding the Middle Way of the True Dharma.
These sons and daughters of good family shall see for themselves all the merit they have produced.
Furthermore, Kauśika,

when sons and daughters of good family write out the Prajñāpāramitā and maintain its scrolls, those gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings who seek the Buddha-way will go to their place to inquire after them, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, pay homage, circumambulate them, and then depart.

The devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who seek the path of the Buddha go to where [the Bodhisattva] is, inquire after his well-being, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.

The devas of the Yāma Heaven who seek the path of the Buddha go to where [the Bodhisattva] is, inquire after his well-being, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.
Good sons and good daughters, you should understand in your hearts this:

"If the countless Buddhas of the ten directions, along with all the devas, humans, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, were all to come here to inquire after the Dharma Master, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, pay homage, and circumambulate him before departing—each of them would receive equal merit without distinction;

likewise, if the devas of the Tuṣita Heaven who seek the Buddha-way were to go there to inquire after [the Bodhisattva], listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, pay homage, and circumambulate him before departing..."

The devas of the Nirmāṇarati heaven who seek the path of the Buddha go to that place, inquire after his well-being, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart;

the devas of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven who seek the path of the Buddha go to that place, inquire after his well-being, listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, perform prostrations and circumambulations, and then depart.

The devas of the Brahma heavens who seek the path of the Buddha—namely, the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha devas—all these celestial beings went to where [the Bodhisattva] was, inquired after his well-being, listened to and received the Prajñāpāramitā, performed prostrations and circumambulations, and then each departed.
Even the Akaniṣṭha devas have all descended to join the ranks of the other gods, let alone Kauśika.

The gods of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm from the three thousand great world-systems all came to inquire after his well-being and to listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā; having paid homage and circumambulated him, they each finally departed.

"Furthermore, wherever those sons or daughters of good family reside, that place shall be secure and firm, and no one shall cause them disturbance; except for the retribution of their own past karma which they have not yet exhausted, nothing else shall be able to move them."
"Good sons and good daughters shall fully receive and attain all such merit; at that time, you should know that the devas and humans will come.
Śakra Devānām Indra said, "How is this so, O God among Gods?"
Good sons and good daughters, you should understand this: why do the devas and humans come to this place to listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, and to pay homage and serve it?
The Buddha said:
"Good sons and good daughters, you should understand this:
'When the devas and humans come to receive the Prajñāpāramitā, they pay homage and serve it.'"
"Why is it necessary to know when the devas and humans arrive?

Sometimes, when a son or daughter of good family is filled with joy, leaping for gladness, and their mind is delighted, they will know that the devas and humans have arrived; knowing this, they should depart, whether it be devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or kinnaras who have come to that place."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
When good sons and good daughters smell the fragrance of ghosts and spirits, they will know that [the spirits] have been perceived.
Good sons and good daughters, the minor ghosts and spirits shall avoid them and depart, while the great ghosts and spirits will come forward."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! Good men and good women should always keep their bodies clean and pure.

Because their bodies are clean and pure, the spirits and deities will all rejoice greatly. When the minor deities see the great deities approaching, they will move aside to avoid them. The majestic majesty of the great honored deities is so sublime that their radiance shines with redoubled brilliance as they proceed slowly and calmly. These celestial beings arrive at the place where the Teacher’s sutras are kept; having entered the place where the sutras are kept, the good men and good women will leap for joy and dwell in that location with complete purity."
Good sons and good daughters shall never suffer from illness; wherever they dwell, they will always be at peace and secure;

they shall never have evil dreams, nor see anything else in their dreams, but only the Buddha, only the stūpas, only hear the Prajñāpāramitā, only see the disciples, and only see those who have attained ultimate transcendence.
One sees only the Buddha seated; one sees only the spontaneous wheel of Dharma; one sees only the time when he was about to attain Buddhahood;
one sees only the various Buddhas who have already attained Buddhahood; one sees only the newly manifested wheel of Dharma; one sees only the various bodhisattvas;
one sees only the various explanations of the six pāramitās; and one sees only what is to be done.
The Buddha saw only other buddha-fields; he saw only that the Buddha’s honored Dharma was perfectly clear and peerless;
he saw in such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a land Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, with several hundred disciples, several thousand disciples, and several ten-thousand disciples.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha preaches the Dharma therein. "Kauśika!

When a son of good family or a daughter of good family has such a dream, upon waking they feel secure and at ease; their body is pure, clean, and light, and they have no desire for food, as their body feels naturally supple, beautiful, and satiated."

“Kauśika! It is like a bhikṣu who has attained dhyāna; upon awakening from that dhyāna, his mind is supple and he does not crave much food, being already satiated by the subtle and exquisite [bliss] within himself.
In this same way, Kauśika!”
Good sons and good daughters, having awakened, do not think much about food, for they perceive their own bodies as supple,
beautiful, and satiated.
Why is this, Kauśika?

Because spirits and deities do not dare to approach his presence, those who wish to grasp the Buddha will see all his merits manifest before them. Those who wish to grasp the Buddha should study the *prajñāpāramitā*, uphold it, and recite it. Even if a son or daughter of good family does not study, uphold, or recite it, but merely writes it down, carries the scroll, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it with offerings—namely, famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags—[they shall likewise attain this].
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose at some time the earth of Jambudvīpa were filled with the relics of the Tathāgata and offered as a gift; and suppose the Prajñāpāramitā were written down and offered as a gift—of these two, which would you take?"
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"One would rather take the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is that?"
I do not dare to fail to revere the śarīra, O God among Gods!
It is from within this that the śarīra emerges to receive offerings; it is from within the Prajñāpāramitā that the śarīra emerges, and from within it that they receive their worship.

For instance, there was a time when I was sitting with the devas in the heavens, occupying a distinguished seat, even my own seat. Whenever any deva or human came to my presence to attend upon me, before I had reached the seat or sat down upon it, all those devas would sit for me; having performed their salutations and circumambulations, they would then depart. This seat is the venerable one of Śakra Devānām Indra; while sitting here, he receives the Dharma, and the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven perform salutations for him.
Thus it is, O God among Gods!
The *tathāgata*, *arhat*, *samyaksaṃbuddha* relics emerge from the *prajñāpāramitā*; the wisdom of *sarvajñatā* is born from within them, for this is the function of the body.
"O God among Gods!
Between these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā.

Even if one portion were filled with the śarīra-relics of the Tathāgatas covering the entire land of Jambudvīpa, and another portion consisted of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra filling the three thousand great world-systems—O God among Gods, from between these two portions, I would take the Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? It is because it results from making offerings to the śarīra produced therefrom.
It is like a debtor, O God among Gods!
He entered and exited together with the king, whom he deeply respected; there was no one who questioned him, nor did he have anything to fear.
Why was this? Because he possessed great power and majesty by the king's side.
O God among Gods!
It is from within the *prajñāpāramitā* that the *śarīra* (relics) emerge, and it is from them that offerings arise. O God among Gods!

This sutra is like a king; the *prajñāpāramitā* is like this king who, being valiant and fierce, receives offerings. The *tathāgata-śarīra* emerges from within *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) and receives offerings.
Thus it is, O God among Gods!
One should know that Sarvajñā (all-knowledge), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is born from within the Prajñāpāramitā; of these two parts, I shall take the Prajñāpāramitā.
“O God among Gods! One who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā is like a priceless maṇi jewel.
Where such a treasure exists, there is nothing equal to it.”
If one holds this [mantra] with attachment, wherever that attachment resides, ghosts and spirits shall find no opportunity to act; they shall not be harmed or struck by ghosts and spirits.
Whether it be a man or a woman, if they hold a maṇi jewel and wear it upon their body, ghosts and spirits will immediately flee.
If one suffers from fever, by holding a maṇi jewel and placing it upon the body, the heat shall be immediately dispelled.
If one suffers from wind-disorders, by holding this maṇi jewel upon the body, the wind will not increase and shall be immediately removed;
if one suffers from cold, by holding this maṇi jewel upon the body, the cold will no longer increase and shall be immediately removed;
if held at night in the darkness, it will instantly become bright.
When held during the heat, the mani-jewel makes whatever place it touches cool;
when held during the cold, it makes whatever place it touches warm;
wherever it goes, poison has no effect there, and the same is true for other such things.
Among them, if there is one bitten by a snake—whether a man or a woman—who is shown a *maṇi* jewel, upon seeing the *maṇi* jewel, the poison immediately departs.
Thus it is, O God among Gods!
The maṇi jewel is most supreme; if there is a person with an ailment—whether eye pain or blurred vision—if they hold the maṇi jewel near their eyes, the eye disease is immediately cured.
Thus it is, O God among Gods! The virtue of the maṇi jewel is sublime and sovereign.

Wherever it is placed, if it is set in water, the water immediately takes on the color of the maṇi jewel. If it is wrapped in silk and placed in water, the water likewise becomes the color of the maṇi jewel; even if it is wrapped in various kinds of silk and placed in water, the water still becomes the color of the maṇi jewel. If the water is turbid, it immediately becomes clear. The virtue of the maṇi jewel is beyond compare.
Ānanda asked Śakra Devānām Indra:
"How so, Kauśika? Is there also the maṇi jewel in the heavens?"
"Is there also a maṇi jewel upon the land of Jambudvīpa?
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Ānanda:
"There are maṇi jewels in the heavens, and there are also maṇi jewels upon the land of Jambudvīpa."

It is beyond words; as I have said, the jewels upon the earth of Jambudvīpa are merely trifles compared to the merit and dignity of that pearl, which exceeds them tenfold, a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, and even by hundreds of millions of billions of times.
As for the maṇi jewel I speak of, wherever it is placed—whether in a chest or in a casket—its...
The radiance shines forth even more intensely; even if one were to lift the jewel and depart for another place, the light would continue as before.
So too is the virtue of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the *sarvajñatā*:
until the *tathāgata*, *arhat*, *samyaksaṃbuddha* passes into *parinirvāṇa*, the veneration of his relics shall remain as it was before. *Sarvajñatā*.
If the relics were distributed throughout the world, they would continue to receive offerings as before.
"Furthermore, Ānanda,

if there are present Buddhas in the countless Buddha-lands of the ten directions whom one wishes to see, that son or daughter of good family should practice the *prajñāpāramitā* and should maintain the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "It is so, Kauśika!
In the past, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas emerged from within this Prajñāpāramitā; they became leaders among men and attained the state of Buddhahood for themselves."

In this way, all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are yet to arise in the future will emerge from within the Prajñāpāramitā; they shall become leaders among men and personally attain the state of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, just as the innumerable Buddhas currently residing in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions have likewise emerged from within the Prajñāpāramitā, becoming leaders among men and personally attaining the state of Buddhahood.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Great Perfection! O God among Gods!
Whatever thoughts are conceived by all people and the classes of crawling and flying creatures, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha fully knows them all through the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said,
"For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā day and night.
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
“Does one practice only the *prajñāpāramitā* and not the other *pāramitās*?
The Buddha said:

“One practices all six *pāramitās*. For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme. When a bodhisattva bestows gifts, the *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses the upholding of morality, patience, diligence, and single-minded concentration; even the distribution of various sūtras to instruct others does not equal a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.”

Kauśika! It is like the various excellent trees upon Jambudvīpa: though their colors are diverse and distinct, their leaves are each distinct, their flowers are each distinct, and their fruits are each distinct; yet the shadows cast by these various branches and twigs do not differ, for those shadows are one and similar to one another.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
The five pāramitās emerge from the prajñāpāramitā, and the prajñāpāramitā gives rise to sarvajñatā; through various successive developments, they attain one another without any difference.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā of supreme and great majesty, O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā of incalculable merit, O God among Gods!”
“O Devātideva, there is no perfection equal to or exceeding the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).

If there is one who writes down the Perfection of Wisdom, holds its volume, takes refuge in it, pays homage to it, and serves and makes offerings to it—namely, with famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags and pennants—and if there is another who writes out this scripture and gives it to others, which of these two would have the greater merit?”
The Buddha said:
"I ask you this on purpose, Kauśika!
Speak freely."
What do you think? If there were one who, having personally made offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata, further distributed them to others and caused them to make offerings;
and another who, having personally made offerings to the relics, did not distribute them to others. Which of these two would generate greater merit?
"Which of these merits is greater?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"O God among Gods!"
“Good sons and good daughters who personally make offerings to the śarīras and further distribute them to others will have great and abundant merit.
The Buddha said,
“It is so, Kauśika!”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, carries its scrolls, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves it with offerings—namely, famous flowers, powdered incense, unguents, blended incenses, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags—and furthermore distributes them to others, their merit will be exceedingly great.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Wherever the Dharma-preacher goes and preaches the sutras and the Dharma, his virtue and merit are exceedingly great, indeed very great.
Furthermore, Kauśika!"
If all the people of Jambudvīpa— whether they be good men or good women— were to cause them all to uphold the ten precepts,
what do you think, Kauśika?
Would their merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Very much, very much,
O Heaven among Heavens!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as when a son or daughter of good family writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, or takes the scroll and gives it to another to write, or reads it for them; their merit will be many times greater."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside the various small kingdoms, middle kingdoms, thousand kingdoms, two-thousand kingdoms, and three-thousand great world systems of the four continents, suppose that all the people in the Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands along the Ganges were made by a son of good family or a daughter of good family to uphold the ten precepts."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to merely write out the Prajñāpāramitā; rather, it is far more meritorious to take this scripture and give it to another so that they may write it out or read it."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all the sons and daughters of good family in Jambudvīpa were to cause them to practice the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the practice of the *prātihāryas*."
"What do you think,
Kauśika? Would that merit not be great?"
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Very much, very much,
O Heaven among Heavens!"
The Buddha said:

“It is not as [meritorious] as when a son or daughter of good family writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, or takes up the scroll and gives it to another person to write, or reads it for them; their merit is many times greater.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside Jambudvīpa, the four continents, small lands, medium lands, a thousand lands, two thousand lands, three thousand great lands, and even as many people as there are in the Buddha-fields of sands along the Ganges—suppose that all these sons and daughters of good family were made to practice the four dhyānas, the four truths, the four bases of psychic power, and the practice of *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, and were all enabled to achieve them."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not increase manifold?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Extremely much, extremely much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to merely write out the Prajñāpāramitā; rather, if they take the scroll and give it to another person so that they may write it, or read it for them, their merit will be many times greater."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If one takes up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another person to copy, or causes them to study it, or studies it oneself, the merit thereof is many times greater."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If there is someone who personally studies the Prajñāpāramitā and understands its profound wisdom, their merit will be many times greater.
Śakra Devendra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods!
How is it that by training in the *prajñāpāramitā* and training in the understanding of its central wisdom, one’s merit becomes many times greater?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods!
How does one train in the Prajñāpāramitā to understand wisdom within?
The Buddha said:
“Good sons and good daughters do not understand how to train. Why is this?

There will be good sons and good daughters in the future who, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, take delight in training in the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet instead receive instruction from evil associates regarding a mere semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked the Buddha:
"What constitutes the branches and twigs of the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:

"In the future age, there will be bhikṣus who wish to study the Prajñāpāramitā; yet evil associates will instead teach them that form is impermanent and that they should practice the impermanence of form. They will practice the Prajñāpāramitā by studying in this manner: that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, and they will practice the Prajñāpāramitā by studying in this manner—that consciousness is impermanent."
"Kauśika! This is the branch of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:

"One who practices the perfection of wisdom does not view form as impermanent through destruction, nor does one view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as impermanent through destruction. Why is this?
Because it is fundamentally non-existent, Kauśika,
one should learn the Prajñāpāramitā with wisdom; its merit will increase manifold.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside the three thousand great lands upon the earth of Jambudvīpa, suppose there were people in as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the Ganges River, and that a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to cause them all to attain the stage of Srotāpanna."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

"It is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to merely write out the Prajñāpāramitā; rather, their merit is many times greater if they take the scroll and give it to others so that they may write it, or cause them to study it, or read it for them."
Why is this? Because the path of the srotāpanna is entirely born from within the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters of Jambudvīpa were all taught and caused to attain the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat, and were all brought to full accomplishment therein;
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be even more manifold?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"It is not so; rather, if a son or daughter of good family writes out this Prajñāpāramitā, and then provides the scroll to another person to write it, or causes them to study it, or reads it for them, their merit will be many times greater."

Why is this? The merit of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is the accomplishment of the merit of the Dharma; all [beings] attain Buddhahood by training in the prajñāpāramitā, and thereby give birth to the path of the srotāpanna, the path of the sakṛdāgāmin, the path of the anāgāmin, the path of the arhat, and the path of the pratyekabuddha.
“Setting aside Jambudvīpa, Kauśika!

Setting aside the people in three thousand great world-systems, or as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges—if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to cause them all to attain the path of srotāpanna, the path of sakṛdāgāmin, the path of anāgāmin, the path of arhat, and the path of pratyekabuddha.”
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.

"It is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to merely write out the Prajñāpāramitā; rather, their merit is many times greater if they take the scroll and give it to others so that they may write it, or cause them to study it, or read it for them."

Why is this? Because they all train in the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby achieve sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) and the virtues of the Dharma; for this reason they become Buddhas, and give rise to the path of the srotāpanna, the path of the sakṛdāgāmin, the path of the anāgāmin, the path of the arhat, and the path of the pratyekabuddha. For this reason, their merit becomes many times greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! Suppose all the people throughout Jambudvīpa were made to practice the Buddha-way;

having already gained faith and entered the Buddha-way, and having given rise to the mind that studies the Buddha-way—if a good man or a good woman takes a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and causes others to copy it, or causes them to study it, or explains it for them, even to an *avaivartika* bodhisattva, by copying the scroll and bestowing it upon them so that they may study from it, enter deeply into the learning of the Prajñāpāramitā, and train in the wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā—then that person’s merit will increase manifold, becoming more and more abundant, and they will fully accomplish the boundless wisdom."
Setting aside Jambudvīpa, Kauśika!

Suppose all the people in three thousand great world-systems, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were to practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and all resolve their minds to walk the path of the Buddha; yet, if a son or daughter of good family, possessing this scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, were to give it to others to copy, or cause them to study it, or explain it to them—even down to an *avaivartika* bodhisattva—by copying the scroll and bestowing it upon them so that they may learn from it, enter deeply into the study of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and cultivate the wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*, thereby increasingly increasing their guarding of the boundless wisdom until it is fully accomplished, then the merit obtained by the former person will be many times greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all the people throughout Jambudvīpa were to practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—that is, they all set their minds upon seeking Buddhahood—and suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family takes up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, causes others to copy it, explains the wisdom within it to them, and instructs them to study it; and suppose they do this even unto the stage of the *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattva, taking up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and bestowing it so that they may enter into wise discernment (*prajñā*), the merit of the latter will be many times greater."

Suppose there were as many people in the great lands of Jambudvīpa—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River in Buddha-fields—each practicing for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all those seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* having resolved their minds for Buddhahood. If a son or daughter of good family were to take a scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and give it to another to copy, causing them to study and enter into wisdom; and if there were an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva who took a scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and, having copied it, bestowed it upon others so that they might study and enter into wisdom, the latter’s merit would be many times greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose all the people throughout Jambudvīpa were made to practice the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva; yet, if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught them to enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*, [the latter would produce greater merit]."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.
"If from among these people a bodhisattva should emerge and say,
'I wish to quickly become a Buddha,' even if they desire to quickly become a Buddha,
if someone were to take a written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and bestow it upon them, their merit would be many times greater."

"Suppose there were as many people as there are inhabitants in the three thousand great world-systems of Jambudvīpa, even up to the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; if a good man or a good woman were to cause them all to practice the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva, yet another good man or good woman were to teach them to enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*. [The latter would generate far more merit than the former]."
"What do you think, Kauśika!
Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"If there were a bodhisattva to emerge from among them and say,
'I wish to quickly become a Buddha,' even if they so desire to quickly become a Buddha,
if someone were to take a written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and bestow it upon them, their merit would be many times greater."
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, O Heaven among Heavens!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is profoundly at peace approaches the Prajñāpāramitā of the Buddha swiftly; if they teach it to others or bestow it upon others, their merit becomes many times greater.”
"For what reason?
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Those who attain the Prajñāpāramitā and draw near to the Buddha are drawing near to the Buddha’s seat.
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Kauśika! Those who are to become honored disciples—bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who receive this teaching—will swiftly become Buddhas.

As for those who act as such, they should emerge from among the Buddha’s disciples; if these people do not seek the Buddha-way, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not study the six pāramitās therein. Without studying these dharmas, one cannot become a Buddha. By studying in accordance with the Dharma, one will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, as you have asked.
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll II;
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll III.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter Four: Encouraging and Assisting through Skillful Means (*Upāyakauśalya*) At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed Subhūti:

"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who encourages and assists others in creating merit—surpassing the merit of those who merely practice giving and maintaining the precepts for their own sake—then his merit becomes even more sublime."
"There is nothing superior to the supreme merit of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s encouragement and assistance.
Subhūti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"Furthermore, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who performs meritorious deeds in the presence of Buddhas in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands—countless Buddhas in each land. From the time they first resolved their minds [for enlightenment] until they themselves attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, became fully awakened (*abhisambuddha*), and finally entered *parinirvāṇa* in the realm of nirvana without remainder, and even until the exhaustion of the Dharma—the merit performed therein is the perfection of merit (*puṇyapāramitā*)."

Furthermore, regarding the various śrāvakas who practice giving and uphold the precepts, cultivating merit for themselves and bringing their remaining merits to the state of *anupadhiśeṣa*; and regarding all those Buddhas who have entered *parinirvāṇa* and the merits they have performed therein—extending from the body of pure precepts, the body of samādhi, the body of wisdom, the body of liberation, and the body manifested through liberated wisdom—the Buddha-dharma is supremely great, and its compassion is immeasurable.

Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, the God among Gods, one further studies all the merits contained within that Dharma; then, taking all the merits performed for the Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa, summing them up and combining them, the act of exhorting and assisting [others] is the most honored, being the supreme and highest among all various virtues.
That which encourages and assists is what constitutes encouragement and assistance.
Having encouraged and assisted, one takes this and applies it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is by means of this that one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He designates this Bodhisattva as a person of virtue who is capable of maintaining his mind; he seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even to the point of forming the thought that there is something to be attained.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
"It is by not seeking in this way that one is able to attain anything.
Those who engage in conceptual thought are considered to lack wisdom."
This thought arises.

Because of conceptualization, one retreats from renunciation; because of faith, one retreats from renunciation. It is solely due to a lack of wisdom that one falls back into the four inversions—perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the empty as substantial, and the selfless as having a self—and for this reason, one retreats through conceptualization, retreats in mind, and retreats in faith.
A bodhisattva should not form the thought that there is anything to be sought.
Since there is no locus for what is sought, how could one seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
"One should not speak these words before newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Why is that?
Or, when there is nothing to believe in, nothing to delight in, nothing to rejoice in, and nothing to practice, one should cultivate [the path] from this very state.

This should be explained for the sake of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it should be explained to such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has long remained in the presence of a virtuous teacher, so that upon hearing it, they are neither terrified, nor alarmed, nor afraid. Such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to provide encouragement and support by maintaining a mind directed toward *sarvajñatā*. When providing such encouragement and support, even the mind itself is extinguished; there is nothing existing and nothing perceived. As for what kind of mind should produce *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and with what mind should it be produced?
"The mind has no duality; it is through the natural spontaneity of the mind that one is able to act.
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"Newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing this, may feel fear or trepidation."
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to cultivate merit, how should they encourage and assist that merit so as to bring it to the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Subhūti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva: “One should provide protection for these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

In the presence of all Buddhas, they shall destroy all evils and sever craving and desire; they shall practice with equanimity as one, subdue the works of Māra, and cast off the heavy burden. Thus, all their former hardships will be completely exhausted, and knowing themselves to be liberated, their minds will follow the reckoning of those who have entered parinirvāṇa under the various Buddhas of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands. Regarding the merit and blessings they have performed therein, and the further merit they perform among the śrāvakas—if one were to calculate and sum them all together, the act of exhortation and assistance is supreme. Among all kinds of virtues, none surpasses exhortation and assistance; such an exhorter is truly able to provide exhortation, and having provided it, they take hold of it to bring about *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
What is this "non-regression in perception," "non-regression in mind," and "non-regression in faith" of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva maintains the mind for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, if that mind is free from any conceptualization, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind can achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Even if one’s mind cognizes itself as being this very mind, that constitutes an act; it is a turning back through conceptualization, a turning back of the mind, and a turning back of what was believed.
Even if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains mindfulness and understands, they should train in this way: to know that all things are exhausted and non-existent.
Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion, with what mind should one perform any action?
When one has realized the mind, what mental factor could have any activity toward phenomena?
As for the Dharma, having conformed to the Dharma, that which is performed is truly performed; it is not a perverted performance. This is the work of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who takes account of and sums up all the merit performed by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; the merit performed by all śrāvakas, down to ordinary worldlings; the merit performed by those among the animals who have heard the Dharma; and the merit performed by those among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and humans or non-humans who have heard the Dharma and resolved their minds [upon enlightenment]; as well as the merit of those who are beginners on the bodhisattva path—adding them all together and accumulating them, this constitutes the supreme.

Those who provide encouragement and assistance are truly able to provide such encouragement; for this reason, they are most honored, as among all various virtues, none surpasses encouragement and assistance. Therefore, that which ought to be encouraged and assisted is indeed provided with encouragement and assistance, and one takes the merit of such encouragement and assistance to cultivate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Even if one further knows this to be the dharma of exhaustion, wherein in all dharmas there is neither arising nor ceasing, and no location—by upholding this dharma of non-arising, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This dharma does not conflict with dharma; by practicing it, one reaches what was previously unattainable—this is the work performed for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not clearly and thoroughly understand the creation of merit..."
Why is this? Because the body is illusory, and the merit of encouragement and assistance is likewise illusory.
A bodhisattva thoroughly understands that which is illusory as being non-existent; therefore, this is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

If one performs meritorious deeds in the presence of various Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa, and maintains these merits with the desire to achieve what is sought, that wisdom will naturally enable one to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

That which is known by the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, is free from conceptual attachment; it has already ceased in the past and possesses no conceptualization, nor does it form concepts. To form such concepts is not a virtue.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study upāyakauśalya; those who have not yet attained the prajñāpāramitā cannot enter, whereas only those who have already attained the prajñāpāramitā can enter.
Do not act for the sake of the body; since the functioning of consciousness has cessation, for this reason there is no body.
For a person of virtue, the presence of conceptualization constitutes an obstruction, as it leads instead to dwelling in suffering.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not delight in performing such meritorious deeds for the sake of providing assistance. Why is this?
Because it is not upright;

one perceives the Buddha in parinirvāṇa and yet still harbors conceptualizations. For this reason, it constitutes an obstruction; the merit thus performed falls short of its goal and results instead in dwelling in suffering.
That which is free from conceptualization is the virtue of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
that which involves conceptualization is like a mixture of poison.

Why is this? Suppose one were to prepare a fine meal and place poison within it; its color would be exceedingly beautiful and its fragrance exquisite, such that there would be none who did not take pleasure in it.

Not knowing that there is poison in the food, a foolish and ignorant person eats it with joy until they are full. When the food begins to digest, after a long time, it will cause great distress to the body.

For one who does not know how to practice virtue, it is exceedingly difficult; if they do not understand how to protect [the teachings], do not understand how to recite them, and do not understand their essential meaning, they will be unable to comprehend them. To practice virtue in such a manner is like food mixed with poison.
The Buddha said to the sons and daughters of good family:

"The Buddhas of the past, future, and present—their bodies of ethical discipline, their bodies of meditative concentration, their bodies of wisdom, their bodies of liberation, and their bodies of the manifestation of the wisdom of liberation—as well as the merit they have performed among the śrāvakas."

"Thus it was said by the Buddha, the God among Gods: if one performs meritorious deeds toward a Pratyekabuddha and fully encourages and assists them, and having so encouraged and assisted them, takes this merit and applies it toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while maintaining a conceptualization of that which has been performed—for this reason, it is like poisoned food."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way: regarding whatever merits of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present there may be, how should one provide encouragement and assistance to create merit so as to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

This Bodhisattva, following the teachings of the Tathāgata, thereby comes to know the spontaneous arising of the Buddha’s merits and all that pertains to his marks and dharmas; by maintaining these blessings as an act of encouragement, and through that encouragement, he personally attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such giving, it is unsurpassed; they shall never be separated from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
One who makes such a gift does so without mixing it with poison.
All that is spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is entirely sincere.

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should make such a gift as is the pure precepts, as is samādhi, as is wisdom, as is liberation, and as is the manifestation of the body through the wisdom of liberation.
There is no realm of desire, no realm of form, and no realm of neither-desire-nor-form;
there is also no past, future, or present;
there is nothing at all, and even the gift that is given is likewise nothing at all.
When one performs such giving in accordance with the Dharma, that Dharma is also non-existent.
One who gives in this manner accomplishes the act of giving so that it is free from the poison of defilement;
whereas one who performs a different kind of giving practices a perverse form of giving.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving in accordance with the Dharma, that which is known by the Buddha, the God among Gods, as true giving, enables him to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”

Acting in accordance with the Buddha is what constitutes the giving of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. If all the people of the trichiliocosm were to maintain thoughts of loving-kindness, compassion, and impartial protection, this would not surpass the supreme gift bestowed by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; this is indeed the most honored.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all the people of the three-thousandfold world system were to become *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [Buddhas], and suppose that as many people as there are in Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were all to make offerings to this bodhisattva—offering fine garments, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick—for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, giving such gifts according to their pleasure.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Would that merit not be great?
Subhūti replied:
“Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"The merit of this encouragement and assistance is such that its blessings surpass all others and are incalculable.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for the merit of one who encourages and assists on behalf of others, even Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not fully contain it."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"

If there is a bodhisattva who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, whatever acts of giving they perform will surpass their previous acts of giving; no one can surpass the excellence of their meritorious assistance, by a factor of a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, or even a hundred billion times.
At that time, twenty thousand beings from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings all bowed their heads at the feet of the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift, O God among Gods!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such giving through skillful means (upāyakauśalya), their merit is exceedingly great and sublime. Why is this?
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and provides encouragement and assistance therein.

The devas and humans of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven took celestial flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, unguents, blended incense, burning incense, celestial silks, flower canopies, banners and streamers, and musical instruments, and used them to make offerings to and entertain the Buddha.
Having made their offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift, O God among Gods!
It is through the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that such a gift is performed; it is a merit of great virtue."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the perfection of wisdom and provide encouragement and assistance therein.

Then the devas of the Yāma Heaven, holding celestial flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, unguents, blended incense, burning incense, celestial silks, flower parasols, banners, pennants, and music, used them to make offerings to and delight the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift, O God among Gods!
That a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva employs such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to perform this giving is a merit of supreme virtue."
"Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the prajñāpāramitā and provide encouragement and assistance therein.

Then the devas of the Tuṣita Heaven took celestial flowers, famous incenses, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, celestial silks, flower canopies, banners and streamers, and musical instruments, using them to make offerings to and delight the Buddha.
Having made their offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift, O God among Gods!
That a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva employs *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) to perform such a gift is a merit of supreme virtue."
"Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the prajñāpāramitā and provide encouragement and support within it.

Then the devas of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven took celestial flowers, famous incense, powdered incense, unguents, blended incense, burning incense, celestial silks, flower-canopies, banners, pennants, and music, and used them to make offerings to and delight the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift, O God among Gods!
That a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva employs such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to perform this giving constitutes a most supreme and venerable merit."
"Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the *prajñāpāramitā* and provide encouragement and support therein.

Then the devas of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven took celestial flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, unguents, blended incense, burning incense, celestial silks, flower parasols, banners, pennants, and music, and used them to make offerings to and delight the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is a most magnificent gift, O God among Gods!
That a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva employs such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to perform this giving constitutes a most sublime and venerable merit."
"Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the *prajñāpāramitā* and provide encouragement and assistance therein.

Then the Brahmā, the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahmā, the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, the Ābhāsvara, the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Anabhraka, the Puṇyaprasava, the Bṛhatphala, the Avṛha, the Atapa, the Sudṛśa, and even the Akaniṣṭha devas—all these celestial beings bowed their heads at the feet of the Buddha and all said:
“Excellent, O God among Gods!
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva to study the prajñāpāramitā is the merit of a truly great gift. Why is this so?
"This is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the prajñāpāramitā and provide encouragement and assistance therein.
The Buddha said to the devas of Śuddhāvāsa:
"Setting aside the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within a trichiliocosm, let alone those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."
Suppose all the people in Buddha-fields were to become *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and furthermore,
suppose there were people from as many other Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges who together made offerings to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— providing them with fine garments,
food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick— as numerous as the sands in the Ganges.
For an eon, one may perform such giving according to one’s own pleasure; yet even if it exceeds this,
it does not equal the gift of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who provides encouragement and assistance for the Buddhas of the past, future, and present— their body of pure precepts,
their body of samādhi, their body of wisdom, their body of liberation, and their body of the wisdom and vision of liberation.
If one were to calculate and sum together all the merits performed by the manifested body and by the śrāvakas within it,
they would not equal those of the one who provides encouragement and assistance.
If one encourages and assists [others], it is because this is most supreme and unsurpassed.
Having performed such encouragement and assistance, one takes hold of it and applies it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If one were to calculate and sum up all that has been spoken by the World-Honored One, there is nothing more supreme than this encouragement and assistance; having fully participated in this encouragement and assistance, what does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain from this?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“A bodhisattva who possesses the Way and its virtue should know that regarding the past, future, and present, dharmas are neither to be grasped nor to be relinquished, neither to be known nor to be attained.”

That Dharma is the dharma of non-arising, and it is also the dharma of non-extinction; it is neither a dharma that arises from anywhere nor a dharma that ceases from anywhere. Within all dharmas, there is absolutely no arising, and dharmas likewise do not cease from having ever arisen. This is the true nature of dharmas. I exhort and assist them on behalf of others; this is what constitutes such encouragement. One who practices such giving will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, Subhūti, the exhortation and assistance [of others] by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is supreme.
Furthermore, Subhūti:

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the presence of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, acts as a substitute for those who practice giving and encourages them; he acts as a substitute for those who maintain morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, and encourages them; he acts as a substitute for those already liberated and encourages them; and he acts as a substitute for those who manifest through the liberation of wisdom and encourages them.
Acting thus as a substitute for exhortation and assistance, that which is liberation is itself giving;
that which is liberation is itself morality; that which is liberation is itself patience; that which is liberation is itself diligence;
that which is liberation is itself single-mindedness; that which is liberation is itself wisdom; that which is liberation is itself liberation.

Prajñā: That which is liberated is the manifestation of the body of liberated wisdom; that which is liberated is already liberated; that which is liberated acts as its advocate and support; that which is liberated is the Dharma.

Therefore, regarding those who will be liberated in the future, as well as the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, currently present in the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands: *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a Mahāyāna sūtra (likely related to the *Prajñāpāramitā* tradition) concerning the nature of liberation and the identity of the liberated one with the Dharma and the manifestations of wisdom.*
Those who are liberated are the disciples of all Buddhas;

those who are liberated were the disciples of past Buddhas, and those who are liberated are the disciples of present Buddhas. Within this Dharma, there is no attachment, no bondage, and no liberation.
Such a Dharma is maintained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that which is bestowed from within it cannot be surpassed by anything, nor can it be destroyed by anything.
Subhūti, this is the supreme form of encouragement and assistance provided by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Suppose there were as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and in each of those fields there were bodhisattvas whose lifespans lasted for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and suppose all the people in those Buddha-fields, numbering as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were to provide offerings to all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick—for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

Subhūti! Even if one maintains the precepts, achieves patience, is untiring in vigor, and attains samādhi in meditation—whether by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or even several tens of billions of times—it would not equal the merit of encouraging and assisting [others]. This latter blessing is most honored and surpasses the former.
Chapter 5: On Niraya. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Five, "On Niraya," Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods, the *prajñāpāramitā* accomplishes much."
Because there is no character that cannot be attained through the *prajñāpāramitā*, O God among Gods!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is the ultimate illumination, O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā dispels darkness, O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is without attachment, O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme, O God among Gods!
O God among Gods! For those who are sightless, the Prajñāpāramitā acts as their eyes.
O God among Gods! For those who are deluded, the Prajñāpāramitā provides them with the way.
"O God among Gods! That which is *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
O God among Gods! The *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
That which is neither produced nor extinguished is precisely this *prajñāpāramitā*, O God among Gods!
It is the fulfillment of the twelvefold wheel of Dharma in its three turnings; it is for the sake of turning this *prajñāpāramitā* that [the wheel is turned], O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā brings peace and security to all who are afflicted; O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā acts as a protector within saṃsāra; O God among Gods!
Since the *prajñāpāramitā* is entirely spontaneous with respect to all phenomena, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell within the *prajñāpāramitā*?
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"The world-mountain (Sumeru) abides because of the Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, those who revere the Buddha should take refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā."
Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"For what reason has the Venerable Śāriputra posed this question?
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed Śāriputra:
"For what reason, Venerable One, do you ask this?
Śāriputra said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!"

The perfection of wisdom is the protection of the bodhisattva; by means of its supportive merit and the preservation of blessings, it brings about omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), surpassing the practices of the bodhisattva—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.

It is like a person who has been blind since birth; whether there be a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even a million such people, if they have no guide and wish to go somewhere or enter a city, they do not know how they should proceed.
Thus it is, Kauśika!

The five pāramitās are like those who are blind and see nothing; separated from the prajñāpāramitā, they likewise desire to enter into sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), yet they do not know how they should proceed.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the protection of the five pāramitās, providing them all with eyes;
the Prajñāpāramitā is their protection, enabling the five pāramitās each to obtain their respective names.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should one maintain oneself while entering into the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"Form is not seen as having an entry point; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise not seen as having an entry point. Even when viewing the five aggregates, they are not seen as having an entry point. This is what it means to guard the Prajñāpāramitā."
"If it is so, O God among Gods!
If one maintains the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, by maintaining it thus, what dharma does one turn back from?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Non-adherence is the dharma of returning; adherence is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If the *prajñāpāramitā* does not return to *sarvajñatā*, it likewise cannot be attained. As for what was asked regarding the *prajñāpāramitā* not reaching *sarvajñatā* and being unable to return—it neither returns nor adheres to birth and death, and there is nothing to which it returns.”
"How should one return?
O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Because there is nothing to which one returns, one is able to return.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"There are few who can equal you, O God among Gods!"
"Just as the Prajñāpāramitā gives rise to no phenomena and extinguishes no phenomena, so too that which should be dwelt upon is a non-dwelling.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"If a bodhisattva at times forms such a thought, he then becomes separated from the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva has some causal basis, he then contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā* upon that basis; knowing that the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty and non-existent, neither near nor far, this is therefore called the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In placing faith in the Prajñāpāramitā, in what dharma does one place faith?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"One who has faith in the Prajñāpāramitā does not believe in form; nor do they believe in the existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. They do not believe in the path of the Srotāpanna, nor do they believe in the paths of the Sakṛdāgāmin, the Anāgāmin, the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha-path."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods! That which is called the ‘Great Perfection’ (mahāpāramitā) is none other than the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“How do you know that the Mahāpāramitā has the Prajñāpāramitā as its cause?
Subhūti replied:

"In form there is neither great nor small; one does not take form as a witness, nor does one act as a witness for form. In sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is likewise neither great nor small; one does not take consciousness as a witness, nor does one act as a witness for consciousness. Thus, one attains the ten powers of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and is no longer subject to weakness."
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is neither broad nor narrow.
Why is it neither broad nor narrow?
Because Sarvajñā knows that within the prajñāpāramitā there is nothing to be practiced.
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent; if a person seeks anything therein, claiming that there is something to be found, this is a great error.

Why is this? Because persons have no place of birth; both the person and the *prajñāpāramitā* are both spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Since the person is ethereal, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise immeasurable. The person is indestructible, and the *prajñāpāramitā* is also thus. One who makes the person like the *prajñāpāramitā* shall attain supreme *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, because the person possesses power, the *Tathāgata* manifests as possessing power.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is most profound, most profound, O Devātideva!
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has faith in this profound Prajñāpāramitā, who neither speaks disparagingly nor harbors doubt, from where has such a person come to be born in this world?”

"How long has it been since they began practicing the bodhisattva path, and how many times have they heard and understood the matters of the *prajñāpāramitā*, such that they have entered into it according to the teaching?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have come from other buddha-fields to be born here. Having made offerings to Buddhas in those other lands and having received and heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from them, they hear the *prajñāpāramitā* once again here, and think to themselves:"
“I am no different from seeing the Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Can the Prajñāpāramitā be seen or heard?”
The Buddha said:
"It cannot be seen or heard.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
“If this bodhisattva follows the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, for how long has he been practicing?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“These are not students of a single kind; each has their own practice. There are those who have already made offerings to several hundred or several thousand Buddhas, having seen them all and having practiced pure precepts under them all.”
If there are those within the assembly who, upon hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, abandon it and depart, they show no reverence for the Dharma of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
When the Buddha teaches the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, such persons likewise abandon it and do not wish to hear it.

Why is this? Because in their previous lives, these people heard the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and abandoned it; they did so neither with their bodies nor with their minds. All of this is brought about by the fault of ignorance.
Because of these offenses, if they hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they further obstruct others and prevent them from teaching it.
To obstruct the *prajñāpāramitā* is to obstruct omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); and to obstruct omniscience is to obstruct the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

Because they have committed the sin of abandoning the Dharma, at death they enter the great hells for several hundreds of thousands of years, several billions of millions of years; there they shall further undergo all manner of unspeakable, agonizing pains within various hells. When their lifespan there is exhausted, they are reborn in the great hells of other directions, and when their lifespan there is again exhausted, they pass on successively to be born in the great hells of yet other directions.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Does this transgression correspond to the five heinous crimes?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"Although their transgressions may be illustrated by metaphors, they cannot be fully compared by analogy; yet when the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being recited or expounded, those whose minds harbor doubts regarding the Dharma will likewise refuse to study it, thinking:
'These words were not spoken by the Tathāgata.'"

"Stop others from speaking thus and do not allow them to study this, for they will destroy themselves and further destroy others; having drunk poison themselves, they further drink poison for others. Such people, having already lost themselves, further cause others to lose themselves; being themselves ignorant of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they in turn destroy others. One should not even look upon such persons."
Śāriputra! One should not sit, rise, speak, or eat together with them. Why is this?
