Those people who slander the Dharma dwell in darkness themselves and further cast others into darkness; they are no different from those who drink poison and kill themselves. If there are those who trust and believe the words of such a person who has severed the Dharma, the retribution for the sin received by both parties shall be equal and no different.
"Why is this? Because by slandering the words of the Buddha, one who slanders the *prajñāpāramitā* has effectively slandered all dharmas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to hear what kind of physical form those who slander the Dharma will receive, and how large their bodies will be.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"If such a person who slanders the Dharma were to hear this matter explained, the boiling blood would immediately gush from his facial orifices; he might even die of fear due to the intense agony he suffers. Upon hearing it, his heart becomes filled with grief and poison until it seems to wither away, just as a severed flower placed in the midday sun quickly wilts and dries up."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will speak of this for the sake of others, so that they may know how the body receives its physical form; let it serve as a great illumination for future generations."
"Those who hear this should feel dread and think to themselves:
'I must not slander and reject the Dharma as that person did.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"This is the great illumination shown to others: that because of one's own sins, one receives a body that is exceedingly foul and hideous, dwelling in a place of extreme toil, suffering, and stench that is truly beyond description; its agony is as immense as a long-lasting, violent torment."
"Once these good men and good women have heard these words and are satisfied with them, they will not dare to slander [the Dharma] again.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "Good men and good women should always protect their body, speech, and mind; it is only because people sit idly by what they say with their mouths that they incur such offenses."

The Buddha said to Subhūti: “These foolish people, having become śramaṇas within my Dharma, instead slander the Prajñāpāramitā, claiming it is not the Path. To obstruct the Prajñāpāramitā is to obstruct the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; to obstruct the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is to sever the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; to sever *sarvajñatā* is to sever the Dharma; to sever the Dharma is to sever the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; and to sever the Saṃgha of bhikṣus is to incur immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sins.”
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"Lord of Devas, if there are those who sever the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
how many factors are there?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Possessed by Māra, these men and women lack faith and do not take delight; because of these two factors, they are able to sever the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are four more things that sever the perfection of wisdom.
What are these four?

Following the words of an evil teacher, they: first, do not study in accordance with the teachings; second, do not accept the ultimate Dharma; third, primarily engage in slander; fourth, seek out the faults of others while being self-conceited.
"These are the four matters.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There are few who have faith in the Prajñāpāramitā, O God among Gods!"
“Because they do not clearly understand this Dharma.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!”
"Those who have faith in the Prajñāpāramitā are few, because they do not clearly understand this Dharma. Subhūti said,
"In what way is it that there are few who have faith in the profound Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. Why is this?
Because form is by its very nature form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation. Why is this?
Because consciousness is by its very nature consciousness.
Past form is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because past form is the very nature of form.
Future form is neither attached to, nor bound by, nor liberated from. Why is this?
Because future form is the very nature of form.
Presently, form is neither attached to, nor bound, nor liberated. Why is this?
Because form is the very nature of form.
Past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because past consciousness is by its very nature spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
Future consciousness is without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because future consciousness is of its own nature.
Present consciousness is now without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation.
Why is this? Because consciousness is by its very nature such.
"For this reason, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound, and few have faith in it. Chapter Six:
Purity The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter on Purity, Number Six. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Those who understand the Prajñāpāramitā are few, because they have not yet become familiar with it.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “So it is, so it is!”
There are few who understand the Prajñāpāramitā; this is due to the fact that they have not yet become familiar with it.
Why is this so, Subhūti?

Because form is pure and the Path is also pure, it is said that form is pure and the Path is also pure; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also pure, it is said that the Path is pure, and therefore consciousness is also pure, and both are pure together with the Path.

Furthermore, Subhūti, because form is pure and omniscience (sarvajñatā) is also pure, one says that omniscience is pure and form is also pure; therefore, the purity of form and the purity of omniscience are equal and without distinction.

Now, because the preceding does not cut off the subsequent, and the subsequent does not cut off the preceding, there is no destruction. For this reason, the preceding is uninterrupted; therefore it is said that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, and all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is also pure. Thus, because all-knowledge is pure, consciousness is also pure; and because all-knowledge is pure, consciousness is also pure. They are equal and without difference. Now, because the preceding does not cut off the subsequent, and the subsequent does not cut off the preceding, there is no destruction. For this reason, the preceding is uninterrupted.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods! This purity is exceedingly profound."
The Buddha said,
“It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Purity is supreme clarity, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
“It is exceedingly pure.”
Śāriputra said:
“Pure and free from defilement, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Extremely pure. Śāriputra said:
"Pure and without blemish, O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“It is pure and non-existent, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
“It is exceedingly pure.”
Śāriputra said:
“O God among Gods, it is through desire that one is purified of desire!
The Buddha said:
"Exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said: "O God among Gods!
It is pure because there is no form within form."
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Non-arising is the utter purity of formlessness, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
“It is utterly pure.”
Śāriputra said:
“O God among Gods, it is utterly pure to have wisdom regarding that which has no wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Extremely pure.
Śāriputra said, "O God among Gods,
it is extremely pure because, regarding wisdom, it is like being without wisdom."
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Regarding form, for one who possesses such wisdom and lacks [false] wisdom, there is utter purity, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
“Utterly pure.”
Śāriputra said:
“Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether they possess wisdom or lack wisdom, they are utterly pure, O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said,
"It is exceedingly pure.
Śāriputra said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is utterly pure; Sarvajñatā neither increases nor decreases, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said, “It is indeed utterly pure.”
Śāriputra said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is utterly pure; it takes nothing at all among all dharmas, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
“Extremely pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods, the self is pure, and form is also pure.”
The Buddha said,
“Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
"Therefore it is said: 'I am pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also pure, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
'They are fundamentally pure.'"
Subhūti said: "The self is pure, and the Way is also pure, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
“Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
“O God among Gods, the self is pure, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is also pure.”
The Buddha said,
"Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
"The self is pure and without beginning, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"It is fundamentally pure."
Subhūti said:
"O God among Gods, the self is pure and boundless, and form (*rūpa*) is likewise boundless.
The Buddha said:
"Fundamentally pure.
Subhūti said: "O God among Gods!
The self is pure and boundless; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise boundless."
The Buddha said,
"Fundamentally pure. Subhūti said:
“O God among Gods! This Prajñāpāramitā is neither there, nor here, nor in between.
The Buddha said:
“It is fundamentally pure.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows this, he is practicing the prajñāpāramitā; however, one who possesses conceptualization has already become far removed from the prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"Where there are letters, there is conceptualization; for this reason, one becomes attached.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, "The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!"
"Peaceful stability is the resolution of attachment.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What constitutes attachment?"
Subhūti said: "To know that form (*rūpa*) is empty is called attachment;

to know that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are empty is called attachment. To know past phenomena as past phenomena is called attachment; to know future phenomena as future phenomena is called attachment; to know present phenomena as present phenomena is called attachment. While suchness (*tathatā*) constitutes a great merit, for a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind [upon awakening] to perceive it in this way is itself attachment."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"What is meant by 'attachment'?
Subhūti replied:
"Kauśika, you know with your mind!
Can that mind which is given away as a gift, and which constitutes the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, perform any action, given that it is fundamentally pure?"
"Good sons and good daughters, by being free from all attachments, they abandon the ultimate limit.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! This causes bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to know that the limit of the beginning (*pūrvakoṭi*) is a matter of attachment to awakening.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
"It is profound and subtle; I shall now speak of it. Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Its words—beginning, middle, and end—are all excellent.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family forms a conceptualization regarding the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and follows that which is so conceptualized, they thereby become attached to the past, the future, and the present."

The Buddha, the God among Gods, exerts sympathetic encouragement (*anumodanā*) on behalf of all phenomena without exception; this is what constitutes sympathetic encouragement toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Because regarding phenomena there is no phenomenon, it is said that there is no past, future, or present. Since nothing can be produced therein, nor can there be conceptualization, nor can there be existence through causes and conditions, it cannot be seen or heard, and can only be known by the mind.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Its essence is profoundly deep and pure, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Originally pure. Subhūti said:
"I now take refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said:
"Because dharmas have no agent, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti said:
"All dharmas truly have no one who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"There are not two dharmas; because they are fundamentally pure by their very nature, they are called 'one. That which is pure has no agent regarding anything, even to the point that there is no purity itself; regarding everything, there is likewise no agent."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Therefore, to be free from all attachments is to abandon the limit of the beginning.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to comprehend, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
“In this way, there is no one who attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”
Subhūti said: "The Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti! It is not something known by the mind. Subhūti said:
“It is because there is no agent, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
“Because there is no agent, there is no attachment.”
Subhūti asked the Buddha,
“How should a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:

"Not conceptualizing the practice of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not conceptualizing the practices of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom. Not fulfilling the practice of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not fulfilling the practices of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom. That form is not fulfilled is the non-practice of form, which is practicing the perfection of wisdom; that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are not fulfilled is the non-practice of consciousness, which is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!
To be attached while having no attachment—this very attachment is indeed non-attachment.”
The Buddha said:

“One who practices without attachment to form is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*; one who practices without attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. This is for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to practice without attachment to form, without attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and likewise without attachment to the paths of the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, *pratyekabuddha*, or the path of a Buddha.”
"Why is this? Because it transcends all attachments and further emerges from within omniscience (sarvajñatā); this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Dharma that has been taught is extremely profound and difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!
That which is spoken does not decrease, nor does that which is not spoken decrease; that which is spoken does not increase, nor does that which is not spoken increase.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
For example, if a Tathāgata were to praise emptiness for the rest of his life, emptiness would not increase; if he were not to praise emptiness, emptiness would likewise not decrease.
It is like praising an illusory person: it does not increase, nor does it decrease if one does not praise them.
Hearing of good, one does not rejoice; hearing of evil, one does not become angry.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When one recites and studies each of these dharmas, the dharmas neither increase nor decrease.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound and difficult practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, if there is one who upholds the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be neither indolent nor fearful, neither terrified nor shaken, and will not turn back.”

Why is this? Because those who guard the *prajñāpāramitā* guard emptiness; therefore, all should pay homage to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Because they have donned the great armor of *saṃnāha*, they battle with emptiness; for the sake of all people, they put on the armor of *saṃnāha* and fight against emptiness. These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have donned the supreme great armor; for the sake of all people, they lift up emptiness. These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly great heroes.
O God among Gods!
By means of the dharma of emptiness, one personally attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieves the state of an *arhat-buddha*.
There may be another bhikṣu who thinks thus: "I should take refuge in the *prajñāpāramitā*, for it is the dharma of non-arising and also the dharma of non-extinction."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva follows the teaching of the perfection of wisdom, what teaching is he following?
Subhūti replied:
"It is for the sake of following the teaching of emptiness.
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
"What is meant by 'following the teaching of emptiness'?"
Subhūti said: “Those who desire tranquility are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who understand the perfection of wisdom.
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
"For how long a period should one who studies the Prajñāpāramitā provide protection?
Subhūti said to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"What do you think, Kauśika!"
"Do you see those dharmas that ought to be protected?
Yet you say you wish to protect them.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:

"No," Subhūti said, "one who dwells in accordance with the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā has already attained protection; neither humans nor non-humans will ever be able to find an opportunity against them."
Subhūti said: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva protects emptiness, he has already been practicing in accordance with the perfection of wisdom.
What do you think, Kauśika?"
"Is it possible to protect an echo?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "It is not."
Subhūti said: "Kauśika!

For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, that dharma is like an echo. Knowing this, one is likewise without conceptualization; practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of being without conceptualization, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakras, Brahmās, and honored devas throughout the trichiliocosm came before the Buddha, paid homage to him, circumambulated him three times, and each stood to one side."

The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the honored devas, all receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, recalled that all those thousand Buddhas were named Śākyamuni, that those bhikṣus were all named Subhūti, and that those who inquired about the Prajñāpāramitā were all like Śakradevendra.
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Exultation (*Nirdeśa-parivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
“When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becomes a Tathāgata, he too shall preach the Prajñāpāramitā at this very place.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya teach the Prajñāpāramitā in this place?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) therein, he does not teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of accepting form (*rūpa*), nor does he teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of emptiness of form. He does not teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of accepting feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), nor does he teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of emptiness of consciousness. Furthermore, he does not teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of liberating form, nor does he teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of binding form. Likewise, he does not teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of liberating feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he teach the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of binding consciousness."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is utterly pure, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"Form is also pure.
Subhūti said, "Therefore,
the Prajñāpāramitā is pure."
The Buddha said:
“Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also pure. Subhūti said:
"Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure.
The Buddha said:
"It is thus the purity of emptiness."
Subhūti said: "Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure.
The Buddha said:
“Form is pure and without blemish; the Prajñāpāramitā is also like this. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure and without blemish; the Prajñāpāramitā is also like this.”
The Buddha said:
"As space is without flaw or defilement, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Those who receive instruction and recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* shall never meet with an untimely death; hundreds and thousands of devas will constantly follow and attend upon them.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family acts as a Dharma teacher and preaches the Dharma on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, they shall obtain incalculable merit.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
The merit attained thereby cannot be further calculated.
If one upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, its merit surpasses that. Why is this?
Subhūti! This is because the perfection of wisdom is itself a precious treasure.
Within all phenomena, there is no agent, nor is there anyone who attains phenomena, nor is there anyone who maintains them.
Why is this? Because the Dharma is profoundly deep.
It cannot be seen, it cannot be apprehended, and there is no one who apprehends it.
Subhūti! Furthermore, one does not perceive the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Subhūti! It cannot be named, nor is there any seeing by which one attains the *prajñāpāramitā*.

That which is sought cannot be found; nor is the *prajñāpāramitā* seen. It is thus profoundly deep and has no place of origination. The *prajñāpāramitā* has nothing upon which it acts, yet there is nothing it does not act upon. The *prajñāpāramitā* likewise has no one who upholds its dharma, nor anyone who guards its dharma. Like space, it is without anything to be grasped and without anything to be maintained; it is without anything seen, yet it is not without contemplation, nor is it without vision.
The sons of the gods from the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems flew above and all beheld him together; they raised their voices in unison and exclaimed:
"For a second time, the Wheel of Dharma is seen turning upon the land of Jambudvīpa!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“There is no turning of two wheels of Dharma, nor does one conceive of the turning of a single wheel of Dharma; this non-turning is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā.”
Subhūti said: “So it is, O God among Gods!
This most peaceful Great Perfection is the unimpeded dharma for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; there is no dharma by which one becomes perfectly awakened.”

What is this Wheel of Dharma? It is that which only the Buddhas see; it is turned as the seeing of the Dharma, turned as the non-returning of the Dharma. Furthermore, there is no dharma therein that causes fear, nor is there any dharma therein that causes sorrow.

Why is this? Because if two dharmas exist, they are unobtainable; what dharma could there be to cause anxiety, and yet no dharma undergoes transformation? Therefore, all dharmas are like space and do not undergo transformation, nor is there any dharma that returns; even all dharmas are non-existent.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"That which is empty has no turning forward, nor does it turn back; it is without conceptualization, without aspiration, without birth and death, and without that from which it arises; it neither turns forward nor turns back."

To speak in this way is to preach the Dharma without anything being preached; there is nothing to be attained, nor is there any realization. To preach the Dharma in this way is neither to enter parinirvāṇa, nor is there any exhaustion in preaching the Dharma in this way.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Perfection of the Infinite, O God among Gods, is like space; it has no limit.”
The first perfection, O God among Gods, is that all dharmas are entirely equal.
The second, the perfection of the fleeting, is that they are fundamentally empty.
O God among Gods!
The three unsurpassed perfections are unattached to all dharmas.
O God among Gods!
"Fourth, the perfection of non-self has no body.
O God among Gods!
Fifth, the perfection of nowhere-going has no destination."
O God among Gods!
The six perfections of non-existence are without anything to be grasped.
O God among Gods!
Seventh, O God among Gods! the perfection of inexhaustibility is without limit.
Eighth, the perfection of non-arising is without cessation.
O God among Gods!
The nine non-active perfections have no creator.
O God among Gods!
Tenth, the perfection of non-knowing is without attainment.
O God among Gods!
Eleventh, the perfection of non-arrival is without reaching.
O God among Gods!
This is because the twelve stainless pāramitās are purified.
O God among Gods!
Thirteenth, the non-attachment *pāramitā* is non-apprehensible.
O God among Gods!
Fourteenth, the dream *pāramitā* is without self.
O God among Gods!
The fifteen pure pāramitās are free from blemish.
O God among Gods!
Sixteenth, the invisible pāramitā has no location.
O Devātideva! Seventeenth, the concentration pāramitā is unshakable.
O God among Gods!
The eighteen aspects of non-conceptualization and the perfections are all equal.
O God among Gods!
Nineteenth, O God among Gods! The dharma of the perfection of immovability does not shift, because it is fundamentally non-existent.
Twentieth, the perfection of desirelessness is so because it is fundamentally non-existent.
O God among Gods!
The twenty-one unborn pāramitās have no destination.
O God among Gods!
Twenty-second, the perfection of tranquility is free from conceptualization.
O God among Gods!
Twenty-third, the perfection of non-anger is free from resentment.
O God among Gods!
This is because the twenty-four perfections of non-self are fundamentally non-existent.
O God among Gods!
Twenty-fifth, the perfection of non-contemplation is that which has no point of origin,
O God among Gods! Twenty-sixth,
the perfection of non-arrival at extremes is that which has no place of abiding, O God among Gods!
Twenty-seventh is the perfection of non-decay, which is indestructible,
O God among Gods!
Twenty-eighth is the perfection of universal penetration, which is beyond the reach of all arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
O God among Gods!
The twenty-ninth, the perfection of non-confusion, is without error.
O God among Gods!
"O God among Gods! In the thirty immeasurable pāramitās, there is not even the slightest dharma.
In the thirty-first, the formless pāramitā, there is no obstruction regarding any dharmas."
O God among Gods!
The thirty-two perfections that are unattainable are non-arising.
O God among Gods!
Thirty-third, the perfection of impermanence is without destruction.
O God among Gods!
Thirty-fourth, the perfection of sufferinglessness is such that all phenomena do not encroach upon one another.
O God among Gods!
The thirty-five perfections of non-self seek nothing among all phenomena.
O God among Gods!
The thirty-six emptinesses and the perfection of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
O God among Gods,
cannot be apprehended within all phenomena; the perfection of non-conceptualization does not emerge from any phenomena.
O God among Gods!
The thirty-eighth power-perfection (bala-pāramitā) is supreme among all dharmas.
O God among Gods!
The thirty-ninth is the immeasurable *pāramitā* of the Buddha-dharmas, which transcends all conceptual calculations regarding phenomena.
O God among Gods!
The fortieth is the spontaneous *pāramitā*; this is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"O God among Gods!
This is because even the forty-first [dharma] has no intrinsic nature within all dharmas.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on Upholding from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Path of Practice. Śakra Devānām Indra had this thought:

“Those who hear this Prajñāpāramitā were all people from the time of past Buddhas; how much more so those who study, uphold, and recite it, and having studied, upheld, and recited it, abide according to the teaching. Such persons have already made offerings to numerous Buddhas in previous lives; now, hearing again this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they study, uphold, and recite it while abiding according to the teaching. These sons and daughters of good family have already posed questions to past Buddhas; therefore, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they do not doubt, do not fear, do not hesitate, and do not tremble.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who believe in and accept the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be regarded as *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive)."
Why is this? O Devātideva!
The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep.

It is because they originally applied diligence and believed in the Prajñāpāramitā that, should there be those who disparage the Prajñāpāramitā, such persons must have already disparaged the Prajñāpāramitā in their previous lives.
Why is this? It is because they do not have faith in or take delight in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which results from their failure to question the Buddha and his disciples.
For this reason, you should know it thus.
Śakra Devānām Indra said to the Venerable Śāriputra:

"The Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound and difficult to fathom. If there are those who do not believe when the profound Prajñāpāramitā is being expounded, such persons have not yet practiced the bodhisattva path; on the contrary, they harbor difficulties within them."
"One who takes refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā has already taken refuge in the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Śāriputra said to Śakra-devānām-indra: "So it is, so it is!"
Kauśika! Those who take refuge in the wisdom of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) are thereby taking refuge in the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
From within this emerges the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Sarvajñā.
This wisdom of omniscience is that which is illuminated by the Prajñāpāramitā; those who abide within the Prajñāpāramitā are none who do not understand wisdom.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in the context of sarvajñatā?
How does he abide within the perfection of wisdom?”
“What is the understanding of wisdom within the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!”
Kauśika! That you have asked such a question—
what I shall now reveal to you is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not dwell in form; that which does not dwell in form is itself the practice. They do not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; that which does not dwell in consciousness is itself the practice. They do not reach a final limit in form; because they do not reach a final limit in form, they therefore do not dwell in form. They do not reach a final limit in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; because they do not reach a final limit in consciousness, they therefore do not dwell in consciousness.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound, O God among Gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to perceive its limits, O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “Form (*rūpa*) is also profoundly deep and non-abiding.

Just as form is profoundly deep and non-abiding, so too is this profound depth and non-abiding of form the very understanding that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also profoundly deep and non-abiding. Just as consciousness is profoundly deep and non-abiding, so too is this profound depth and non-abiding of consciousness the very understanding that form is also profoundly deep and non-adherent. Just as form is profoundly deep and non-adherent, and form is profoundly deep and non-abiding—just as form is profoundly deep and non-abiding—this is what is meant by form being profoundly deep and non-adherent. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also profoundly deep and non-adherent. Just as consciousness is profoundly deep and non-adherent, and consciousness is profoundly deep and non-abiding—this consciousness being profoundly deep and non-abiding is what is meant by consciousness being profoundly deep and non-adherent.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, O God among Gods!
It should be expounded before irreversible bodhisattvas; upon hearing this dharma of wisdom, they will neither doubt nor be deluded by it.”
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Śāriputra:
"If one were to speak of this before a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet received the prediction [of enlightenment], what difference would there be?"
Śāriputra said:

“This bodhisattva has sought Buddhahood for a very long time and has already received a prediction (vyākaraṇa). Even if he has not yet received it, upon hearing this, he will receive a prediction therein before long; whether he sees one Buddha or two Buddhas, he will immediately receive the prediction and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have not yet received their prediction of enlightenment, upon hearing this, will become terrified and immediately abandon it and depart.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "So it is, so it is!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have sought the Buddha-way for a very long time—whether they have already received their prediction or have not yet received it—all hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I too rejoice in hearing these words, O God among Gods!
You bring peace and security to those who delight in the Dharma.”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"If you wish to speak, do so in my presence.
Śāriputra replied:
“Suppose, O God among Gods, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees himself in a dream sitting upon the seat of a Buddha;
he knows then that he is close to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will attain the state of an Arhat-buddha.”
Thus it is, O God among Gods!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* has practiced for a very long time; it will not be long before they now receive their prediction [of enlightenment], and their merit is about to reach full completion.
“A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should understand it thus: for one who has attained this profound Prajñāpāramitā, their merit shall be brought to full completion.
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!”
"Śāriputra! That you delight in making such a statement is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Suppose, O God among Gods, there is a man traveling ten thousand *li*.

As he counts those ten thousand *li*, he arrives at a vast, empty wilderness. From afar, this man sees cowherds or shepherds, or he sees boundary markers, or houses, or groves of trees. He then forms this thought:
‘This looks like a commandery; it looks like a district; it looks like a village.’”
"If one wishes to see or hear [them], one should form this thought; as one proceeds step by step and draws closer, one no longer fears robbers or thieves.
O God among Gods! It is the same for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has attained the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Now the time for his prediction of enlightenment is not far off, nor does he fear falling into the stages of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because he possesses the superior conceptualization of having heard and seen the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
It is as if, O God among Gods, a man wishing to see the great ocean were to travel toward it;
if he sees trees and perceives them as trees, or sees mountains and perceives them as mountains, one should know that the great ocean is still far away.

As he proceeds further, he no longer sees trees nor has the perception of trees; he no longer sees mountains nor has the perception of mountains. His mind also knows that the great ocean is near and will not be far off. Along the way, there are no more trees nor any perception of trees, and no more mountains nor any perception of mountains. Although this man has not yet seen the great ocean, it is certain that he is about to arrive. In this same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand.
O God among Gods!
If one hears and attains this profound Prajñāpāramitā, even if they do not see the Buddha bestowing the prediction of enlightenment upon them, it means that they shall become a Buddha before long.
If one hears that they have attained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, O God among Gods! it is like a tree in the springtime:
its leaves are gradually about to sprout, and before long there shall be flowers and fruit.

Why is this? This tree is an auspicious omen; one may know that before long it shall have leaves, flowers, and fruit. The people of Jambudvīpa all rejoice greatly, having seen this tree and knowing that its leaves, flowers, and fruit will soon reach maturity.
Thus it is, O God among Gods!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the vision of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their merit is about to reach fulfillment; they now bring this to personal accomplishment within the *prajñāpāramitā*. It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, in past lives, studied the *prajñāpāramitā*, and it is due to the resulting fulfillment of that merit that they have attained this state.

For this reason, when they again hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there are none among the devas in the heavens who do not rejoice on their behalf. They imagine seeing the past bodhisattva-mahāsattvas receiving their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and they know that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is now likewise receiving his prediction and will, before long, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Just as, O God among Gods, when a woman is pregnant, her belly gradually grows large and her body becomes heavy;

because she is no longer as she was before, her movements become inconvenient, her desire for food and drink diminishes, she is unable to walk far, she experiences slight pains, her speech becomes soft and slow, and she is restless in lying down or rising; as these pains increase, one should know that this woman will give birth before long.”
So it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, O God among Gods!

If one who wishes to fulfill their merit hears or sees this profound Prajñāpāramitā and practices its recollection, you should know that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will before long receive the prediction of enlightenment and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!”
"Whatever has been spoken is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!"
Tathāgata! Arhat! Samyaksaṃbuddha!
You have already fully and clearly designated [the stages] for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva day and night brings to mind that all those in the world may attain peace and security, and he takes pity upon those in the heavens above and the world below. For this reason, he personally attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and when he has become a buddha, he preaches the Dharma for all.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods! How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* practice so as to achieve accomplishment?”

The Buddha said to Subhūti: “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he does not perceive a fault in form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a fault in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive an absence of fault in form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive an absence of fault in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. He does not see these dharmas; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, he does not see what is non-dharma; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods!
That which has been spoken is incalculable.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Form is also incalculable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also incalculable.
Not knowing form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not knowing feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Who, O God among Gods, would believe this?
Is this the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What is it that constitutes 'practice'? Even if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices, he merely acquires a name.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā does not approach power; he does not approach the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), nor does he approach them; he does not approach the buddha-dharmas, nor does he approach them; he does not approach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor does he approach it."

Why is this? The powers are incalculable; the four grounds of self-confidence are also incalculable; the Buddha-dharmas are also incalculable; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is also incalculable; form (*rūpa*) is also incalculable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) are also incalculable; all phenomena (*dharmas*) are also incalculable; and the mind (*citta*) is also incalculable.

Even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, it is practicing nothing at all; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Even if one practices in this manner, it is merely for the sake of obtaining a name.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Prajñāpāramitā, O Devātideva, is the king among all most profound and precious jewels."
The Prajñāpāramitā is the king among great generals.
O God among Gods!
When the Prajñāpāramitā engages in battle with emptiness, there is none who can prevail over it.
"O God among Gods!
From this, cessation cannot be attained.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! Those who wish to quickly transcribe this sutra should do so until the end of one year, or even until its completion."
"Why is this? Because these sons of good family, amidst their precious treasures, will encounter many causes and conditions that lead to their interruption. Subhūti said:
"In the midst of the Prajñāpāramitā, Māra the Evil One constantly seeks to cause its interruption.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Even if Māra the Evil One should wish to interrupt this sūtra, he will ultimately be unable to overcome the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
Śāriputra asked the Buddha:
"By whose majestic spiritual power and grace is it that evil Māra cannot interrupt them midway?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"This is all due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, as well as the present Buddhas of the ten directions in incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands, who further lend the grace of their majestic spiritual power; all these Buddhas together keep him in mind, together bestow upon him, and together protect him. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already obtained the protection bestowed by the Buddhas."
Śāriputra! Māra the Evil One will not be able to cut it off midway. Why is this?

The Buddhas currently residing in the incalculable lands of the ten directions all together protect the Prajñāpāramitā; whether there are those who contemplate, explain, or recite it, or those who study, receive, or transcribe it, all these are brought about by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recite this, or uphold, study, or transcribe it, they shall be protected by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“All this is due to the grace of the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas. You should know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who study the prajñāpāramitā are protected by the protection of the Buddhas.”
Śāriputra said:
"If there are those who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha beholds them all with his eye.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"The Tathāgata beholds with his Buddha-eye those who study, uphold, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, as well as those who, at the very end, write down and uphold this sūtra; you should know that all such persons have already been seen by the eyes of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“Those bodhisattvas of supreme virtue who study, receive, and uphold this sutra—these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are now seated near the Buddha for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, if there are those who copy and uphold this sutra at the very end [of the teaching], such people shall be most honored and attain great merit.”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
After the Tathāgata has passed away, this Prajñāpāramitā shall remain in South India.
Once those who have studied it there have mastered it, it shall be transmitted from South India to West India.
"Once you have mastered it, you shall transmit it from Western India to Northern India.
Those who would study it should learn it.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Śāriputra.

"When the Dharma is on the verge of being extinguished in the future, I shall fully know those who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā; if there are any who write it down at the very end, the Buddha will foresee them all in advance and praise and extol them."
Śāriputra asked the Buddha,
"In the final age, will this Prajñāpāramitā reach Northern India?
The Buddha said:
"When you arrive in Northern India, those who are there shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā;
you should further inquire about it and know that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has practiced the Mahāyāna for a very long time, and for that reason is receiving the Prajñāpāramitā once again."
Śāriputra asked:
“In Northern India, how many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will there be who study the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"In Northern India as well, there are very many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, but few who study the prajñāpāramitā.

If there are those who explain it, and one hears it without fear, without difficulty, and without dread, such a person must have heard of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in a previous life. Because this bodhisattva is a person of supreme virtue who maintains the precepts in their entirety, they desire to act as a foundation for all people and bring about the liberation of many."
As for those people who seek the Way of the Buddha, I know that these sons and daughters of good family are now close to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
Those who train in this manner will constantly study this Dharma wherever they are born, and shall thus practice *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

These sons and daughters of good family shall be most noble and honorable; Māra will ultimately be unable to do them anything, nor can he move them or cause them to abandon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When these sons and daughters of good family hear this *pāramitā*, they attain supreme honor; through their encouragement and delight in the merit of the Mahāyāna, they draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Although these sons and daughters of good family do not see me in person, those who obtain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in future lives have already beheld the Buddha face-to-face; what is spoken here is no different from his own words. This is that which a bodhisattva should practice and carry out.

Should there be several hundred or several thousand people who seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should instruct them together, encourage and gladden them together, and preach the Dharma for them so that they all rejoice and study the Buddha-way.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“I exhort and assist these good men and good women who study the bodhisattva path toward supreme virtue; for those who provide such instruction, their minds will successively illuminate one another.”

If there are good sons and good daughters who provide assistance and encouragement to those who wish to practice the bodhisattva path—whether they be several hundred or several thousand people seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—one should instruct them together, encourage and delight them together, and cause them to joyfully study the Buddha-way.

These sons and daughters of good family who experience such leaping joy and rapture in their hearts aspire to be born in Buddha-fields in other directions. Because they are born in those other regions, they shall behold the Buddhas face-to-face as they preach the Dharma; furthermore, they shall hear the *pāramitās* and understand them all clearly. Moreover, in those fields, they shall teach hundreds of thousands of people, causing them all to practice the path of the Buddha.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is difficult to reach, O God among Gods!

Because there is nothing you do not understand regarding the dharmas of the past, future, and present, you fully know the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the future, causing these beings to study and enter the six pāramitās with tireless diligence."
The Buddha said:
"If these sons and daughters of good family practice this Dharma, whatever they seek will certainly be attained; even that which they do not seek will naturally be obtained."

This is due to the power of the original vows of these good sons and good daughters; they do not depart from this Dharma, and although they do not seek anything, they naturally attain the six pāramitās.
Śāriputra asked the Buddha,
"Can sūtra scrolls be produced from within this pāramitā?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"These sons and daughters of good family who have deeply entered the Prajñāpāramitā shall, from within it, individually extract each profound dharma and form them into sūtra scrolls."
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Those who possess the teaching of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are able to instruct all people, exhorting and assisting them by preaching the Dharma, causing them all to rejoice and study the Buddha-way.
These good sons and good daughters shall themselves further study this Dharma; by virtue of this, in whatever place they are born, they will increasingly attain the six *pāramitās*.

Chapter Nine: Awakening (*Bodhi*) In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Chapter on the Practice of the Way, the Ninth Chapter: Awakening (in the *Dān* [Old] edition, the Chapter on Awakening Mara). Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"When good sons and good daughters are engaged in their studies, there ought to be efficacious signs."
"O God among Gods!
How should one awaken to its difficulty?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If the mind is not joyful, one should recognize it as the work of Māra;
if the mind of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva suddenly gives rise to delusions, one should recognize it as the work of Māra;
if there is fear of thunder and lightning while a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is copying this sutra, one should recognize it as the work of Māra."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is transcribing this sutra, if they engage in mutual joking and playfulness, they should recognize this as the work of Māra;
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is transcribing this sutra, if they engage in mutual comparison and disparagement, they should recognize this as the work of Māra;
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is transcribing this sutra, if they look around to the left and right, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva writes this sutra, if their mind is distracted by improper thoughts, they should recognize this as the work of Māra;
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind is not fixed upon the sutra and repeatedly rises from their seat, they should recognize this as the work of Māra;
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thinks to themselves:
"I have not yet received the prediction [of enlightenment] within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thinking thus, his mind becomes distracted and he departs; he should recognize this as the work of Māra.
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects to himself:
"If my name is not found within the Prajñāpāramitā," and the mind feels no joy or delight,
one should recognize this as the work of Māra.
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects to himself:
"I have not heard the Prajñāpāramitā in my home village, district, kingdom, county, or town; nor have I ever heard it in the place where I was born.
Thinking thus with regret, he immediately departs.
That person shall have to wait for further kalpas before they attain anything; for some time during those kalpas, they will take pleasure in studying other sutras and will not abide in sarvajñatā.
If one abandons the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and departs for it, studying other sūtras instead, this is to abandon the root in order to grasp the branches;
yet those who study the *prajñāpāramitā* also understand worldly phenomena (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) and further understand the dharmas of the Path (*mārga-dharma*).
It is just as if a dog, having received food from its master, refuses to eat it and instead seeks food from those who perform manual labor.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

In the future, there will be bodhisattvas who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead seek out derivative and peripheral *prajñāpāramitās*, following divergent scriptures and arts; they will thereby fall into the stages of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* paths.
"It is as if a man were to see an elephant and examine its feet. Subhūti, what do you think? Would that man be considered clever?
Subhūti replied, "He would not be considered clever."
The Buddha said:

"This bodhisattva is a person of virtue who, among the two classes [of practitioners], abandons the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead practices and studies other sūtras, thereby attaining the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha. Subhūti, what do you think? Is this bodhisattva wise?"
Subhūti said, "It would not be wise.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, one should recognize the work of Māra.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Suppose, for example, there were a man who wished to see the great ocean, but having never before seen the great ocean, upon seeing the water of a large pond, he were to say:"
"Could this water perhaps be the great ocean?
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that man be wise? Subhūti replied:
"It is not wise," the Buddha said.

"If a bodhisattva who possesses such virtues abandons the *prajñāpāramitā* and instead studies other sutras, falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha paths—Subhūti, what do you think? Is this bodhisattva mahāsattva wise?"
Subhūti said, "It would not be wise.
The Buddha said:
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.

For example, suppose there were a master builder capable of constructing palaces who intended to design and build a palace like those of the sun and moon, so lofty that it could not be missed by anyone. Subhūti, in your opinion, would he be able to do so?"
Subhūti said: "The palaces of the sun and moon are exceedingly high; they could never be made.
The Buddha said:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Would that man be wise?
Subhūti replied, “He would not be wise.”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! In the future,

those who practice the bodhisattva path and hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* will find it disagreeable and abandon it, instead clarifying the teachings of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and seeking *sarvajñatā* therein.”
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is this bodhisattva wise?
Subhūti replied, "He is not clever."
The Buddha said:
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.

It is like a man who wishes to see a cakravartin king, but before seeing the cakravartin, instead sees a minor king; he contemplates the latter’s appearance and attire with great attention and then calls out, 'This is the cakravartin.'"
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is this man wise? Subhūti replied, “He is not wise.”
The Buddha said: “It is so, Subhūti!

In the future, there will be bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, will instead find it disagreeable and abandon it, entering into the teachings of the śrāvakas while seeking *sarvajñatā*.”
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is this bodhisattva wise?
Subhūti replied, "He is not wise."
The Buddha said:
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.
It is like a man who, being greatly hungry, obtains food of a hundred flavors yet refuses to eat it, preferring instead to eat food of sixty flavors."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would this man be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, "He would not be wise."
The Buddha said: “So it is, Subhūti!

In the future, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, find it displeasing and abandon it; they then enter among the teachings of the śrāvakas, seeking *sarvajñatā* with the desire to become buddhas.”
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is this bodhisattva mahāsattva wise?
Subhūti replied, "He is not wise."
The Buddha said:
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.
It is like a man who obtains a priceless maṇi jewel, yet takes a crystal and compares it with it, wishing to make them identical."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is this man wise? Subhūti replied, "He is not wise."
The Buddha said:

"In this way, there will be those in the future who practice the bodhisattva path; having heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they instead hold fast to these śrāvaka dharmas, desiring to attain *sarvajñatā* and become buddhas within the framework of the śrāvaka dharmas."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is this bodhisattva mahāsattva wise?
Subhūti replied, "He is not wise."
The Buddha said:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
When copying the *Prajñāpāramitā*, if any gain or profit arises, and upon hearing such talk one abandons [the task] and departs, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva creates an obstacle for himself.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
“In this way, can one write out and complete the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
"If one cannot succeed in writing it out, this good son should recognize that this is the work of Māra.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
If a son of good family writes out this sutra in whatever measure, and says:

"I am writing the Prajñāpāramitā," and therein conceives thoughts of hearing its definitive resolution or desires to gain something from it, he should recognize this as the work of Māra; for one who acts with such conceptual seeking falls into the realm of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when copying the Prajñāpāramitā,

one might think of one's hometown, or think of other regions, or think of other countries, or think of a king, or think of bandits, or think of armies, or think of battles, or think of parents, brothers, sisters, relatives, and kin, or have other such thoughts."
Māra further intensifies that thought, distracting the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva and creating obstacles for them.
One should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If there should come wealth and profit—namely, garments of fine silk, food and drink, bedding and furniture, and medicines for the sick—all provided in abundance, and these reach the ears of the bodhisattva and cause their mind to become distracted, they will be unable to study, recite, or master the Prajñāpāramitā.
One should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are profound dharmas of the Buddha;

Māra will follow them and create confusion, causing the bodhisattva-mahāsattva no longer to delight in attaining upāyakauśalya (skillful means), and thus he will not take pleasure in inquiring about the prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said:

"I have extensively explained the matters of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Those who wish to learn *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) should seek it from the *prajñāpāramitā*; those who do not accord with the *prajñāpāramitā* should abandon it and go their way, for they would be seeking *upāyakauśalya* within the path of the śrāvakas."
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is this bodhisattva wise?
Subhūti replied, “He is not clever.”
The Buddha said: “It is so;
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
If the person receiving the sūtra wishes to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, yet the Dharma-preacher’s body becomes uneasy, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when the Dharma-preacher has settled down and wishes to bestow the Prajñāpāramitā, but the recipient of the scripture wishes to depart, they will not be in harmony; thus, the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be written out and completed."
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a person who studies the sūtras comes wishing to receive the Prajñāpāramitā with a joyful heart, yet the Dharma master intends to go to another region; thus, these two do not harmonize, and they are unable to study and transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā to completion.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize such things as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if the Dharma-preacher intends to obtain something—

such as clothing or material gain— and the person receiving the scripture has no intention to give, these two will not be in harmony, and they will not succeed in studying and perfecting the Prajñāpāramitā.
In this way, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should recognize the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if the person receiving the sutra has no sense of attachment or stinginess, yet does not oppose the wishes of those who seek it, while the Dharma Master is unwilling to reveal his own copies of the scriptures nor to explain them accordingly, the recipient of the sutra will find no joy; thus, the two will not be in harmony and shall not be able to study, transcribe, or complete the Prajñāpāramitā.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize and understand that this is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a Dharma teacher wishes to speak something, but the person receiving the teaching does not wish to hear or know it, such a lack of harmony between the two means they shall not hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize these as the deeds of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti,

if the Dharma-preacher is physically exhausted and lies down, wishing not to rise, and takes no pleasure in speaking, while the person receiving the teaching wishes to hear the *prajñāpāramitā*, such a lack of harmony between the two means that the *prajñāpāramitā* will not be heard.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize them as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when one wishes to write or recite the Prajñāpāramitā, if someone should happen to come among the assembly and instead speak in opposition and slander it:
"To study for this reason is to undergo much toil and suffering.
He spoke of the immense toil and suffering in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts (preta), saying to people:
"One should quickly sever the root of birth and death."
"In such cases, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when one wishes to write or preach the Prajñāpāramitā, if someone comes and sits among the assembly, praising the pleasures of the heavens where the five desires may be indulged to one's heart's content, saying that those who practice dhyāna will attain rebirth among the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and those who contemplate emptiness and stillness will attain rebirth among the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [the bodhisattva should realize] these are all dharmas of impermanence and diligent suffering. It is not as good as seeking here the path of a srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat, so that one shall no longer be occupied with birth and death."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Dharma Master thought:
"I am noble and honorable; if there are those who come to pay homage and take refuge, I shall bestow upon them the Prajñāpāramitā;
but if there are those who do not pay homage and take refuge, I shall not give it to them."

The person receiving the sutra returned home and paid homage with deep reverence, not shirking even when faced with hardships. The Dharma Master, however, felt regret and did not wish to give the sutra to his disciple. Hearing that grain was expensive in another country, he said to the person receiving the sutra:
"Good son, do you know this?"
"Can you go with me to that place?
Reflect carefully upon this; do not let yourself regret it later.
When the disciple heard these words, he was filled with great sorrow and distress, and he thought to himself:
"I have read all the sutras, yet he refuses to give them to me; what shall I do?
Thus, because the two were not in harmony, they were unable to study and complete the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
When the Dharma Master was about to reach an extremely perilous place, he said to the person receiving the scripture:
"Good son, do you understand?
That place has no grain; it is filled with tigers, wolves, many bandits, and the five kinds of empty marshes. I wish to go there."
"Reflect carefully for yourself: is it truly diligent and arduous to follow my patience?
Then, speaking with words that were profound and pleasing, he caused the disciples to become weary of their own hearts; no longer finding delight in them, he gradually granted them leave to return.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By creating such an obstacle, one is unable to study the Prajñāpāramitā.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize it as the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there may be a Dharma-preacher who is diligent in his travels for alms and possesses many skillful means, yet he is utterly unwilling to give the sutras to his disciples. On the contrary, wishing to become indolent and abandon them, he says to the person receiving the sutra:
'Good son, do you know this?'"
"I must go somewhere," he thinks,
and then he asks questions.
In this way, the two are not in harmony, and he cannot study the book to complete the Prajñāpāramitā.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize and understand the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
Māra the Evil One constantly seeks out opportunities to prevent those in training from reciting and receiving the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"For what reason does Māra constantly seek out opportunities to prevent those in training from reciting and receiving the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Māra, the Evil One, habitually engages in slander, claiming that these are not pāramitās, saying:
'I possess various profound sūtras whose excellence is beyond words; therefore, these alone are the pāramitās.'"
"In this way, Subhūti,
Māra the Evil One practices slander, causing the minds of newly initiated bodhisattvas to become filled with doubt, so that they no longer study, recite, or transcribe this sūtra."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize and understand this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when an instance of Māra’s activity arises,
it causes a deeply trained bodhisattva to realize the limit of existence (bhūtakoṭi) and thereby fall among the śrāvakas, attaining the path of a srotāpanna.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize and understand them as the work of Māra.
*The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines*, Scroll Four;
*The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: Illumination. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Ten: Illumination.
The Buddha said:
"In the Prajñāpāramitā, there are many causes and conditions for the arising of Māra, even to the point of causing [the practice] to be severed.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Tathāgata has said, if there are Bodhisattvas, there will be much harm and peril."
Why is this? Because that which is most supreme and honored is difficult to encounter, it may even lead to harm.
It is the same with the Prajñāpāramitā, O God among Gods!

Many who have many causes for arising, as well as those newly trained and having first resolved their minds, possess very little knowledge; their minds do not enter into the Great Dharma, nor do they recite the Prajñāpāramitā. Such persons are considered to be possessed by Māra.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"As you have said, those who have newly resolved their minds know very little; their minds do not enter into the Great Dharma, nor do they recite the Prajñāpāramitā. This is because they have been seized by Māra, and they themselves give rise to the causes and conditions for Māra, leading until their [practice] is cut off."
If good sons or good daughters take up, uphold, study, recite, and read this Prajñāpāramitā, it is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha. Why is this so?
Evil Māra cannot restrain it so as to cause its severance;
this is because it is sustained and upheld by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

It is like a mother who gives birth to children one by one, numbering up to ten; while her children are still small, she falls ill and is unable to protect them, and there is no one to look after them. If the mother recovers and remains at peace, she herself nurtures and raises her children so that they may survive, guarding and attending to them against cold, heat, dryness, and dampness—this is what is manifested in the world.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha keeps the *prajñāpāramitā* in mind; and whoever upholds it, whether by reciting or writing it, the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions likewise constantly keep the *prajñāpāramitā* in mind. This is how the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifests within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained omniscience (sarvajñatā) by means of this; those who have become Buddhas, those who have not yet become Buddhas, and those who are about to become Buddhas—all have attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) through the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—this illumination brought about by the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)—arises entirely from the Prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, he manifests in the world.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha illuminates the world through the Prajñāpāramitā.”
"What is meant by the Prajñāpāramitā illuminating the world?
And what is it that the Tathāgata sustains in the world?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"The Tathāgata manifests the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) to appear in the world.
Subhūti asked: "How does he manifest the five aggregates within the Prajñāpāramitā?"
"What is it that constitutes the manifestation of the *prajñāpāramitā* within the five aggregates?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"It is manifested by way of non-destruction; yet there is no manifestation through non-destruction either."

Emptiness is neither subject to destruction nor does it possess destruction; it is without perception and without aspiration, and it is neither destroyed nor does it undergo destruction. For this reason, it manifests within the world.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“As for incalculable persons and incalculable minds, the Tathāgata fully knows them all; they are all naturally born persons, such as these naturally born persons.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata clearly knows incalculable persons and incalculable minds.
The Tathāgata, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, manifests the maintenance of the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if there are minds that are agitated or distracted, the Tathāgata knows them all.
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the minds that are diseased and the minds that are disturbed?
As for the fundamental nature of phenomena (dharmas), they are neither diseased nor disturbed; it is for this reason that he knows them.
What is meant by knowing the agitated mind and the distracted mind?
That which ought to be exhausted is known as being exhausted; for this reason, one knows them.

When there is a mind of craving and desire, one knows it as a mind of craving and desire; when there is a mind of hatred and anger, one knows it as a mind of hatred and anger; when there is a mind of delusion and ignorance, one knows it as a mind of delusion and ignorance.

One knows that the root of the mind of desire is the absence of a mind of desire; one knows that the root of the mind of hatred is the absence of a mind of hatred; one knows that the root of the mind of delusion is the absence of a mind of delusion.
Subhūti, it is this Prajñāpāramitā that has enabled me to attain sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). Why is this?
The Tathāgata has no mind of craving or desire; because he possesses no mind of craving or desire, he fully knows the fundamental nature of all minds, which likewise lacks any craving or desire.
For this reason, the mind of the Tathāgata is free from craving and desire.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has no mind of anger; by means of this mind free from anger, he fully knows the root of all minds, which likewise possesses no mind of anger.
For this reason, the mind of a Tathāgata is free from anger. Why is this?
Because a Tathāgata has no deluded mind; by virtue of having no deluded mind, he fully knows the fundamental nature of all minds, and likewise possesses no deluded mind.
For this reason, the mind of the Tathāgata is free from delusion.
Thus, Subhūti, it is by means of the prajñāpāramitā that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifests and sustains the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
because the Tathāgata acts for the sake of sentient beings, through the Prajñāpāramitā his mind is vast and there is nothing he does not know."
What is meant by saying that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā so that his mind is vast and there is nothing he does not know?

That mind is neither broad nor great; it neither departs nor arrives anywhere. For this reason, the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā so that his mind is vast and there is nothing he does not know.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the Tathāgata acts for the sake of sentient beings, through the perfection of wisdom he expands his mind so that there is nothing he does not know."
What is meant by saying that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, relies upon the *prajñāpāramitā* to broaden his mind so that there is nothing he does not know?
That mind comes from nowhere and abides nowhere.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, expands his mind so that there is nothing he does not know.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
because the Tathāgata takes into account immeasurable persons and immeasurable minds, he knows all things through the Prajñāpāramitā."
What is meant by saying that the Tathāgata, because of his immeasurable persons and immeasurable minds, knows all things through the *prajñāpāramitā*?
That mind abides nowhere and has no place from which it comes or to which it ceases; because it is without remainder, there is nothing he does not know.
Because his mind is like space, he knows all that cannot be calculated— both persons and minds. In this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata,
by means of the prajñāpāramitā, knows all that cannot be calculated— both persons and minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, for the sake of sentient beings,
the Tathāgata, by means of the prajñāpāramitā, fully knows all invisible minds."
What is meant by saying that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, knows through the Prajñāpāramitā how to fully know the invisible mind?
That mind is fundamentally pure, and thus it is devoid of conceptualization.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, knows all unobservable minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
For the sake of beings, the Tathāgata, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, knows all invisible minds."
What is meant by the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, knowing through the Prajñāpāramitā that he fully knows the invisible mind?
That mind cannot be seen with the eye, just as it has come from.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata, by means of the prajñāpāramitā, knows all unobservable minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is because of sentient beings that the Tathāgata, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, knows; desiring to attain this, he brings about the full knowledge of all things."
What is meant by this? It is that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, through the Prajñāpāramitā, knows how to attain what he desires to attain;
he knows that all form arises from being unobtainable, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise arise from being unobtainable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
How does the Tathāgata know that those who wish to attain this reach it through these causes?
From death to death, this is form (*rūpa*); from death to non-death, this is also form; from non-death to non-death, this is also form; neither having death nor not having death, this too is form.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—from death to death, these are also form; consciousness—from death to non-death, these are also form; consciousness—from non-death to non-death, these are also form; consciousness—which neither has death nor lacks death, these are also form.

To perceive that there is consciousness but no person and no self in the world is also form (*rūpa*). To perceive that there is no person but there is a self in the world is also form. To perceive that there is hope but no self in the world is also form.

To perceive neither hope nor the absence of hope and no self in the world is also form.
