To perceive that there is hope, a person, and a world with feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness is also form. To perceive no hope, no self, no world, and no consciousness is also form. To perceive neither the absence of hope nor the presence of hope and no self-consciousness is also form. To perceive both a self and a world and the absence of a world is also form.

"The self and the world are finite; this is also form (*rūpa*). The self and the world are both finite and infinite; this is also form. The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this is also form.
It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

That "the self and the world-consciousness are finite" is also form; that "the self and the world-consciousness are both finite and infinite" is also form; that "the self and the world-consciousness are neither finite nor infinite" is also form.
"That which is life is the body," this is also form; "that which is not life is not the body," this is also form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Tathāgata knows that those who wish to attain this will reach it by means of these causes.
What is meant by "the Tathāgata knows that those who wish to attain this will reach it by means of these causes"?
The Tathāgata knows that form is fundamentally non-existent; as he knows that form is fundamentally non-existent, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What is meant by "knowing consciousness"?
The essence of knowledge is fundamental non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*). What is this fundamental non-existence?
That which seeks to attain something is also fundamentally non-existent; even the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent, abiding as such through wisdom.
What is meant by "originally non-existent"?
The world, too, is originally non-existent.
What is it that is originally non-existent?

All dharmas are likewise originally non-existent. Just as all dharmas are originally non-existent, the path of the Srotāpanna is also originally non-existent; the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin is also originally non-existent; the path of the Anāgāmin is also originally non-existent; the path of the Arhat and the path of the Pratyekabuddha are also originally non-existent; even the Tathāgata is likewise originally non-existent. This single original non-existence is without distinction; there is nothing it does not penetrate, for it fully knows all things.
Subhūti, this Prajñāpāramitā is itself original non-existence (*prakṛti-niḥsvabhāva*).
It is by means of the Prajñāpāramitā that the Tathāgata has attained the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and illuminates and sustains the world; this is what is manifested.
By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata fully knows that the world is fundamentally non-existent and without differentiation.
Thus, Subhūti, because the Tathāgata fully knows fundamental non-existence, he is given the title "Buddha."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods, the fundamental non-existence is profoundly deep;
yet the Buddha and Bodhisattvas fully understand all such matters by themselves.”
Who would believe this?
Only those who have attained the path of Arhatship, or those who are Avaivartika (non-retrogressive), or Tathāgatas who have achieved perfect enlightenment (Abhisambuddha), are able to speak of it.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"That which is fundamentally non-existent has no time of exhaustion; that which is spoken by the Tathāgata likewise has no limit or end.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, together with ten thousand sons of the gods of the desire realm, and the Brahmakāyika devas, together with twenty thousand sons of the gods, approached the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side. Then the sons of the gods from the desire realm and the Brahma heavens addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“The Dharma taught by the God among Gods is exceedingly profound; how, then, is its characteristic to be formed?
The Buddha spoke to the devaputras, saying:
“Listen now to how its characteristic is formed.”
Having donned it, one is without conceptualization, without aspiration, and not born of birth-and-death; there is nothing possessed and no place of abiding—this is its characteristic mark.
As for that mark, it dwells like space; it is the mark of the dwelling place of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, which neither devas, asuras, nāgas, nor ghosts and spirits can shake or move.

Why is this? This mark cannot be made by the hand; form cannot create the mark, nor can sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness create it. This mark cannot be created by either a human or a non-human being.
The Buddha said to the sons of the gods,
"If one were to say that this emptiness has an agent, would you be able to believe it?
The sons of the gods replied to the Buddha:
"One does not believe that there is a creator of emptiness. Why is this?
Because there is no one capable of creating emptiness."
The Buddha said:
"So it is, O sons of the gods!

Those marks are eternally abiding; whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the marks remain as they were. Because they abide thus, and because the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Tathāgata is named 'the Thus-Come One who is fundamentally non-existent' (*mūla-abhāva-tathāgata*)."
The devaputras addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This mark is profound; it is from this that the Tathāgata has attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). All that the Tathāgata knows—the wisdom that is without obstruction—arises entirely from the Prajñāpāramitā; this is the treasury of the Buddha."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"The Tathāgata manifests and sustains the world by means of the Prajñāpāramitā.
It is thus, Subhūti!"

The Tathāgata reveres and serves this Dharma, thereby attaining his own realization; all of this proceeds from the *prajñāpāramitā*. For this reason, that which the Tathāgata reveres is the cause by which he attained Buddhahood; thus, it constitutes the repayment of his debt of gratitude.
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s repayment of gratitude?

It is because the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and became an *arhat samyaksaṃbuddha* through this very vehicle (*yāna*), and it is because he has become free from all attachments through this very vehicle that he manifests the repayment of gratitude.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows that dharmas have no agent;

for this reason he has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Nor is it through non-action that he has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; rather, it is for the sake of repaying his debt of gratitude to the Tathāgatas that he manifests the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has no expectations regarding any phenomena; all [his activities] proceed from the Prajñāpāramitā, and for this reason he manifests the sustenance of the world.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since all dharmas are unknowable and invisible, what does it mean to say that the Prajñāpāramitā emerges from the Tathāgata and manifests to sustain the world?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"That which is spoken of as all dharmas being unknowable and invisible means that all dharmas are entirely empty; for this reason they are unknowable.
All dharmas cannot be grasped or maintained; for this reason they cannot be seen."
All dharmas that are unknowable and invisible arise from the Prajñāpāramitā.
It is thus, Subhūti!

That all dharmas are unknowable and invisible is because they emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā so that the Tathāgata may attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment and manifest as the sustainer of the world.
Form is invisible, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also invisible; this is how the Prajñāpāramitā manifests and sustains the world.
Subhūti said: "What is meant, O God among Gods,
by 'form is invisible'?"
"What is meant by saying that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are 'unseeable'?
The Buddha said:

"One does not see consciousness arising with form as its condition; therefore, form is unseeable. Likewise, one does not see consciousness arising with feeling, perception, or mental formations as their conditions; therefore, consciousness is unseeable."

Just as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not seen, so too this world is not seen in its characteristics; nor is anything manifested in this world seen, for all of it arises from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
What is meant by this Prajñāpāramitā manifesting and sustaining the world?

That which is the concern for the world is itself empty; that which is the concern for the world is itself evanescent; that which is the concern for the world is itself quiescent; that which is the concern for the world is itself pure—this is what constitutes the manifestation of the world.
Chapter Eleven: The Incalculable. From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Dōgyō-kyō*, Chapter Eleven, "The Incalculable. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The ultimate perfection of the Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā) is an ultimate that is incalculable, an ultimate that is immeasurable, an ultimate that has no equal, and an ultimate that is boundless."
The Buddha said:

“The ultimate perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the ultimate that is incalculable, the ultimate that is immeasurable, the ultimate that has no equal, and the ultimate that is boundless. It is the peaceful perfection of wisdom, the incalculable ultimate; it is the omniscience (sarvajñatā) of the Tathāgata which requires no teacher. For this reason, the perfection of wisdom is the incalculable ultimate.”
What is the immeasurable perfection of wisdom?
The Tathāgata’s unconditioned, teacherless omniscience is immeasurable, inconceivable, and incomparable; therefore, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable and ultimate.
What is this perfection of wisdom that is secure and ultimate, with nothing equal to it?
Among the Tathāgatas, who could surpass it? Therefore, this perfection of wisdom is ultimately peerless.
What is the boundless and ultimate nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Because the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is boundless and without teacher, the *prajñāpāramitā* is therefore boundless and ultimate.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of the Tathāgata—being without a teacher—inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless?"
The Buddha said:

"Form, sensation, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are incalculable; all dharmas are also incalculable. Since all dharmas are ultimately without any dharma-nature, they are precisely incalculable therein.
Form, sensation, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are inconceivable; all dharmas are also immeasurable."
Form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are boundless, and all phenomena are likewise boundless;
the limits of form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness are utterly unattainable, and the limits of all phenomena are utterly unattainable.
For what reason are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness without limits, and why are all dharmas without limits?

Why is it that the limits of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended and have no point of exhaustion, and why the limits of all dharmas cannot be apprehended and have no point of exhaustion?
For what reason are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—indeed all phenomena—utterly unobtainable? What is the limit, the extent, or the temporal duration of this state?
The Buddha asked:
"Can the realm of empty space be calculated to its limit?
Subhūti replied:
"Emptiness is immeasurable and inexhaustible.
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas are immeasurable, incomparable, and without limit. For this reason, the dharma of the Tathāgata is likewise; it is immeasurable, incomparable, and without limit."
The Tathāgata’s arousal of the mind and his undertaking of training are incalculable, incomparable, and boundless; fundamentally, there is no mind and no thought.
For example, as space has neither mind nor thought, so too, were there a mind and thoughts, they would follow along with this cycle of birth and death without end.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is like space and has no boundaries; this Dharma, being like space, is incalculable. Thus it is said to be incalculable, incomparable, and boundless.

When the Buddha preached this sutra, five hundred bhikṣus and thirty bhikṣuṇīs all attained arhatship; sixty upāsakas and thirty upāsikās all attained the stage of srotāpanna; and thirty bodhisattvas all attained the joy of the dharma that is unborn, and all shall receive their prediction of enlightenment during this Bhadra Kalpa.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep, supremely great, peaceful, and ultimate.
The Buddha said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep, supremely peaceful, and ultimate; Sarvajñatā, the paths of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha—all emerge from this sutra.”

For example, regarding that which a Cakravartin king ought to accomplish, all his subordinate ministers, as well as the people of all his provinces and kingdoms, belong to the king; thus, he has nothing further to worry about.
Arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas, as well as all dharmas, all emerge from within the Prajñāpāramitā; they are all established by this sūtra.
The Buddha said:

"Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not grasped and not entered; the paths of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and sarvajña are not grasped and not entered."
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"What kind of sarvajñā does one not accept?
What kind of sarvajñā does one not enter?"
The Buddha said,
“What do you think, Subhūti?
Do you see the place where an Arhat enters?”
Subhūti said: “I do not see them, O God among Gods!
I do not see any such dharma as a place into which I have entered.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Subhūti! I, too, do not perceive any place where the Tathāgata enters."
"Just as I, the Tathāgata, have no place of entry, so too omniscience (sarvajñatā) has no place of entry.
The Devaputra of Desire and the Brahmā-devaputra both addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods!..."

The Prajñāpāramitā is profound and difficult to comprehend. Regarding the merit performed during the time of past Buddhas, if those people who hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā in this present age have faith in it—even if all the inhabitants of the trichiliocosm were to believe in everything they ought to do, and having so believed, were to practice for the duration of an entire kalpa—the merit of delighting in this profound Prajñāpāramitā for a single day would surpass that immeasurably. It would leave the former merit far behind.
The Buddha said to the devaputra of Desire and the devaputra of Brahma:

"Even if there were another person who, upon hearing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, attained realization and remained firm in their faith and joy for the duration of one kalpa, their merit would not equal that of these [latter] groups."

The devaputra of Desire and the devaputra of Brahmā both came forward, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Having walked back a great distance, they finally turned back and each returned to his own celestial realm, singing praises of the merits of the Buddha’s teaching.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are bodhisattvas who have faith in the profound Prajñāpāramitā, from where do they come to be born in this world?"

The Buddha said: "One who has such faith has no doubt in their mind; they feel neither aversion nor mere pleasure, but delights in hearing [the teaching]. They keep the teacher of the sūtra in mind and do not wish to be separated from them, just as a newborn calf never wishes to leave its mother. This bodhisattva has come from among human beings to be born here; having been a student in previous lives, they now encounter this profound *prajñāpāramitā* again and, with faith and joy, do not depart from it."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are bodhisattvas who at times return their merit, or those who come from other buddha-fields, or those who have made offerings to the Buddhas—would there be any such as these who come from there to be born in this interval?"
The Buddha said: "There are.

These bodhisattvas have made offerings to Buddhas in other buddha-fields and have come from there to be born in this world; by means of these merits, they attain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* right here."

Furthermore, if there are bodhisattvas who have come from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born in this world, or who have heard the wisdom within these profound sūtras from the Bodhisattva Maitreya and have now been born here, they maintain these merits and have now attained the profound Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who, during the time of a previous Buddha, heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* but did not inquire about its inner wisdom, and is now born in this world, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, his mind immediately becomes doubtful; he does not have faith or delight in it, and he does not inquire about its inner wisdom.
Why is this? Because they had doubts in previous lives.

Furthermore, if there are bodhisattvas who, having heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, questioned its central wisdom for one day, two days, three days, or up to seven days, and by virtue of these merits, now again attain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will always delight in hearing it, rejoice in questioning it, and faithfully accept it.

Furthermore, if there are bodhisattvas who at times wish to hear the *prajñāpāramitā* and at other times do not wish to hear it, their minds becoming distracted and repeatedly wavering like a scale that suddenly dips and suddenly rises—because such people have only recently begun their studies and have not yet set their resolve, they possess little faith and take no pleasure in attaining the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. They then become weary, unwilling to study, and abandon it; thus they will ultimately achieve nothing and fall into the paths of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Chapter Twelve: The Parable. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Practice of the Path*, Chapter Twelve, "The Parable," the Buddha said:
"Suppose, for example, a ship in the great ocean were suddenly wrecked; one would know that all those on board would fall into the water and drown, never being able to cross over to safety."

If there is a plank or a mast in that ship, and a strong person seizes it, they can mount it and, following the current, fall into deep water to escape; one knows that such a person will ultimately not drown and die in the water.
Why is this? Because they have used a wooden mast.

Although a bodhisattva possesses faith and joy, concentration and practice, and diligence, if they desire to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi but do not obtain the profound prajñā-pāramitā and do not study upāya-kauśalya (skillful means), that bodhisattva will fall into the path of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha.

If a bodhisattva possesses faith and aspiration, possesses the practice of meditative concentration, and possesses diligence, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and studied *upāyakauśalya*, this bodhisattva will never become weary or indolent along the way; they transcend the paths of the arhats and pratyekabuddhas and abide precisely within *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is, for example, like a person carrying an unbaked clay jar to fetch water; one knows that this jar cannot endure long and will break along the way.
Why? Because the jar has not yet been fully formed.

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses faith and joy, who practices concentration, and who possesses diligence, yet desires to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without obtaining the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and without learning in *upāya-kauśalya*, that bodhisattva will ultimately be unable to reach *sarvajñatā*; they will instead become weary midway and fall into the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.
It is like a person carrying a finished jar to fetch water; one knows that they will safely return with the water.
Why is this? Because the jar is already complete.

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses faith and joy, who practices meditative concentration, and who possesses diligence, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and who trains in *upāyakauśalya*—know that such a bodhisattva will never, midway, become weary, slacken, or cease, nor allow their mind to run wild, but will correctly advance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

It is like an old, dilapidated boat in the great ocean that has not been repaired; one pushes it into the water, places goods within it, and intends to sail to a destination. Knowing that this boat will ultimately never reach its goal and will instead break apart midway, causing the goods to be lost and scattered.

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses faith and joy, who practices meditative concentration, and who possesses diligence, yet desires to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without obtaining the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and without learning *upāya-kauśalya*, know that this bodhisattva will grow weary midway and lose the precious jewel, abandoning the great treasure and departing.
What constitutes a great treasure? It is the Buddha.
Such a bodhisattva would then fall midway into the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.

It is like a wise person who takes an old, dilapidated boat from the seashore, repairs it, pushes it into the water, places goods within it, and boards it with the intention of reaching a destination; knowing that this boat will not break apart mid-journey, he will certainly arrive at his intended place.

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses faith and joy, who possesses the practice of concentration, and who possesses diligence, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and who has learned the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the profound *prajñā-pāramitā*, one should know that this bodhisattva will never grow weary or indolent along the way, but will abide right within *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva possesses single-minded faith and delight, possesses the practice of meditative concentration, and possesses diligence; therefore, they will never again fall into the paths of the arhats or pratyekabuddhas, but proceed directly toward the gate of the Buddha.

Suppose there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, whose body was so frail from extreme old age that it could not find rest; if this person were afflicted by a feverish illness and confined to a bed, would they be able to rise and move about on their own?
Subhūti said: "No, it could not. Why is that?"
Because this person is extremely old and lacks strength, even if his illness were to be cured, he would still be unable to rise, sit, or walk about by himself.
The Buddha said:

“If a bodhisattva possesses faith and joy, possesses meditative practice, and possesses diligence, yet desires to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without learning the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, he will ultimately be unable to reach Buddhahood; he will instead rest midway and fall into the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.”
"Why is this? Because they have not attained the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) for studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:

"However, when a person has recovered from a wind-cold illness and their body is strong and healthy, and they wish to rise and walk, there may be two strong men, each supporting one flank and each holding one arm, who together support them as they walk slowly."
The man said to the sick person:
"Set your mind at ease and do not fear; I shall support you myself until we reach our destination, for it is my duty not to abandon you midway."
“Would such a person be able to reach the place they wish to go?
Subhūti replied:

“If a bodhisattva possesses faith and joy, possesses settled practice, and possesses diligence, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and if they train in *upāyakauśalya*, this bodhisattva will never become weary or slacken midway; they will be able to ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* therein.”
Chapter 13: On Discernment (*Vibhaṅga*) The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Course of Practice*, Chapter Thirteen: On Discernment. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva of the present age train in the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said:
"One should attend upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), one should delight in spiritual friends, and one should wholeheartedly follow the instructions of the Prajñāpāramitā."
What is following the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā?

It is that whatever this bodhisattva gives in alms, he should give it for the sake of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and must not become attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) are without attachment.

If one maintains morality, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom, one should maintain these for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; do not become attached to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because in sarvajñā (all-knowledge) there is no attachment, and one does not obtain the joy of the path of the arhat or pratyekabuddha.
It is in this way that the bodhisattva of the present gradually enters into the prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti said: "The bodhisattva undergoes hardships, desiring to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
“The Bodhisattva undergoes hardships with humility; he brings peace and security to the world, acting as its refuge, its shelter, its crossing, its platform, and its guide.”
What is meant by the Bodhisattva being a protector of the world?
To protect, instruct, and deliver all beings from the hardships of birth and death is to be a protector of the world.
What is meant by being a refuge for the world?
To deliver all beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death—this is what constitutes a refuge for the world.
What is the shelter for the world?
When a Bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieves the title of *tathāgata*, he preaches the sūtras for the sake of the world without attachment; this is the shelter for the world.
What is meant by "non-attachment"?

Form is neither attached to nor bound; this form has no place from which it arises and no place from which it ceases. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise. All phenomena are thus neither attached to nor bound.
What is the worldly transcendence?
It is the transcendence of form as non-form; it is the transcendence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as non-consciousness. This transcendence constitutes all dharmas.
Subhūti said: "As the Buddha has taught, one attains unexcelled perfect enlightenment by means of the deliverance of all dharmas.
For what reason?"
"Is there nothing to which he is attached?
The Buddha said, "It is so.

A Bodhisattva who is without attachment undergoes diligent toil and remains tireless in his mindfulness of the Dharma. Having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he preaches the sutras; this, too, is the deliverance of the world."

What is the "worldly platform"? It is like a platform in the water, which the water flows around on both sides. Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—past, future, and present—are severed on both sides. When these are thus severed, all dharmas are also severed. If all dharmas are severed, this is concentration; this is the ambrosia; this is *nirvāṇa*. When a bodhisattva contemplates the Dharma without slackening and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is called the worldly platform.

What is meant by being a guide for the world? When a Bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he teaches that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; he teaches that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty. These [phenomena] come from nowhere and go nowhere. All phenomena are empty; all phenomena are without conceptualization; all phenomena have no location; all phenomena have no consciousness; all phenomena have no source of arising. All phenomena are empty; all phenomena are like dreams; all phenomena are like a single [reality]; all phenomena are like illusions; all phenomena are without limit; all phenomena are without suchness—they are all equal and without distinction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound; who will be able to fully comprehend it?
The Buddha said:

“Bodhisattvas have sought this for a very long time; from the time they first performed meritorious deeds under past Buddhas until now, only such persons as these can truly understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Subhūti asked: "What is meant by 'having sought it for a very long time'?
The Buddha said:
"When one is detached from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, such that they no longer exist, only then does one clearly understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti said: "Is this bodhisattva a guide for the world?"
The Buddha said:
"In this way, a bodhisattva attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and acts as a guide for incalculable, asaṃkhyeya beings. Subhūti said:
“Does a bodhisattva undergo great hardship because this constitutes the donning of the great armor (*mahāsaṃnāhasaṃnaddha*),
or because he brings immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of people to parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha said:

"In this way, the Bodhisattva undergoes austerity; this is the great *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha* (donning of the armor). Therefore, it is the unbound *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unbound; nor is there binding with respect to Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, nor with respect to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). All dharmas are unbound; therefore, it is called the *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*."
Subhūti said: “A bodhisattva seeking the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should not seek it in three places.
The Buddha said:
"For what reason should a bodhisattva seeking the profound *prajñāpāramitā* not seek it in three places?

Subhūti replied: "The *prajñāpāramitā* is extremely profound; it neither has a protector nor lacks a protector. From within the *prajñāpāramitā*, there are no dharmas that emerge. To protect the *prajñāpāramitā* is to protect emptiness; to protect the *prajñāpāramitā* is to protect all dharmas; to protect the *prajñāpāramitā* is to protect non-existence; to protect the *prajñāpāramitā* is to protect non-attachment."

The Buddha said: "One who dwells within the *prajñāpāramitā* should be known as an *avaivartika* bodhisattva. Within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they have no attachment or clinging; they never follow the words of others nor believe in other paths. Their minds are neither terrified nor indolent. Having questioned the wisdom within this profound sutra from Buddhas of the past, now that they hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds continue to be without fear or indolence."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, does not feel fear or dread and remains free from indolence, by what causes and conditions should they contemplate and observe within this prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said:
“To direct the mind toward sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is what constitutes the contemplation of the prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti said:
"What is meant by 'directing the mind toward sarvajñatā'?
The Buddha said:
"Directing the mind toward emptiness is what constitutes contemplating sarvajñatā; contemplating sarvajñatā is itself non-contemplation."
The incalculable *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is like how the incalculable form (*rūpa*) is non-form;
it is like how the incalculable feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are non-consciousness. It neither enters nor exits;
it is neither attained nor known; it is neither possessing knowledge nor lacking knowledge; and it is neither produced nor...
There is nothing that can be destroyed, nor is there anything that acts; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
it is neither seen nor located. Thus, emptiness is immeasurable, and *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is incalculable;
one cannot calculate that there is anyone who acts as a Buddha, nor anyone who attains Buddhahood. There is none.
One who attains Buddhahood does so not from within form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does one attain Buddhahood through the perfection of giving,
the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor,
the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.
The devaputra of Desire and the devaputra of Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound; it is difficult to comprehend, difficult to understand, and difficult to know.
The Buddha said to the various devaputras:
“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is extremely deep; it is difficult to comprehend, difficult to understand, and difficult to know.

The Tathāgata’s peace and profundity lie in this sutra: it fully knows that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is without action, and that in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is no such thing as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This sutra is as profound as space, with nothing equal to it; like all dharmas, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.”
The devaputras of the Desire Realm, the devaputras of the Brahma Realm, and others addressed the Buddha, saying:

"It is rare for people of the world to have faith in such a profound sutra as this. Since worldly people are attached to all that they desire, we pray that you will preach this profound sutra out of compassion for them."
The Buddha said:
"It is so, O sons of the gods!

It is rare for people of the world to have faith in such a profound sūtra. Because they are attached to whatever they desire, it is out of compassion for these people of the world that I shall preach this profound sūtra."
Chapter 14: On Original Non-existence (*Mūlapratiṣṭhāna*) In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Course of Practice*, Chapter Fourteen:

On Original Non-existence. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “All dharmas follow in succession without attachment; all dharmas are without conceptualization, like space. This sūtra has no place from which it arises; when one searches for all dharmas, they cannot be apprehended.”
The devaputra of Desire and the devaputra of Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The disciple Subhūti has spoken thus; the teaching of the Tathāgata speaks only of the wisdom of emptiness.”
The Buddha said,
"So it is, O sons of the gods!
Follow the teaching of the Tathāgata."
The devaputras asked the Buddha:
"What is called the teaching of the Tathāgata?
Is that which is in accordance with the dharma—being without any place of origination—the following of the Tathāgata’s teaching?"
The Buddha said:
"So it is, O sons of the gods!
All dharmas are without origin; this is to follow the teaching of the Tathāgata."
To follow the teaching of the Tathāgata is to realize that all things are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*). This fundamental non-existence neither comes from anywhere nor goes anywhere.
The Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent, and all phenomena (*dharmas*) are also fundamentally non-existent;
all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, and the Tathāgata is also fundamentally non-existent. There is no difference between this fundamental non-existence and suchness (*tathatā*).

Subhūti follows original non-existence (*tathatā*); this is the original non-existence of the Tathāgata. The original non-existence of the Tathāgata abides thus. Subhūti abides following the teaching of the Tathāgata; the original non-existence of the Tathāgata is without distinction, for original non-existence is without distinction. All dharmas are without distinction, without distinction.
The Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent and free from all obstructions; all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and free from all obstructions.
The Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent, and all dharmas are fundamentally unobstructed; these fundamental non-existences are equal as one, with no difference in their fundamental non-existence.
There is no agent; all things are fundamentally non-existent, and even this fundamental non-existence is itself non-existent.
Such is the fundamental non-existence of the Tathāgata: it is neither destroyed nor does it decay, for all dharmas are ungraspable.

Subhūti follows the teachings of all dharmas: the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent, all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; they are equal and without distinction, for within the true dharma, they are fundamentally non-existent.
Subhūti follows the teaching of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent, having no past, future, or present, for all dharmas are fundamentally without past, future, or present.

Subhūti follows the teaching of the Tathāgata: the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent; the past is fundamentally non-existent; the future is fundamentally non-existent; and the present Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent. These are equal and without distinction; this equality and lack of distinction is true fundamental non-existence.
When the Bodhisattva attained this True Non-arising (bhūtatathatā), which is called "Tathāgata," the earth shook in six ways.
The Tathāgata preached Non-arising, and Subhūti followed the teaching of the Tathāgata.

Subhūti does not grasp at form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness; he does not grasp at the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha. In this way, Subhūti follows the teaching of the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra said:
"This fundamental non-arising is profound, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
“This fundamental non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*) is profound, most profound!

When this fundamental non-existence was being taught, two hundred bhikṣus all attained arhatship; five hundred bhikṣuṇīs all attained the stage of srotāpanna; five hundred devas and humans all realized the joy of the dharma of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and sixty newly initiated bodhisattvas standing therein all attained the path of arhatship.

The Buddha said: “These sixty bodhisattvas, in past lives, each made offerings to five hundred buddhas; they practiced giving seeking form, and they practiced precepts, patience, and diligence seeking form. They practiced dhyāna without knowing emptiness or being detached from emptiness, and they did not attain the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*. Now they have all taken the path of the arhat. There is a path for bodhisattvas that attains emptiness, attains the formless, and attains wishlessness; yet these bodhisattvas, failing to attain the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, have midway attained the path of the arhat and will no longer return.”

Suppose there were a great bird, its body eight thousand li or twenty thousand li long, yet it had no wings; it wished to throw itself down from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to reach the ground of Jambudvīpa.
“Before it has reached its destination, if this bird regrets its course and wishes to return halfway to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
would it be able to return? Śāriputra replied, “It could not return.”
The Buddha said,
"If this bird were to descend from here to the ground of Jambudvīpa, could it possibly do so without its body suffering pain?"
Śāriputra said, "It could not;
as this bird descends, its body would inevitably suffer pain, and it would either faint in extreme agony or die. Why is this?"
“His body will become large and tall, and he will have no wings.
The Buddha said:
“Even if this bodhisattva, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, practices giving in pursuit of form, maintains the precepts, and...”
If a bodhisattva practices patience and exerts diligence in the pursuit of form, yet does not enter emptiness through dhyāna, and fails to attain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*,
they may give rise to the mind desiring to seek the Buddha-way and intend to become a Buddha for all beings,
only to attain the path of an arhat or pratyekabuddha midway; such a bodhisattva, regarding the past...
Regarding the precepts, diligence, samādhi, and wisdom maintained by the Buddhas of the future and the present,
and having heard of the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they all conceive thoughts seeking after form; this constitutes not maintaining the precepts,
diligence, samādhi, and wisdom of the Tathāgata, and failing to understand omniscience, but merely conceptualizing it as such.
Upon hearing this sound, they immediately desired to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through it;
however, they were unable to do so, and instead attained the path of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha midway.
"Why is this? Because they have not attained the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra said:

“As the Buddha has taught, because the bodhisattva Smṛtimatī lacked the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), she attained the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha. If there is a bodhisattva who, having adorned themselves with the requisites for awakening, desires to attain anuttarasamyaksambodhi, they should diligently study the perfection of wisdom and skillful means.”
The devaputra of Desire and the devaputra of Brahma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to comprehend, difficult to understand, and difficult to know; it is difficult to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi when one seeks it.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to comprehend, difficult to understand, and difficult to know. As I contemplate the wisdom within it, I think that attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi would be easy.”

Why is this? Since there is nothing that exists, from what could one obtain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? All dharmas are empty; though one searches for them, they are utterly unobtainable, yet one shall attain *abhisambodhi*.
Seeking the Dharma, one finds nothing to be obtained; there is no one who performs the act of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there anyone who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If there are those who hear that all dharmas are empty, they will find it easy to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"According to what Subhūti has said, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain."
Why is this? Emptiness does not think, "I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This dharma of emptiness would be easy to obtain. Why is this?
“Just as all the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have attained it.
Subhūti said: “How so, Śāriputra?”
"Is it attained by means of form?
No. Is it attained by means of dharmas apart from form?"
"No. Have they attained feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness? "No."
"Is it possible to attain that which form is fundamentally non-existent? No.
Is it possible to attain a dharma that form is fundamentally non-existent?"
"No. Are sensation, perception, mental formations, volitional formations, and consciousness fundamentally non-existent such that they could ever be attained? No."
Apart from consciousness, can one attain that which is fundamentally non-existent?
No. Can one cause that which is fundamentally non-existent to be attained? No.
"No. Apart from the fundamental [nature], is there any dharma that can attain [it]? No."
"If these dharmas are unattainable, what dharma is there that can be attained?
Śāriputra said: "According to the Dharma as taught by Subhūti, there is no bodhisattva who attains it."

Regarding the three types of virtuous persons spoken of by the Buddha—those who seek arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and buddhahood—these three do not calculate themselves as three; as Subhūti has said, they constitute but a single path.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra:
“Subhūti speaks of a single path; you should question him.
Then Śāriputra addressed Subhūti:
"I ask this because of the single path spoken of by Subhūti.
Subhūti replied, "How so?
Within that which is fundamentally non-existent, do you perceive three paths?"
Śāriputra said,
"I do not see them. Why is this?"
"Within original non-existence, these three things cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti said, "Can even a single thing be apprehended within original non-existence?"
"No. How could one obtain even a single path within that which is fundamentally non-existent? No."
Since these truths are ultimately unattainable, it is for this reason that the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha are further mentioned.
It is spoken thus because the Path is fundamentally non-existent and without distinction.
"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing that the mind is fundamentally non-existent, remains free from indolence, this bodhisattva shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha said:
"What Subhūti has spoken is entirely sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; it is through this power that he is enabled to speak thus."
"When a Bodhisattva hears that all things are fundamentally non-existent, equal, and without distinction, their mind does not become indolent, and they shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
Śāriputra asked:
"In what way does a Bodhisattva accomplish Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What constitutes the accomplishment of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:

“Within the impartial regard for all people, one should engage them in conversation with a virtuous mind; one must not harbor harmful intentions, but should always speak with a heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), free from anger. One should always maintain a benevolent and equanimous mind; a bodhisattva should abide in this manner.”
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Five;
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
15. Chapter on the Avaivartika: The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Fifteen, on the Avaivartika.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way should an avaivartika bodhisattva be compared?”
How should one observe their conduct?
How should one examine them?
And how can one know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:

"An avaivartika bodhisattva is like one who has attained dhyāna and is unshakable—whether in the stage of an arhat, the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or the stage of a buddha. This stage of a buddha is as it is from the beginning, ultimately never moving."
The Buddha taught that all things are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*); hearing this, one does not say it is wrong.

Emptiness is this fundamental non-existence; entering into fundamental non-existence, one regards what is fundamentally non-existent as being like fundamental non-existence, and likewise does not say it is wrong.

Entering thus into this state, one enters by means of hearing that this is fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*). When the mind turns toward other objects of hearing, it ultimately harbors no doubt; it neither asserts "it is" nor denies "it is not. In this way, fundamental non-existence abides as fundamental non-existence.
What he speaks is not frivolous; what he says does not concern other matters, but only what is correct for others. He does not observe the deeds performed by others.
By these comparisons and by these signs of conduct being fully perfected, one knows him to be an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.

An avaivartika never mimics the physical appearance or facial features of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; he does not perform sacrifices or prostrate before deities, nor does he offer flowers or incense to deities, nor does he instruct others to do so.

One shall not be born in an evil realm, nor take birth as a woman; one should uphold the ten precepts—abstaining from killing, theft, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, intoxicants, harsh words, false speech, and frivolous talk, and refraining from envy, anger, and reviling. One shall not harbor doubt nor teach others to do so. Having personally upheld the ten precepts without doubt, one further teaches others to observe them. One protects the ten precepts even within dreams, and likewise beholds the ten precepts face-to-face within dreams.

The mind of an avaivartika studies all dharmas; he preaches the sutras for the sake of the people of the world so that they may abide in peace and security, upholds and transmits the profound sutras, and causes them to attain and dwell in merit. He ensures that all fulfill their vows to obtain the sutras, so that they may utilize them to attain and dwell in merit.

When an avaivartika bodhisattva hears the exposition of profound sutras, they never doubt; they do not say they do not believe, nor do they feel fear. Their speech is gentle, subtle, and most profound.

Whether sleeping, walking, entering, or exiting, his mind is settled in concentration and free from distraction; he raises his feet slowly when treading upon the ground, and his glances are composed and steady.
His garments and robes are clean and pure, free from dust and filth, and his body is devoid of the eighty kinds of parasites.
"As all merits gradually increase and become full, one receives them all with an extremely pure mind; those merits transcend the world.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "In what way is the bodhisattva’s mind pure?"
"How can this be known?
The Buddha said:

"The merit performed by this bodhisattva increases ever more; his mind is supremely exalted, sovereign, and free from all obstructions, such that he fully attains all merits. This mind is exceedingly pure, its purity surpassing even that of the paths of the arhats and pratyekabuddhas."
Thus, when those who come to make offerings to an avaivartika bodhisattva do so, he does not indulge in the joy of receiving them, being entirely free from stinginess and greed.
When preaching profound sutras, he never experiences weariness or exhaustion therein.
Deeply penetrating into wisdom, if there are others who wish to inquire about profound sutras, they should take up this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and explain it for them;
if there are matters that other paths cannot correctly resolve, they should take up this profound *prajñāpāramitā* to rectify them;
and regarding all phenomena arising from within this sutra, they should speak to others using the characteristics of impermanence.
That which cannot be understood through any of the worldly scriptures, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is maintained as the means to explain it.

For this reason, Māra the Wicked comes to where this bodhisattva is and, standing at the side, conjures eight great hells (*niraya*). Within each of these hells, he conjures several hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, and then points them out, saying:
"These individuals were all *avaivartika* bodhisattvas who received their prediction from the Buddha; yet now they have all fallen into the hells."
The Buddha grants them [the prediction], though they are but those destined for hell.
Suppose there were a bodhisattva who has received the prediction of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), yet he should quickly utter words of regret, saying:
"I am not an *avaivartika*."
“If one repents, saying ‘It was so,’ then one shall no longer fall into the hells, but shall instead be born in the heavens.
The Buddha said,
“If the mind of such a bodhisattva does not waver or change, he is an avaivartika.”
The Wicked Māra again transformed himself into the Bodhisattva’s teacher; wearing the same robes, he went to where the Bodhisattva was and spoke deceptively:
"All that you previously heard and received from me, you must now completely abandon; none of it is fit for use."
If you repent your transgression, you must do so with swift remorse.
If you follow my words, I shall come every day to inquire after your health; if you do not heed my words, I shall never come to visit you again.
"If you do not wish to speak of this matter again, I no longer wish to hear it; therefore, I say that all these things were not spoken by the Buddha, but are merely external matters.
You should now once more accept what I say: everything I have spoken is the word of the Buddha."
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing these words, has a wavering mind, they have not received the prediction from past Buddhas; they have not yet ascended to the stage of a bodhisattva, nor do they abide on the level of *avaivartika*."
If this bodhisattva’s mind remains unshakable and does not waver, one should know that this is brought about by the emptiness of this profound sutra.
Engaging in such reflection, he will ultimately not believe the words of others.

It is, for example, like a bhikṣu who has attained arhatship and no longer follows the words of others, clearly seeing all the realizations within the sūtras; this is brought about by emptiness and can never be shaken. Just as with the dharmas contemplated on the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha, one can never again regress.
This bodhisattva dwells in the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), abiding correctly and facing the gateway of the Buddha, never again to turn back; this is called ultimate transcendence.
By means of these analogies and by means of these characteristics and practices being fully complete, one knows this to be an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there may be a corrupt Māra who transforms himself into another person and goes to where the bodhisattva is, saying these words:
"That which you seek involves only toil and suffering; it is not the seeking of the Buddha-dharma."
If you have borne this toil and hardship in vain, for what purpose did you undergo such difficult labor?
Having been in the evil realms for a very long time, you have only just now attained human form; should you not reflect upon this, and should you not feel weary and disillusioned with it?
"Where else could one seek this body again?
Why did you not earlier attain the path of Arhatship; what use is the Buddha for seeking such a thing?
If the mind of this bodhisattva does not waver or change upon hearing these words, know that he is an avaivartika (non-retrogressive).
The evil Māra was unable to move him or cause him to abandon his resolve, so he employed further expedients, manifesting as several bodhisattvas who stood by his side, pointing them out and saying:
"Do you see these or not?"

These were all bodhisattvas who had made offerings to buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, providing them fully with robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines; they had received and practiced the Dharma from those buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, inquiring after wisdom, acting according to what was to be done, abiding in accordance with the Dharma, and seeking in accordance with the Dharma. They all entered into this practice, training in this way, receiving it in this way, and acting in this way, yet even by all of this, they were still unable to attain Buddhahood.
"If you have only recently begun your training, by what cause could you possibly attain Buddhahood?
When the Bodhisattva hears these words and his mind does not waver, the evil Māra again departs and, not far away, transforms himself into various bhikṣus and shows them to him, saying:

"These are all arhats who, in past lives, all sought the path of a bodhisattva but were unable to attain Buddhahood; they have now all attained arhatship. How then could bhikṣus such as these ever attain Buddhahood?"
"If the Bodhisattva hears these words and his mind does not waver or shift, he should recognize this as the work of Māra.
The Buddha said:

"One who trains in this way, seeks in this way, and practices in this way, abiding within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with a mind that does not waver or shift—and who is thus endowed with such signs and conduct—should be known as an *avaivartika* (one who is non-retrogressive)."
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should train in this way and seek in this way; they should protect these teachings and receive the Buddha's instruction, and should mindfully practice in other regions."
Hearing such words from Māra, his mind did not waver or shift; he was unshakable, realizing that this was the work of Māra.
The Bodhisattva trains in this way, thinking: "If one does not attain Buddhahood, then the words of the Buddha must be otherwise."
The Buddha’s word is never deceptive.
Māra the Wicked again went to where the Bodhisattva was and spoke these deceitful and vexing words:
"The Buddha is like space; this sutra has no boundaries and no limit can be found. I already know all within this sutra—it is nothing but emptiness."
If you undergo diligent toil within this [teaching], or do not, you should recognize that Māra is acting for this purpose;
Māra has fabricated this sūtra—how could one wish to become a Buddha through it?

"This is not what was taught by the Buddha. The Bodhisattva should clearly perceive and know that this is the work of Māra. When a Bodhisattva practices the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas and samādhis, they transcend the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) and do not follow or record these four dhyānas. These dhyāna-practiced samādhis are for the sake of transcending ordinary people; because they enter into the midst of desire, they are merely dhyāna-samādhis. Such a Bodhisattva never follows the teachings of dhyāna, for their merit far surpasses that of the dhyānas.
He does not rejoice when his name is praised by others, nor does he feel sorrow when it is not praised; his mind remains forever undisturbed, as he constantly keeps in mind the people of the world.
He is skillful in his movements, whether walking, sitting, or rising; he always maintains an upright mind and correct resolve, with little lustful intent.
When at home, upon seeing women, his heart finds no pleasure or joy, and he is constantly filled with a sense of dread.

When engaging with women, one should reflect that their impure secretions are foul-smelling and unclean; this is not my Dharma. For the remainder of my life, I shall no longer associate with them, for I must escape from within these foul secretions.
It is as if there were a person traveling through a vast wilderness, fearing bandits, who thinks to himself:
"When shall I escape from this perilous path?"
One should abandon and distance oneself from such lewdness, fearing it as if walking through a vast, desolate wilderness, and one must not speak of that person’s faults. Why is this?
Because all those in the world desire to be made peaceful and secure.
The Buddha said:
"Such a bodhisattva attains this through the perfection of merit; all of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which causes them to form such a thought."

This Bodhisattva is followed by the Vaiśravaṇas who transform themselves into various spirits and ghosts, yet they do not dare to approach or draw near him. The Bodhisattva never loses his resolve, his mind does not give rise to delusions, and his body remains complete and free from sores or leprosy; he is exceedingly heroic and fierce, and he never seduces the wives of others.

If there are those who practice healing arts, incantations, or the administration of medicines, one does not perform these oneself, nor does one instruct others to do so; furthermore, upon seeing others performing them, one’s heart feels no joy.
They never speak of men or women as being for the sake of sexual desire, nor do they speak of unrighteous matters, nor are they reborn in evil realms.
By these comparisons, by these signs, and by the fulfillment of their conduct, one knows them to be irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattvas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason is a bodhisattva called ‘avaivartika’ (non-retrogressive)?
The Buddha said:

“A Bodhisattva does not engage in affairs with kings, nor with people in secular cities, fortresses, or villages; he does not engage in affairs with thieves, nor with military commanders or weapons; he does not engage in affairs with men or women; he does not engage in affairs with other practitioners, nor with those who perform sacrifices to spirits, nor with wine, meat, or grain-based foods; he does not engage in affairs with perfumes, incense, silks, profit-seeking enterprises, or frivolous amusements; he does not engage in affairs regarding the ocean or various sensual desires; he does not engage in affairs with those who are base, malicious, ungrateful, or fond of quarreling and causing discord. Rather, he engages only in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, never departing from it in mind, for *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is always present within it.”
They do not fail to aspire to always practice the Middle Way with rectitude, nor is there a time when they do not do so.

They constantly praise those who are virtuous and good as supreme; they always follow spiritual friends and do not associate with evil associates; they constantly seek the Buddha-dharma, aspiring to be born in the Buddha-fields of other directions.
For this reason, they constantly see the Buddha and make offerings to him.

From the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the realm of space, they come from those places to be born in the Central Land; they are always born among virtuous and wise people, into families that are skilled in discourse and well-versed in the scriptures.
He never takes pleasure in worldly affairs; throughout his life he does not violate the law; he is always born in great kingdoms and is never born in the borderlands.

Because he is endowed with these analogies and these marks of conduct, for this reason he is called an *avaivartika* bodhisattva. Yet he never says, "I am an *avaivartika*," nor does he say, "I am not," nor does he doubt that he is not on the stage of an *avaivartika*, nor does he say, "I am on the stage of an *avaivartika*."

It is as if there were a person who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; while remaining in that stage, they never doubt the works of Māra. As soon as such thoughts arise, they immediately recognize them; though Māra gradually approaches, he is not permitted to follow.
In the stage of the avaivartika, one never doubts nor becomes indolent.

It is like a person who commits a heinous crime; throughout their entire life, their mind can never be turned to do good or to cease thinking of evil, for that evil intent persists until death without ceasing.

This bodhisattva dwells in the center of correctness and abides on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*); his mind cannot be moved, and throughout the ten directions, none can ever again turn his mind away. Possessing his own ground of the Way, he never doubts that there are no arhats or pratyekabuddhas; his mind does not find it difficult to recollect the Buddha; his mind is vast and limitless, dwelling securely and firmly in that stage, such that no one is able to subdue him.
Abiding in this way, there is no one more wise than such a person.
For this reason, Māra the Evil One is filled with great sorrow and distress, saying:
"The mind of this bodhisattva is as hard as steel and cannot be turned."
He then again assumed the form of a Buddha and went to speak to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Why do you not realize the fruit of Arhatship here?

If you have not yet received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and if you do not possess these analogies or these signs—yet it is by means of these analogies and these signs that a Bodhisattva fulfills his practice—and even with such [fulfillment], one still does not attain Buddhahood."
"By what cause would one obtain it?
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva hears these words of Māra and their mind remains unmoved, this bodhisattva has received a prediction from a past Tathāgata and has already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, they recognize that this is Māra who has come in the form of a Buddha to speak, and they know: 'This is not a Buddha; it is merely Māra.'"
"You may wish to cause my mind to waver, but my mind cannot be moved.
The Buddha said:

"This Bodhisattva whose mind cannot be moved or turned back has received a prediction from a Tathāgata of the past; he has already been granted the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and abides on the stage of Avaivartika."

Why is this? Because they are endowed with these analogies, these marks, and these practices, one knows that these *avaivartika* bodhisattvas have fully attained the Dharma and practice with perfect rectitude; they should, for the sake of the Dharma, not begrudge their own bodies or lives. These bodhisattvas have received and mastered all dharmas, and they maintain and protect all the teachings of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
For this reason, one should not begrudge one's own body or life, never being indolent and never growing weary.
When the Tathāgata and his disciples preach the sūtras, one’s mind shall never harbor doubt, nor shall one ever say that it was not spoken by the Buddha.
Upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds never harbor doubt, nor do they say it is not so.
Such a bodhisattva attains the joy of the dharma of non-arising; abiding therein and maintaining this, they are fully endowed with all merits.
"By means of these analogies and by means of these characteristics and practices being fully perfected, one is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
Chapter 16: The Laywoman Dakkhiṇā From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter on the Laywoman Dakkhiṇā, the Sixteenth. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"An *avaivartika* bodhisattva arises from supreme great merit; he constantly expounds the profound teachings for bodhisattvas and enters into the profound."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
If one leads bodhisattvas inward to enter the profound, what constitutes the profound?
Emptiness is the profound; so too are signlessness, wishlessness, and the absence of consciousness; that which is neither arising nor ceasing—Nirvana—is the limit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Nirvāṇa is the limit; it is not among all dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas are profound; form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profound.
In what way are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness profound?"
"Just as they are originally non-existent, so too form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are originally non-existent;
for this reason, they are profoundly deep.
Subhūti said, "It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!"
"Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—when these delusions are eliminated, that is Nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:

"One should contemplate and keep in mind that which is profoundly deep and in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā; one should train by abiding in this manner according to the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā. If a bodhisattva practices accordingly and contemplates as taught therein for even a single day, how many kalpas of birth and death will that bodhisattva cast behind?"

For example, suppose there is a lecherous man who has made an appointment with a beautiful woman whom he deeply loves; if that woman, being unable to act of her own accord, misses the appointment and does not arrive, would that man not still keep her in his thoughts?
Subhūti said: “That person has thoughts;
they think of reaching him, desiring to see him, to sit or rise with him, to dwell together with him, and to converse with him.
The Buddha said:
“Before that person has arrived, how many thoughts and mental activities could arise?
Subhūti replied,
“Those thoughts would be very many, indeed very many!”
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva contemplates the profound *prajñāpāramitā* such that their mind does not waver for even a single day, they will retrogress from birth and death for as many eons."

When a bodhisattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, if they contemplate it according to its instructions and as it is taught, and practice accordingly for even a single day, they thereby eliminate evils and eradicate transgressions.

If there were another bodhisattva who remained far removed from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and practiced giving for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the merit of this latter bodhisattva would not equal that of the former bodhisattva who follows the teachings of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a single day; the merit of the latter surpasses the former.

Furthermore, if there were another bodhisattva whose lifespan lasted for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and who, while maintaining all the aforementioned acts of giving, offered them to stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas, yet did not obtain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
and if there were yet another bodhisattva who practiced in accordance with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to its teaching, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former.
Furthermore, suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, practiced giving as previously described and was fully endowed with the precepts;
yet if there were another bodhisattva who sought the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and preached the sūtras arising from mindfulness, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former.

Furthermore, if there is another bodhisattva who practices the giving of the sutra, their merit becomes even more superior, and they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Because this bodhisattva, while practicing the giving of the sutra, has deeply entered into it and follows its teachings, their merit surpasses that of the former;
whereas if there is another bodhisattva who gives the sutra as a gift but does not deeply enter into it, they do not even come close to matching it.

Furthermore, if there is another bodhisattva who, upholding this sutra, practices giving and penetrates deeply into its meaning, never being separated from it even for a moment, and is protected by the Prajñāpāramitā, their merit will be exceedingly great, indeed exceedingly great.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Between that which is cognized and that which is characterized by attachment, which of these two possesses greater merit?
The Buddha said:

“Regarding what is known by a bodhisattva: if one seeks the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, delights in emptiness, delights in non-existence, delights in exhaustion, and delights in impermanence—recalling these constitutes not being separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*. In this way, a bodhisattva attains incalculable, asankhyeya merits.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the difference between ‘incalculable’ (*asaṃkhyeya*) and ‘immeasurable’ (*aprameya*)?
The Buddha said:
" 'Asaṃkhyeya' means that its number cannot be exhausted;
'incalculable' means it cannot be measured or calculated, such that its limits or boundaries can never be found."
"Therefore, they are incalculable *asaṃkhyeya*. Subhūti said:
"The Buddha has taught that 'incalculable' applies to form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Regarding what you have asked, for what reason are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness uncountable and immeasurable?"
Subhūti asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'immeasurable'?
The Buddha said:
"If one calculates it in terms of emptiness, it is immeasurable; if one calculates it in terms of signlessness and wishlessness, it is likewise immeasurable.
Subhūti said: "It is so;
calculated as empty, this dharma is immeasurable."
The Buddha said,
"Why do you say that I have not always spoken of the emptiness of all dharmas? Subhūti replied:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is entirely empty.
The Buddha said, "All dharmas are entirely empty; they are inexhaustible and incalculable."
In the sutras there are no individual wisdoms and no individual differences; the Tathāgata merely speaks through differentiation. Emptiness is inexhaustible and immeasurable.

Whether it be this perception, this vow, this consciousness, this birth, this desire, this cessation, or this nirvāṇa—he teaches according to what each finds pleasing. He provides these explanations, manifests these demonstrations, and offers these instructions; such is that which the Tathāgata has spoken.
Subhūti said: "It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!
The sūtra is fundamentally empty."
"How is it that you further preach this sutra in mid-air, a sutra that cannot be grasped?
As I understand the Buddha's words, all dharmas cannot be grasped.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! All dharmas are unattainable.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! All dharmas are simply unattainable emptiness;
this is what is meant by 'unattainable. Subhūti said:
“As the Buddha has taught that what is fundamentally non-existent cannot be attained, I pray that you explain whether this unattainable wisdom increases or decreases.
The Buddha said, “No.”
Subhūti said:

"If there were an unattainable wisdom that increased or decreased, then the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā would increase or decrease; yet they neither increase nor decrease."
If the perfections do not increase, for what cause would a bodhisattva draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
By what condition would they attain abhisaṃbodhi?
If the perfections were not diminished, for what reason would a bodhisattva draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and by what cause would they draw near to the seat of *abhisambuddha*?

The Buddha said: "This wisdom that is beyond attainment neither increases nor decreases. If a bodhisattva seeks the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and maintains it, such a bodhisattva, through this skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), does not think of the *dānapāramitā* as increasing, nor does he think of it as decreasing. Furthermore, he reflects thus: 'It is merely a name for the thought of giving that constitutes the *dānapāramitā*. Taking these merits and dedicating them, he brings about *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.'"

When giving in this manner, and likewise with the *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, and *dhyānapāramitā*, if a bodhisattva seeking the *prajñāpāramitā* maintains it and attains *upāyakauśalya*, they do not conceive of the *prajñāpāramitā* as having increase or decrease; it is merely called the *prajñāpāramitā*. Seeking it and maintaining it, they give rise to the thought and, holding these merits, dedicate them toward *anuttarasamyaksambodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'?
The Buddha said:
"Fundamentally, this does not exist.

This fundamental non-existence neither increases nor decreases; by constantly following this mindfulness without departing from it, one draws near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, sitting upon the unattainable Dharma and the unattainable wisdom."
If the Prajñāpāramitā neither increases nor decreases, and the bodhisattva remains mindful of this without departing from it, they are close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does a bodhisattva approach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by maintaining the initial thought, or by maintaining the final thought?"
The Buddha said:
"The initial thought and the subsequent thought—these two thoughts have no counterpart. Subhūti said:
“Regarding the later mind and the initial mind, since there is no mutual opposition between them, by what merit are they produced and brought to growth?
The Buddha said:
“It is like lighting a lamp wick; does the light first emitted burn the wick?”
"Is it by means of the later light that the wick is burned?

Subhūti replied, "It is not by means of the initial light that the wick is burned, yet it is not apart from the initial light; it is not by means of the later light, yet it is not apart from the later light."
The Buddha asked Subhūti:
"Is it so, or not? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

"A bodhisattva does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the initial thought, nor does he attain it apart from the initial thought; he does not attain it by means of the final thought, nor does he attain it apart from the final thought."
The Buddha asked:
"In what way does this constitute attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti replied:

"The profound state of *abhisaṃbodhi* is based on these causal conditions: a bodhisattva does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the initial thought, nor do they attain it apart from the initial thought; they do not attain it by means of the subsequent thought, nor do they attain it apart from the subsequent thought."
The Buddha asked, "How is it, Subhūti?
Does the mind that has previously ceased arise again later?
Subhūti replied:
"No," [he replied].
The Buddha said:
"Can the mind that has just arisen be extinguished?"
Subhūti said, “It can be extinguished.
The Buddha said:
“Can that which is to be extinguished be made not to be extinguished? Subhūti replied, “No.”
The Buddha said:
"Since they are fundamentally non-existent, can they possibly be made to abide?
Subhūti replied:
"If one wishes to abide in original non-existence, one should abide as one does in original non-existence.
The Buddha said:
"Even if one were to abide within original non-existence, could one thereby cause [the resolve] to become firm and steadfast?"
In this original non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*), is there mind or no mind?
Without departing from original non-existence, can there be mind?
Do you perceive this original non-existence?
"Is seeking in this way a profound seeking?
Subhūti replied,
"O God among Gods!"
To seek in this manner is to have no seeking at all. Why is this?
Because these dharmas are ultimately unobtainable and cannot be seen.
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva seeks the prajñāpāramitā, what is it that they seek?
Subhūti replied:
“I seek emptiness.
The Buddha said:
“If it were not empty, what would you seek?”
Subhūti said: “It is for the sake of seeking conceptualization.
The Buddha said:
“How do you regard the perception of going?
[Śāriputra: No, for this bodhisattva does not go toward the perception. Subhūti said:
"One does not form such seeking-thoughts.
