Why is this? If the thought of seeking were exhausted, or if the thought were extinguished, it could indeed be extinguished, and one would thereby become an Arhat. This is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of not extinguishing the thought of attainment while realizing it; thus, one proceeds toward the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*) in accordance with this teaching."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If there are bodhisattvas who possess three things that lead toward the gate of samādhi and guard the gate of samādhi:
first, emptiness; second, signlessness; and third, wishlessness."
These three things are beneficial to the Prajñāpāramitā; it does not increase only during the day, but it should also increase even during dreams at night. Why is this?
“The Buddha has said that there is no difference between day and night, or between waking and dreaming. Subhūti said:
“If a bodhisattva benefits from the *prajñāpāramitā* during the daytime, they will likewise benefit from it within the dream at night.”
Śāriputra said:
"How could there be anything attained from what is done within a dream?
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are like everything that exists within a dream."
Subhūti said:
"The wholesome deeds performed in a dream bring benefit when one rejoices upon waking; the unwholesome deeds performed in a dream bring diminution when one does not rejoice upon waking."
Śāriputra said:
"Suppose one kills a person in a dream and feels joy in his heart; upon waking, he says:
'Was it not a pleasure for me to kill this person?'"
"How is this so? Subhūti replied, "No, they all have their causes and conditions;
the mind is not empty. These things must have causes and conditions—whether seen, heard, or thought of—as their causes and conditions; it is for this reason that one knows them."
From within this, one causes the mind to have attachments and causes the mind to have no attachments; this is called "not forgetting," for all of these have their respective causes and conditions.
Śāriputra said:
"All that is created is merely empty; for what reason, then, would the mind have any causal conditions?
Subhūti replied:
“With perception as a condition, the mind arises from this as a condition.
Śāriputra said:
“If a bodhisattva gives a gift in a dream and dedicates that gift toward attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, does such a gift exist or not?”
Subhūti said: "The Bodhisattva Maitreya is present nearby; he shall succeed to the Buddha’s position in the near future. Therefore, you should know that you ought to question him.
Śāriputra then addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"What I asked, Subhūti said:
'The Bodhisattva Maitreya will be able to explain it.
Maitreya then spoke:
"Should I be understood by my name Maitreya?
Or should I be understood through wisdom by means of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Or is it by means of this body that I am to be understood?"

Whether it be emptiness or form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—through wisdom one understands that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty. There is no power in what is to be understood; these dharmas are not seen at all, nor is there anyone seen who is to understand them, nor is there anyone seen who shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra said: "Does what the Bodhisattva Maitreya has spoken constitute realization?
Maitreya replied:
"No, I have not attained realization through the Dharma I have preached.
Śāriputra then thought to himself:
"The wisdom entered by Maitreya Bodhisattva is exceedingly profound."
"Why is this? Because it has been a very long time since he has constantly practiced the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra:
“How is it? Do you see yourself when you have become an arhat? Śāriputra replied, “I do not.”
The Buddha said:
"In this way, a bodhisattva does not form such a thought:

'I have received the prediction regarding this dharma, and I shall therein attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi),' nor is there anyone who attains unexcelled perfect enlightenment."

"When a Bodhisattva practices in this way for the sake of seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, they never fear that they will not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Following the teachings within this Dharma, they seek the Prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, I have nothing to fear."
When a bodhisattva encounters great and extreme peril amidst tigers and wolves, they ultimately feel no fear or dread, thinking to themselves:
"Even if there should be one who devours me, it shall be for the sake of practicing giving and fulfilling the *dānapāramitā*, drawing me closer to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"I vow that when I later become a Buddha, there shall be no realm of birds or beasts within my land.
When the Bodhisattva arrives among the bandits, he is never afraid. Even if he were to die therein, he would think to himself:

"This body must inevitably be cast aside; even if I am killed by these bandits, I shall harbor no anger. For the sake of fulfilling the practice of patience, the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, I shall draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"May it be that when I later attain Buddhahood, there shall be no thieves or bandits within my buddha-field.
When the Bodhisattva reaches a place where there is no water or drink, his mind is not afraid or terrified; he thinks to himself:
"It is because people lack virtue that there is no water or drink here."

May it be that when I later attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, my buddha-field shall be filled with water and juices, and may all the people within my field obtain the eight-flavored water of omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
When the Bodhisattva encounters times of famine, his mind is not afraid, and he thinks to himself:

"I shall apply myself with diligence to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so that within my buddha-field there shall never again be famine; and so that for the people in my buddha-field, whatever food or drink they wish for or seek shall appear before them, just like the food and drink in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
When the Bodhisattva is amidst an epidemic, he thinks to himself:

"I shall have no fear at all; even if my own body should perish therein, I must certainly practice diligence to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so that within my buddha-field there shall be no years of famine or epidemics, and I shall surely subdue the hosts of Māra."
The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva hears that this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this unexcelled perfect enlightenment, will only be attained after a vast and long period of time has passed, his mind feels no fear; for from the moment he first resolved to train until now, it has not been long.”
It is, for example, like the duration of a single mental movement.
Why is this? Because there is no fundamental limit [to its beginning].
When the Buddha had spoken these words, a female lay follower rose from her seat, approached the Buddha, paid homage to him, knelt with her right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Having heard this, I am neither afraid nor terrified; I shall surely descend upon those places of fear. Seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, once I have attained abhiṣambodhi, I shall preach this sutra."

The Buddha smiled, and golden light issued from his mouth; the upāsikā then took golden flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, yet by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, none of the flowers fell to the ground.
Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his *kāṣāya*, and stepped forward to pay homage to the Buddha. Kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; since you have smiled, there must be something to be said."

The Buddha said, “In a future age called the Constellation Kalpa (Tārakā-kalpa), there shall be a buddha named Suvarṇapuṣpa. At that time, this upāsikā will cast off her female body and receive a male form.”

In the future, they shall be born in the buddha-field of Akṣobhya; from the buddha-field of Akṣobhya, they shall go again to another buddha-field, and from one buddha-field, they shall be born again in another buddha-field, continuing in this manner without end.
For example, it is like a Cakravartin king who travels from one palace to another, never letting his feet touch the ground from birth until death.
Likewise, this upāsikā travels from one buddha-field to another, never failing to behold a Buddha.
Ānanda thought to himself:
"The assembly of bodhisattvas in the buddha-field of Akṣobhya Buddha is indeed a true assembly of Buddhas.
The Buddha, knowing what Ānanda was thinking, said:
"These bodhisattvas in this assembly have all already transcended birth and death.
This upāsikā shall later become the Buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa, who will deliver incalculable arhats, leading them to parinirvāṇa."

At that time, within that Buddha-field, there were no beasts of prey or thieves; there was no lack of water or drink, nor were there instances of high grain prices or pestilence; all other evil matters were entirely absent.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"From which Buddha onward has this upāsikā performed meritorious deeds?
The Buddha said:
"In the past, when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara first resolved his mind to seek Buddhahood, he performed meritorious deeds.
During the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he likewise took golden flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, making this vow:
'By the merit of this offering, may I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
The Buddha said:

"Just as I took five flowers and scattered them over the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I immediately attained the joy of the dharma of non-arising and stood therein. He then conferred upon me the prediction, saying:
'After incalculable kalpas, you shall become the Buddha Śākyamuni.'"
At that time, when this upāsikā saw me receive the prediction from the Buddha, she also thought to herself:
"I too shall receive a prediction and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; such is the manner in which bodhisattvas receive their predictions."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“This laywoman Dakṣā first conceived the original aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-abhisaṃbodhi in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.”
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“Has this laywoman Dakṣā attained what she sought?
The Buddha said:
"Already crossed.
*The Sūtra on the Practice of the Perfection of Wisdom*, Scroll Six;
*The Sūtra on the Practice of the Perfection of Wisdom*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter 17: Guarding Emptiness. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Seventeen: Guarding Emptiness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, what constitutes entering emptiness?
What constitutes maintaining the samādhi of emptiness?
The Buddha said:

"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty; they should practice this contemplation with a single-minded focus. While practicing this contemplation, they do not perceive any phenomena. Thus, not perceiving any phenomena, they do not realize [nirvana] within those phenomena."
Subhūti said: "The Buddha has taught that one does not realize [the truth] within emptiness; how then can a bodhisattva dwell in samādhi and yet not realize realization within emptiness?"

The Buddha said: “A bodhisattva fully possesses mindfulness of emptiness but does not realize it; making this contemplation, they do not take realization as their goal. Making this contemplation, they contemplate the points of entry; when they are just about to incline toward it, they do not take realization as their goal, nor do they enter samādhi. Their minds are without attachment, and at that time they do not lose the fundamental nature of the bodhisattva’s dharma, nor do they attain realization midway.”
Why is this? Because his original vow was to protect all sentient beings and because he possesses the utmost compassion.
He thought to himself:
"I am fully endowed with all merits; at this time, I do not realize [nirvana].
When a bodhisattva attains the Prajñāpāramitā, they obtain immense merit and fully acquire the power of wisdom.

It is like a person who is courageous and brave enough to repel the enemy; he is exceptionally handsome, fierce, and strong, capable of everything, and proficient in the art of war, knowing and practicing all sixty-four maneuvers, and is thus revered by all people.
Wherever he goes, there is no place where his power does not prevail.
Having attained something, he distributes it to others with a joyful heart.
If there is some other matter requiring him to go away with his parents and wife through a great and perilous road amidst hardships, he brings safety and peace to his parents and says to his wife:
"Do not be afraid; we shall all emerge from this calamity together.
Once they had emerged, they were able to escort their parents, wives, and children back to their hometowns; upon arriving home without encountering any evil, there was no one who did not rejoice.
Why is this? It is because such a person is courageous, possesses great wisdom, and is astute and vigorous.

This bodhisattva practices supreme great compassion; with his mind focused on all sentient beings (*sattva*) throughout the ten directions, he at that time maintains a compassionate heart and bestows everything upon others as the highest gift. This bodhisattva transcends the stage of the arhat and emerges from the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
Abiding in samādhi, he feels compassion for all sentient beings (sattva) while perceiving nothing; therein he does not realize [nirvana], but enters deeply into emptiness without becoming an arhat.

When a Bodhisattva practices in this manner, they practice the samādhi of emptiness and turn toward the gate of nirvāṇa; yet, while not harboring perceptions of existence, they do not enter emptiness to realize a fixed attainment.

It is like a flying bird soaring through the air without encountering any obstruction: when the Bodhisattva practices, they are about to head toward emptiness and reach emptiness to face non-perception, yet they do not fall into emptiness nor do they fall into non-perception, for they desire to fully possess all the dharmas of a Buddha.

It is like a skilled archer who shoots into the air; his arrow remains suspended in mid-air, and as he shoots subsequent arrows, each one strikes the preceding one. As he continues to shoot, each later arrow hits the one before it. The man wishes for the first arrow to fall, and only then does it fall.

When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, being protected by upāyakauśalya (skillful means), they do not realize the truth midway through their own stage, nor do they fall into the levels of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha. Sustaining these merits, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; when their merits are fully perfected, they then become a Buddha.
"A bodhisattva contemplates within the sūtras and does not realize [nirvāṇa] midway.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"A bodhisattva undergoes hardships and trains in this manner, yet does not realize [nirvāṇa] midway."
The Buddha said:
"These bodhisattvas all act for the protection of all sentient beings, maintaining the samādhi of emptiness and turning toward the gate of nirvāṇa, while discerning through mental reflection.
What is this discernment? It is as follows:"

To maintain the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness—this is what is called skill-in-means (upāya-kauśalya), which prevents this bodhisattva from attaining realization midway.
Why is this? Because they protect themselves through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), they bring to mind all *sattvas*.
By maintaining these thoughts, they attain *upāyakauśalya* and do not realize [nirvana] midway.

If a bodhisattva enters deeply into contemplation, maintaining the samādhi of emptiness directed toward the gate of nirvāṇa, the samādhi of signlessness directed toward the gate of nirvāṇa, and the samādhi of wishlessness directed toward the gate of nirvāṇa—for this reason, having discerned the conceptualizations regarding causes and conditions held by people since remote antiquity, they seek to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preach the sūtras so as to cause others to distance themselves from these causes and conditions. They maintain the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness, directing them toward the gate of nirvāṇa, yet none of them realize the fruit of verification midway.

In this way, when a bodhisattva contemplates people of the distant past, they perceive them as having the notion of permanence, the notion of peace, the notion of self, and the notion of beauty, each according to its own fundamental nature.

When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall preach the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may sever the perception of existence, the perception of security, the perception of self, and the perception of beauty, and completely sever all seeking.
How does one sever them?
One contemplates that what is permanent is impermanent, that what is pleasant is entirely suffering, that what is the self is not the self, and that what is beautiful is entirely ugly.
Thus the Bodhisattva reflects within his own mind:
"In order to attain *upāyakauśalya*, one maintains the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, turning toward the gate of *nirvāṇa* without realizing the fruit midway."
If there is a bodhisattva who thinks:

"A person has set out from afar; they seek causes and conditions, seek perceptions, seek desires, seek perceptions of accumulation, seek perceptions of emptiness, and seek this perception—all of these are present."

The Bodhisattva said: "I desire that all such things may not exist in the world. It is by means of this mindfulness of persons that one attains *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means). This dharma contemplates emptiness, perception, volition, and consciousness as being without origin or limit. Such a Bodhisattva does not realize [nirvana] midway; one should understand the dharma in this way."

"How does a bodhisattva seek the prajñāpāramitā? They should practice with clear understanding within the dharmas; with what should the mind take as its object when seeking it, and how should the mind enter it? Maintaining the samādhi of emptiness, maintaining the samādhi of signlessness, and maintaining the samādhi of wishlessness, they should head toward the gate of nirvāṇa, yet not realize the fruit midway."

He dwells in the samādhi of non-perception, he dwells in the samādhi of non-arising; because this bodhisattva has not yet attained decisive penetration, he dwells in the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, the samādhi of wishlessness, the samādhi of non-perception, and the samādhi of non-arising.

When one has finished contemplating this samādhi, if there is someone who comes to question them and they do not immediately provide an explanation with an incalculable mind, know that this person is not an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because the mind of an avaivartika is immeasurable and all-knowing; since he does not possess such conduct, one knows that this bodhisattva has not yet attained the state of avaivartika.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is a bodhisattva who can understand this, they shall be an avaivartika.
The Buddha said:
"If one hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, or even if one does not hear it, is able to understand it, such a person is an *avaivartika* (one who will not regress). Subhūti said:
"Countless people seek the path of the bodhisattva, yet few are able to understand it."
The Buddha said:

"Those who are able to understand this receive the prediction [of enlightenment]. Because they possess the most excellent knowledge of the Dharma within these merits, they cannot be surpassed by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, nor can they be reached by gods, asuras, nāgas, or yakṣas; this is the mark of an Avaivartika (non-retrogressive Bodhisattva)."
Chapter 18: On Detachment. From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Practice of the Path*, Chapter Eighteen: On Detachment.
The Buddha said: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

In his dreams, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not enter the stage of an Arhat, nor does he enter the stage of a Pratyekabuddha; he takes no pleasure in seeking therein, nor does he instruct others to enter therein. His mind does not dwell upon any phenomena within the Prajñāpāramitā even while dreaming; he does not take the Prajñāpāramitā as a basis for realization, but his mind remains constantly fixed on the Buddha.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
An irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva should know these to be the marks of irreversibility.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva may, in a dream, be seated in the midst of a gathering of several hundred disciples;
or be seated in the midst of a gathering of countless thousands of disciples, or countless hundreds of thousands of disciples, preaching the sūtras;
or be followed by a community of bhikṣus, leading them at the very front.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has fully revealed this in the sūtras.
It is likewise so, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is an avaivartika should know these to be the marks of an avaivartika.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva may, while in a dream, sit in the highest reaches of space and preach the sūtras to an assembly of bhikṣus; he may see for himself a radiance seven feet high and manifest transformations at will; and in other places, he may act as if preaching the sūtras like a Buddha—this is what a bodhisattva mahāsattva does within a dream."
It is likewise so, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible should know these to be the marks of irreversibility.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva experiences no fear, terror, anxiety, or dread even in dreams. Even if they see in a dream commanderies and districts where armies have risen up and are attacking one another, or where fires break out; or if they see tigers, wolves, lions, and other wild beasts; or if they see those who are decapitating people; or if they see various other such transformations involving great suffering, many who are destitute, hungry, or thirsty, and all beset by calamities—even when seeing all these things, their mind is not afraid, not terrified, not startled, and does not waver.
Seeing this in a dream, he immediately rises from his seat upon awakening and thinks:
"All that was seen in the dream pertains to the three realms; when I become a Buddha, I shall preach the sutras for them all and teach them everywhere."
"It is likewise so, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible should know these to be the marks of irreversibility.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By what means is it known that when this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becomes a Buddha, there will be no evil minds whatsoever within his realm?
At that time, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees in a dream animals devouring one another or when there is an epidemic among the people, his mind gradually gives rise to this aspiration, and he forms this thought:
"I shall certainly become a Buddha. When I have become a Buddha, may there be no evil whatsoever within my realm."
"It is by this that one knows. Furthermore, Subhūti,
it should be known that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
“Furthermore, Subhūti, the complete elimination of all evils is also a mark of an avaivartika bodhisattva. Moreover, Subhūti,”
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has awakened from sleep and sees a city or town on fire, he then forms this thought:
"What I have seen in my dream, by means of this analogy and these signs, shows that I am not afraid; by means of this analogy and these signs, I am complete in my practice."
"In this way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses these marks; this is the characteristic of an Avaivartika (non-retrogressive).
Possessing these comparisons and practicing with these characteristics fully, he is called an Avaivartika Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."

Now I have examined, scrutinized, and thoroughly investigated that which I am directed toward: this city wall shall surely be extinguished, surely be dissolved, and surely be removed, so that it no longer appears, because of me.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, suppose that fire has been extinguished, has vanished, and has departed; one knows this.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has received the prediction, and the past tathāgatas, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas have conferred upon him the anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi, one knows these to be the marks of an avaivartika.”
If the fire does not go out, does not subside, and does not depart, know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet received the prediction.
If the fire deity burns one house and leaves another house, or again leaps across to burn one *li* and leaves another *li*, know this, Subhūti!

This was caused by his family members having interrupted the recitation of the sutras in their previous lives. These people saw for themselves all the karmic results of their past deeds; the evil they had committed in former existences was entirely eliminated and forgiven. From that time forward, the remaining retribution for interrupting the sutras was completely exhausted, and all the evils of those past lives were utterly extinguished.
In this way, Subhūti,
one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet attained the state of non-retrogression (avaivartika) or unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

By means of these analogies and by means of these characteristics and practices being fully accomplished, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should regard [them] in this way; and by means of these analogies and these characteristics, he should explain them so that others may come to know them."
Furthermore, Subhūti, if at any time a man or woman is possessed by or afflicted with spirits, that bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Perhaps I have received the prediction, just as the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas conferred upon me the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for all that is contemplated in this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is utterly pure."

If I am to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), my thoughts shall all be pure; this unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment sets aside the mind of an arhat and sets aside the mind of a pratyekabuddha.

Even if one were to set aside the mind of an arhat and set aside the mind of a pratyekabuddha, one will certainly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment and become a buddha; it is impossible not to become a buddha.

Regarding those who shall become Buddhas through *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are none among the present Buddhas of the *asaṃkhyeya* lands in the ten directions who does not know them, does not see them, or does not realize them.

Now the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha fully knows my thoughts and recollections; I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become a Buddha. Just as I have truly declared, just as I have truly practiced, and just as I have truly spoken, this spirit-demon shall depart because of me.
He then asked:
"By which spirit or ghost is this man or woman possessed?
Thereupon, the spirit departed immediately.

Subhūti, you should know that if this is not the case—that is, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart when these words are spoken—then this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet received the prediction;
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have not conferred upon him the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If that person is truly sincere, Māra the Evil One will approach and stand before this bodhisattva mahāsattva, speaking these words:
'If you originally dwelt in this way, if your original name was such-and-such, or if you have already received the prediction of enlightenment.'"
Desiring to confuse him, that bodhisattva should speak these words:
"If I am truly such at this time, the spirits and deities shall follow my words; I have certainly received the prediction that I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"If it is truly as my sincere words state, then these ghosts and spirits shall depart immediately.
Thereupon, that evil Māra thought to himself:
"I must cause these ghosts and spirits to leave."
Why is this? Because Māra is exceedingly venerable and possesses majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), which the spirits and deities do not dare to confront.
Māra thought to himself: "Because of Māra's majestic spiritual power, the spirits and deities have departed."
"In this way, the bodhisattva thinks:
'It is by the power of my own majestic spiritual authority that the spirits and ghosts have departed.
" The Buddha said:

"Unaware that he had departed by means of the Māra’s supernatural power, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva, believing himself to be truly so, became arrogant; he held others in contempt, laughed at them without restraint, and said to people:
'I have already received my prediction from the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, whereas all these other people have not yet received their predictions.'"

Because of this, they become self-satisfied and arrogant; conversely, anger arises, and their resentment gradually increases. Thus, they remain far removed from *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and lose the wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

These bodhisattvas lack *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); their anger arises again, and they give rise to these two stages, whereby they will fall to the stage of an arhat or fall to the stage of the path of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, these individuals do not uphold [the teachings];
such Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should recognize this as the work of Māra.

They abandon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), do not speak with spiritual friends, do not attend to spiritual friends, and do not record the instructions of spiritual friends; for this reason, one knows they are held fast by Māra.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra. Why is that?
When one perceives this matter, one should know that Māra has come before the bodhisattva; at times Māra changes his appearance and approaches, speaking these words:
"The past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have predicted for you the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
your original name was such-and-such, your mother’s name was such-and-such..."
The father’s courtesy name was so-and-so; or the elder brother’s courtesy name was so-and-so; or the elder sister’s courtesy name was so-and-so; or the younger brother’s courtesy name was so-and-so;

or the name of a close relative was so-and-so; or the name of an acquaintance was so-and-so; or the courtesy names of the parents and elder brother were so-and-so; or the courtesy names of the ancestors back through seven generations were so-and-so;
or the courtesy names of the mother’s maternal family were so-and-so; or the courtesy names of the father’s maternal family were so-and-so.
Whether born in a certain city, a certain country, a certain district, a certain county, or a certain village;
whether one always speaks with gentle words, or speaks such words now,
or likewise spoke such gentle words in former lives, or was at times of high talent.
Then he again followed his form and said:

"If in a previous life you were also eminent and wise—whether you saw your own name, or saw [the practice of] begging for food, or sometimes eating at a single place, or sometimes going to where food was served; whether you first ate fruits and vegetables and then ate rice, or sometimes stayed among burial mounds, or sometimes on a quiet road, or sometimes dwelt among the trees; whether you accepted invitations, or sometimes did not accept invitations; whether you took a small or large amount to satisfy yourself, or sometimes did not apply sesame oil to your body; whether your voice was pleasant, or whether you were skilled in conversation."
Seeing this, Māra spoke these deceptive words:
"If it was so when you were in previous lives that you were skilled in such eloquent speech, and if it was likewise so when you practiced the Dharma in previous lives."

Why is this? If one attains [this state] now because of pure conduct in a previous life, it is due to the merit resulting from having practiced purity in a previous life; thus, what is attained now is simply that very merit.

If in a previous life one was the son of such-and-such a family, of such-and-such a clan, and also had such-and-such a name, and if in that previous life one performed such conduct, then in this present life one likewise attains such purity.
That bodhisattva then forms this thought:
"Could it be that I have attained [this]?
Thereupon, that evil Māra speaks these words again:

"If one has received the prediction of non-retrogression (avaivartika), then by virtue of the fact that the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have already bestowed this prediction upon them, they thereby attain purity."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Regarding the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) as I have described them—if one examines them by means of these comparisons, these marks, and these practices, and yet what I have described is not fully met, and they instead rely on their own [limited] understanding, you should know that such bodhisattvas will ultimately not achieve success; you should know that they have been ruined by Māra.”

Why is this? Because by means of these comparisons and these characteristics, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible (avaivartika) knows that they cannot be grasped; yet, because Māra speaks of their merits and mentions their names, such bodhisattva mahāsattvas, hearing what Māra says, feel joy in their hearts and consider it to be truly so. They then act with haughty arrogance toward others, treating their fellow students with contempt and becoming conceited themselves.
Because that bodhisattva accepts this designation, he loses his fundamental practice and falls into the net of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, because he accepts this designation,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva fails to recognize the deeds of Māra and, conversely, claims for himself that he has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Māra further speaks these words:
"If you are to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, when you become a Buddha, your name shall be such-and-such.
Upon hearing this name, the bodhisattva forms this thought in his mind:
"Is it not so with me? I too previously thought thus; I originally formed this intention, and having originally formed this thought."
The Buddha said:
"Such a bodhisattva has little wisdom; such a bodhisattva lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and instead conceives this thought:
'When I become a buddha, my name shall be as it was previously conceived by me; I will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and my name shall be such-and-such.'"
The Buddha said:
"If it is as the Māra has instructed, or if the Māras and devas have acted together, then this bhikṣu is deluded by Māra.
The Buddha spoke to Subhūti:

"Regarding the bodhisattvas whom I have designated, by means of these comparisons and these characteristics, I did not instruct them to act in such a way; yet they failed to understand what I taught, losing these comparisons and missing these characteristics. Instead, they rely on these mere words and thus conceive the thought in their own minds: 'I am an avaivartika.'"

He then disparages other bodhisattvas; because of this contempt, he distances himself from the Buddha, distances himself from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), distances himself from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-jñāna (the wisdom of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment), and distances himself from upāya-kauśalya (skillful means). Having lost the Prajñāpāramitā and lost his good spiritual friends, he instead acquires evil spiritual friends; such a bodhisattva will inevitably fall into the path of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha.

If, after a long period of great hardship and toil, one is able to seek Buddhahood again, then by virtue of the grace of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one shall again attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and personally realize Buddhahood.
The Buddha said:

"At that time, when one conceives such a thought and receives this name, if one does not immediately awaken to it, does not immediately correct it, and does not immediately repent, one will thus fall into the path of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha."
The Buddha said:

"If there is a bhikṣu who teaches the four grave prohibitions or other matters, yet violates and destroys these prohibitions, he no longer constitutes a śramaṇa and is no longer a son of the Buddha; such a person ruins those among the bodhisattvas, and his transgression is greater than that of the four grave offenses of a bhikṣu."
If this bodhisattva says,
"I was born in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a district, such-and-such a county,
and such-and-such a village," and when forming such thoughts and conceptions, their transgression is most grave; it should be understood in this way.
Setting aside these four grave matters, there are the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); when such a thought arises in the mind, its transgression is heavy.
Because this bodhisattva has accepted that title and, with mental conviction, gives rise to such a thought, his transgression is great; one should understand it thus.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Because of these words, Māra enters into deep transgression.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the virtue of detachment, Māra the Evil One approaches again and speaks these words:
"The Dharma of detachment is indeed thus; it is that which is praised by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“I do not speak of such seclusion as when I instruct bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to dwell in solitary places, to dwell among trees, or to dwell in quiet retreats.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way, O God among Gods!
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain far removed?"
Is there yet another form of seclusion?
It is neither dwelling in solitude, nor dwelling among the trees, nor dwelling in a quiet place. What, then, is this other form of seclusion?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Suppose there were Arhats each practicing this mindfulness, each Pratyekabuddha practicing this mindfulness, and each Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in seclusion outside the city, each practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva such that no evil whatsoever may be committed; each practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, whether staying in a solitary place, staying among the trees, or staying in a quiet location—this is the dharma of seclusion for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who practices with clear comprehension.”
I desire that you practice this conduct; I do not desire that you travel far to dwell in remote, uninhabited places.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, maintaining this seclusion, should practice day and night and should practice with clear comprehension. For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices away from the vicinity of cities.

Holding to these analogies, each of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice accordingly: whether dwelling in solitude, dwelling among the trees, or dwelling in a secluded place—each practicing as a bodhisattva-mahāsattva—in this way is the dharma of seclusion that I have taught.
At that time, Māra the Evil One will go to instruct them in the practice of seclusion, saying:
"Whether you dwell in a solitary place, or dwell among the trees, or dwell in a quiet location, you should practice in this manner."
This bodhisattva, following the teachings of Māra, then loses the dharma of detachment.

Māra speaks these words: "Take up the dharma of an Arhat with this same thought of non-differentiation; you should follow this practice. Take up the path of a Pratyekabuddha with this same thought of non-differentiation; you should also follow this practice. Take up the path of a Bodhisattva with this same thought of non-differentiation; you should also follow this practice. The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to comprehend and enter; if you should practice in this way, you will abandon the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said:

"This bodhisattva has not yet attained his original vow, yet he acts contrary to it; he lacks thorough understanding of the Dharma, and this bodhisattva-mahāsattva instead relies on his own [limited] views, treating other bodhisattvas with contempt, thinking to himself:
'Who can surpass me?'"
[The Buddha said: "One should not look down upon a bodhisattva who dwells near a city.

A bodhisattva dwelling near a city is thoroughly pure and clean; his mind is free from discursive thought. He does not abide within the dharma of the arhats, nor does he abide within the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas. He does not accept any evil thoughts; he abandons [worldly] meditative joy for the sake of concentration, fully attains all samādhis, and completely fulfills all his vows."
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), even if they dwell for a hundred years, a hundred thousand years, or a hundred thousand million years—or even longer—within a wilderness of hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, in a place where birds and beasts do not go, where bandits do not go, and where *rākṣasas* do not go; though they remain there, if they do not understand this dharma of seclusion, it will ultimately be of no benefit."

This is the failure of a bodhisattva to fully realize seclusion; though they claim to have attained it through their own thoughts and actions, because they do not understand that they are unaware of themselves, they are actually lost.
To abide in the practice of seclusion while remaining self-centered is merely double-tongued speech; it is not true seclusion.
It is not that I do not approve of this mind of the bodhisattva; rather, it is not as you say regarding my teaching on the distancing of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
This distancing is not fully understood, and within this distancing, nothing at all can be apprehended; such is what constitutes the three kinds of distancing.
Thereupon, that evil Māra flew up into the air and stood there, saying these words:
"Excellent, noble son!
This is the true dharma of seclusion, as taught by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. You should indeed practice this seclusion; in this way, you will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Upon hearing these words, that bodhisattva was delighted and immediately rose from his secluded retreat to go to where another secluded bodhisattva lived near the city. That bodhisattva bhikṣu was one who had accomplished virtuous qualities, yet [the first bodhisattva] went to him and spoke with contempt, saying:
"The Dharma you practice is not correct."
The Buddha said:

"Among such virtuous ones, there may be a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who clearly understands and practices accordingly, yet others call him wrong; or there may be one who acts contrary to the truth and calls it right, honoring those who should not be honored and showing anger toward those who should be honored.
Such a person says to that Bodhisattva: 'I practice seclusion, and a flying being came and said to me:'"
“Excellent, excellent!
If you have truly discerned this Dharma of seclusion, you should indeed practice accordingly.
It is for this reason that I have come to speak with you.”

If you were now to follow my practice, there would be nothing to compare with it. If you were to walk about the outskirts of a city, who would come to say to you, "Well done," or who would come to tell you, "Excellent"?
The Buddha said: "Subhūti,
this bodhisattva is a person of virtue, yet he instead treats such a person with contempt."

A bodhisattva should understand this: such a person is like a caste of corpse-bearers who, having nothing of value within, merely shout back in response; they possess deficiencies and are the enemies of bodhisattvas, those who revile bodhisattvas, and for this reason, they are the great thieves of the world above and the world below.
Even if they wear the robes of a śramaṇa, they are no different from thieves;
among those bodhisattvas who possess virtue, they are likewise thieves.
Subhūti, one should not engage in affairs with such people as these;
one should not converse with them; nor should one even look upon them with respect.
Why is this? Because when much anger arises, it ruins a person's good heart.
Such people as these should be understood in this way.
In what way, Subhūti,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not abandon sarvajñatā,
nor set aside anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

Because this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not abandon sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment) and acts as a protector for all sattvas (beings).
One should not associate with those corrupted bodhisattvas; one should not revere them, nor should one meet with them. One must protect the Dharma and firmly uphold it oneself.

One should always maintain an urgent sense of purity and establish oneself therein; whatever the mind habituates itself to, one should always hold fast to that with discernment. One should always maintain a correct mind and always stand in awe of places of suffering and toil, never entering into such places, nor entering into the three [evil] states. Toward wherever those corrupted bodhisattvas may be, one should always maintain a heart of loving-kindness toward them, always pitying them so as to bring them peace and security. One should take compassion for them and cherish them with thoughts of loving-kindness, while always protecting and reflecting upon oneself:
"May I never give rise to such evil thoughts; may my mind be free from all blemish and defilement; and should I possess any unwholesomeness, may I quickly cast it away."
"Thus it is, Subhūti!
One should understand that all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are supreme.
Chapter Nineteen: Good Friends. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter on Good Friends, Number Nineteen. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is engaged in practice and desires to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should attend upon and serve a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), honoring and attending to them.
Subhūti asked the Buddha,
“By what means should one recognize the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“The Buddha, the God among Gods, is the good spiritual friend of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
whoever explains the prajñāpāramitā and instructs others to enter into this sūtra is the good spiritual friend of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the six pāramitās are the good spiritual friends of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
One should understand it thus: the six pāramitās are the sūtra;

the six pāramitās are the path; the six pāramitās are the protection; the six pāramitās are the unity; the six pāramitās are the guide. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past emerged from the six pāramitās;
all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are yet to come in the future shall likewise emerge from the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently existing in the incalculable lands of the ten directions have likewise all emerged from the six pāramitās and attained sarvajñatā.
All take the path through these four matters and employ these four matters to protect all sentient beings (*sattva*).
What are the four matters?
First, giving to others; second, bringing joy to others; third, benefiting others; and fourth, impartiality in giving.
These are the four. Thus, Subhūti, for this reason the bodhisattva mahāsattva is a śāstṛ,

for this reason he is a mother, for this reason he is a father, for this reason he is a shelter, for this reason he is a terrace, for this reason he is a deliverer, for this reason he is a refuge, for this reason he is a guide, for this reason he is the six pāramitās, and for this reason he is the deliverance of all beings (sattvānām).
For what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the six pāramitās?
Because they desire to completely sever the roots of those beings who have no ultimate limit, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all train in the prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"What is the characteristic of the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Being without obstruction is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti said: “One who attains the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of this characteristic likewise attains all dharmas by means of such a characteristic.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, Subhūti!
One attains the Prajñāpāramitā through the mark of non-existence; this is the mark by which all dharmas are attained.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
All dharmas are distinct from one another; all dharmas are each empty.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
These respective characteristics are each empty; this is the characteristic of the prajñāpāramitā, for all dharmas are each empty.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
These characteristics of the prajñāpāramitā are each empty, and in accordance with these characteristics, all dharmas are each empty.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
“Furthermore, O God among Gods!

Since all dharmas are each empty, for what reason do sentient beings desire to be born without end, without ever diminishing, and without ever reaching an end? Space never increases, space never ceases, and within each instance of emptiness there is no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or *abhisambuddha*. It is not from within this respective emptiness that these dharmas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or become *abhisambuddhas*.”
"How is it, O God among Gods!
By what means should this Dharma be known with certainty?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Thus, Subhūti!
Day and night, people desire to obtain this and bring about this;
they seek it in this way. Subhūti said:
"So it is, O God among Gods!
Day and night, people desire to obtain this cause and bring about this, seeking it in this way.
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Do you see me as desiring this emptiness?
Subhūti replied:
"No, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said: "Is it not so?"
“Subhūti! Is this emptiness attained by one’s own making?
Subhūti replied:
“Thus it is, O God among Gods!
It is empty.
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Is it not for this very reason that they desire to obtain this and bring about this, so that these people undergo diligent toil and suffering without any time of release?"
Subhūti said:
"O God among Gods, those people who desire to attain such supreme peace and security undergo such diligent toil that there is no time of rest."
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!
Because of what people desire, they become attached; you should understand it in this way.”

That which gives rise to sentient beings arises fundamentally from this; within this, there is nothing to be grasped. Since there is nothing to be grasped, one does not attain anything through it; thus, it is utterly non-existent.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
There is no time of diminution or exhaustion; within this, there is absolutely no arising or increase.
To understand it in this way is for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“One who understands in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, does not seek form, nor does he seek feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”

Understanding this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* performs an equal practice that no arhats or pratyekabuddhas can attain. This is the path traveled by those possessed of virtue; it is supreme and transcendent, and the excellence therein is such that none can reach its limit.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
"Having attained the Prajñāpāramitā, I shall practice in this manner.
By practicing day and night in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly approach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said:
“What do you think, Subhūti?

Suppose all the people of Jambudvīpa and those in the four directions—including every crawling and creeping insect—were made into human beings. Once they had each attained the human state, suppose they were all led to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having resolved their minds to seek the Buddha-way, each of them practiced giving for the duration of their lives, dedicating these acts of giving toward the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. What do you think?”
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the merit of this bodhisattva mahāsattva who performs such giving not great?
Subhūti replied, "It is very great, very great!"
"O Devātideva!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as great as when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attained the prajñāpāramitā, observes it for even a single day—even if it is the very last day—practicing according to the instructions within the prajñāpāramitā and forming such thoughts; the merit of this exceeds that of the former."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the prajñāpāramitā and practices with such mental attention toward these dharmas, they are preeminent among the entire assembly.
Why is this? Because no other person is able to equal this loving-kindness; setting aside the Buddhas, there is no one who can be the equal of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

This son of good family has entered deeply into knowledge and clearly understands that this wisdom is fully perfected. Seeing all those in the world who undergo suffering, he then feels profound compassion. With his eye of mindfulness piercing through to see immeasurable beings, he remains fully endowed with diligence at all times; because of this lack of indolence, he attains this practice.
At that time, one should feel profound gratitude and bring all sentient beings (sattvāḥ) to mind; yet one should not abide by means of these signs, nor should one abide by any other state. Subhūti!

The wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is of supreme brilliance; although they have not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, their clarity is such that by practicing accordingly, they are honored and exalted by all buddha-fields.

While they are correctly heading toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not yet fully reach it, yet they receive from others robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for illness—all provided in full abundance.
This Prajñāpāramitā is that in which the mind stands; it completely eliminates all that is received through giving and draws one near to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The food consumed by the bodhisattva mahāsattva is free from fault and brings benefit; he reveals the path to all *sattvas*—a path that is boundless and reaches no limit—illuminating it all clearly.
He desires to deliver all those who are within prisons and to show the eye of wisdom to all *sattvas*.

One should contemplate and practice the Dharma within this Prajñāpāramitā, and one should follow these instructions; by means of such contemplation and practice, those who enter into this Prajñāpāramitā engage in immovable conduct and unshakable conduct.

Why is this? Because one should practice according to this immovable conduct; do not harbor thoughts or conceptualizations, and do not entertain divergent views or hold onto shortcomings while entering into the *prajñāpāramitā*. One should practice in this manner, entering into the *prajñāpāramitā* day and night without ever becoming weary or ceasing.
It is as if, Subhūti, a man were to obtain a maṇi jewel; having not possessed it previously, he later obtains this maṇi jewel and leaps for joy.

Having obtained this maṇi jewel, he later lost it again; because of this, he was deeply afflicted by grief and anxiety, dwelling in sorrowful contemplation as if he had lost the seven treasures, and he thought:
"Why have I suddenly lost this precious gem?"
"In this way, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to seek precious jewels should always firmly maintain a mind that neither gains nor loses sarvajñā (all-knowledge), and should always enter into this state of mindfulness."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If that which is contemplated results in the loss of the self,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) without such loss?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus understands the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they do not lose the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Why is this?"
"Subhūti! The prajñāpāramitā is like space; this prajñāpāramitā neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti said:

"This Prajñāpāramitā is empty; how then does it give birth to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and how does the Prajñāpāramitā bring their practice to fulfillment so that they draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha said, “No,
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva neither increases nor decreases.”

Furthermore, Subhūti, when this sutra is being preached, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears it and neither fears nor is terrified, you should know this: that son of good family is practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is this prajñāpāramitā a practice of emptiness? "No, Subhūti!"
“Is there a practice that attains [enlightenment] apart from the perfection of wisdom?
“No, Subhūti. “Is it the practice of emptiness?”
"No, Subhūti! Is it apart from the practice of emptiness? "No, Subhūti!"
“Does it practice the destruction of form?
No, Subhūti. Does it practice the destruction of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?”
“No, Subhūti! Is there any practice apart from form? “No, Subhūti!”
“Is there any conditioned formation whatsoever apart from feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness? “No,
Subhūti,” he replied.
“How, O God among Gods,
does one practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
“What do you think, Subhūti?
Do you perceive any such dharma—that is, what dharma practices the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:
“I do not see it, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said: “How so, Subhūti?”
“[The Buddha] replied, ‘No, Subhūti— do you not see which bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom? Subhūti said,
‘I do not see them, O God among Gods!’”
The Buddha said:
"Suppose, Subhūti, one were to see universally: is this a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti said: "I do not see them, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
“Suppose, Subhūti, that one does not see any dharma anywhere that has arisen. Do you see such a thing?
Subhūti replied:
“I do not see them, O God among Gods! The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the joy of the dharma of non-arising; he is fully endowed with such joy. Having received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) from that which does not arise, he reaches the destination of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, where there is no further fear. He provides this protection for himself. The bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks in this way, practices in this way, and exerts power in this way, in order to attain the Buddha-wisdom, the supreme great wisdom, the sovereign wisdom, the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñatā-jñāna*), and the Tathāgata-wisdom.”
"If one were to see that no Buddha is attained, would the words of the Buddha then be different?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all dharmas are such that they do not arise from anywhere, can one receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
“No. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Do you see [anyone] who is destined to receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti said: "I do not perceive any dharma that should attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti! So it is with these dharmas; they are not obtained from anywhere.
A bodhisattva does not form such a thought:"
"Those who uphold this Dharma shall receive the prediction [of enlightenment], yet they do not receive the prediction.
*The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 7;
*The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 8.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: Śakra-devānām-indra. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Twenty: Śakra-devānām-indra.
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha from within the assembly, saying:
“The profound Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to comprehend and difficult to know.
The merit of those people is not small who, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, write it down, uphold it, and study it.”
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"What do you think, Kauśika!
If all the people of Jambudvīpa were to fully observe the ten precepts, would their merit not be great?"

If one were to possess such merit, even multiplied a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten thousandfold, a hundred millionfold, or a trillionfold, it would not equal that of these good sons and good daughters who hear, write down, uphold, and study this Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu among those seated there said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Is the merit of these sons and daughters of good family greater than that which has gone beyond you, O Kauśika?"
Śakra Devānām Indra replied to that bhikṣu, saying:
"If one turns the mind back even once for a single thought, one has already surpassed me; how much more so for those who hear, write down, uphold, and study the Prajñāpāramitā."

Having heard the Prajñāpāramitā, by following this Dharma and establishing oneself according to the teachings of this Dharma, one rises entirely above all devas, asuras, and the people of the world; one is preeminent and most honored among all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they not only surpass the devas, asuras, and the people of the world, but they also surpass all those up to and including the srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not merely surpass the arhats and pratyekabuddhas; they also surpass those bodhisattvas who practice the dānapāramitā, even if they lack prajñāpāramitā and upāyakauśalya. Furthermore, they surpass them.

Not only does he transcend the dānapāramitā, but he likewise transcends even the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, and dhyānapāramitā; for the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has lost the prajñāpāramitā and lost upāyakauśalya also transcends these [perfections] above.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, even if all the devas, asuras, and people of the world were to assemble together, they could never surpass this bodhisattva mahāsattva, for he dwells in the constant cultivation of the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, if they maintain this firm resolve as they have become familiar with the *prajñāpāramitā* therein, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly approach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). That bodhisattva mahāsattva is not far from the name of the Tathāgata; that bodhisattva mahāsattva, thus protecting [the teaching], is not far from the seat of a Buddha. All indolence that might arise in that bodhisattva mahāsattva shall no longer occur. When that bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they train for the sake of Buddhahood; they do not train in the dharma of the arhat, nor do they train in the dharma of the pratyekabuddha.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way: the Four Heavenly Kings should inquire after them, saying, "Train in this swiftly! The fourfold assembly of disciples should be those whom they deliver; they should sit upon the seat of the Buddha and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, the Four Great Kings will constantly go in person to inquire after them, let alone other sons of gods; the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will keep such a bodhisattva mahāsattva in mind as they practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, and they shall cause such a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner.
Furthermore, when all the various afflictions and pains that exist in the world arise, this body remains entirely without resentment; this is the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Ānanda had this thought:
"Is Śakra Devānām Indra speaking this by his own wisdom,
or is he speaking through the Buddha's majestic spiritual power?"
Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what Ānanda was thinking, said to him:
"Is it by the Buddha’s majestic power that I have spoken?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Ānanda!
Was it not by the Buddha’s majestic power that Śakra Devānām Indra spoke these words?
It is exactly so, Ānanda!"
At times, a bodhisattva mahāsattva deeply contemplates the prajñāpāramitā, practices the prajñāpāramitā, and trains in the prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, within this trichiliocosm, all the wicked Māras felt grief and malice in their hearts, desiring to jointly disrupt and confound this bodhisattva mahāsattva. They deliberated among themselves, saying:
"By what means can we cause this bodhisattva to prematurely realize the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha midway, and prevent him from becoming a Buddha?"
Chapter 21: On Arrogance (*Abhimāna*) The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Practice of the Path*, Chapter Twenty-one: On Arrogance. The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"When a bodhisattva wishes to study the *prajñāpāramitā* at the appropriate time, and wishes to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with the Dharma, at that moment, the Māras within each of the Buddha-fields will each be startled and think to themselves:
'We must cause this bodhisattva to attain the fruit of an arhat midway; do not let him quickly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, do not let him quickly become a Buddha.'"
"Furthermore, Ānanda,
Māra the Evil One becomes afflicted with grief and distress upon seeing the Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, Ānanda..."

At that time, the various wicked Māras will release fire and wind from the four directions to terrify this bodhisattva; if they cause him fear, his hair shall stand on end, and they will cause his mind to turn back, so that his distracted thoughts may recur.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Māra does not universally disturb all bodhisattvas; there are those whom he disturbs and those whom he does not.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Which bodhisattvas are disturbed by Māra?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not take delight in it, then the evil Māra will come and attempt to destroy them.”
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, feels doubt in their heart and thinks to themselves:
'Does it exist, or does it not exist?'"
"In this way, Ānanda,
a bodhisattva provides an opportunity for Māra the Evil One to gain the upper hand.
Furthermore, Ānanda..."

If there is a bodhisattva who distances himself from a virtuous teacher, that bodhisattva will have no desire to hear the profound matters of the *prajñāpāramitā* he has heard; he will neither understand them nor know them. How, then, could he maintain the *prajñāpāramitā*?
For this reason, Ānanda,
Māra the Evil One gains an opportunity over such a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Ānanda:
If there is a bodhisattva who associates with an evil teacher, for this reason, the wicked Māra gains an opportunity against that bodhisattva.
That bodhisattva says:
"This is precisely the teacher I delight in; he shall fulfill my aspirations. As for the many other bodhisattvas, they are not my close friends."
"For this reason, Māra the Evil One will once again gain access to that bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, [if one] instructs other bodhisattvas [in such a way]: "
"Using this as study and using this as writing, I myself do not yet understand this matter; can you understand it?
Or if at times a bodhisattva speaks to another bodhisattva with mutual contempt, saying:
"What I practice is correct, while what you practice is incorrect."
At that time, the evil Māras were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. Then the evil Māra assumed the appearance of a person in strange attire and came before him, addressing the Bodhisattva:
"You were born in such-and-such a country, into such-and-such a family."
Upon hearing these words, that bodhisattva then treats with contempt other bodhisattvas who have achieved [the path] and are free from pride.
Such a conceited bodhisattva possesses meager merit and lacks the marks of an avaivartika.
This bodhisattva possesses little merit among those who are irreversible (avaivartika), yet he is conceited and disparages other bodhisattvas, saying:
"You do not equal my practice."
For this reason, the evil Māra rejoices greatly and says:
"Now, those who fall into the hells, the realm of animals, and the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) are not few.

The evil Māra shall further increase his thoughts; of what he says and proclaims, many will believe and accept it, and among those who hear it, there are none who do not follow his words. Those who train in this way will have their anger increase all the more, and the actions of their minds will become inverted.
For this reason, the actions performed by body, speech, and mind become light and contrary [to the truth].
For this reason, that person’s transgressions increase further within the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
For this reason, the evil Māra rejoices and leaps for joy beyond measure.
If one who seeks the path of a bodhisattva disputes with one who seeks the path of an arhat, at that time the evil Māra thinks to himself:
"The bodhisattva is far from sarvajñatā; though he is far, he is not very far."
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva disputes with another bodhisattva, at that time Māra the Evil One thinks:
'Both have distanced themselves from the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If a bodhisattva who has not yet attained *avaivartika* status quarrels with a bodhisattva who is *avaivartika*, and reviles that *avaivartika* bodhisattva—because of that bodhisattva’s reviling, which follows from his own thoughts, he harbors resentment; for every single such thought, he must endure one *kalpa*."

"Although a bodhisattva may harbor such evil thoughts, they do not abandon sarvajñatā (all-knowledge); rather, after an incalculable number of kalpas have passed, they shall once again begin from the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one has conceived an evil thought in the mind, is it possible to repent for it midway?"
"Will one then have to wait until that kalpa?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Within my Dharma, even the most grave offenses can be repented."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“If there is a bodhisattva who harbors malice and resentment, yet rejoices within himself and speaks of it to others, that person can no longer be made to repent.”
If a bodhisattva is reviled or met with hatred and resentment, they should think to themselves:
"Alas! What I have done is without benefit."
"From then on, I never again dared to act in such a way.
Furthermore, I reproached myself:
'Human birth is difficult to obtain; for this reason, one ought to endure all things from others.'"
How much less, then, should I engage in verbal disputes with others?
I shall act as a bridge for the people of the ten directions, so that they may all tread upon me and cross over.
Since I have this intention, how could I ever again engage in disputes with others?
One should stand firm like a deaf sheep, enduring all evils and never committing any evil thought.
When I become a Buddha, I shall establish all people of the ten directions in parinirvāṇa; I shall no longer contend with others nor harbor anger toward them, for the sake of the path of the Arhat.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When bodhisattvas dwell together with one another, what should their practice be?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"When Bodhisattvas look at one another, they should regard each other as they would the Buddha, thinking in their hearts:
'We share the same teacher, the same boat, and the same path; what is studied by this one, I too shall study.'"

"Thus, if there are other bodhisattvas who wish to take pleasure in training in the path of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha, and if they associate with them, even if such persons exist, I shall not associate with them.
However, those who wish to seek the Buddha-way in every lifetime should follow one another and train in this way, for we share a common Dharma."
Chapter 22: On Training. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Two, "On Training," Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does a bodhisattva train in impermanence as training in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)?"
Is training in non-arising training for the sake of *sarvajñatā*?
Is training in the departure from lust training for the sake of *sarvajñatā*?
Is training in cessation training for the sake of *sarvajñatā*?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Regarding what you asked:
'Is training in impermanence training for sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)?'"

Regarding this, Subhūti, what do you think? This *tathāgata* is originally non-existent (*abhāva*); it is through following causes and conditions that one attains the state of a *tathāgata*. Could there ever be an end to the word "originally non-existent"?
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “No, World-Honored One; as the Buddha has said, it is not so.
The Buddha spoke to Subhūti:

"To train for the sake of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is to train thus in the prajñāpāramitā; to train thus is to train in the state of a tathāgata, to train in the powers, to train in the fearlessnesses, and to train in all the Buddha-dharmas."
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they practice all the dharmas of training.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, Māra and his retinues cannot destroy them midway;
by training thus, the bodhisattva will swiftly attain the stage of *avaivartika*.
A bodhisattva who trains in this way will swiftly approach the seat beneath the Bodhi tree;
a bodhisattva who trains in this way is training in the entirety of the Buddha-way;
a bodhisattva who trains in this way is practicing the Dharma.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they exercise supreme great compassion;
thus they train in equanimity.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they turn the twelvefold wheel of Dharma in its three aspects.
"When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they train to deliver and extinguish all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
when a bodhisattva trains in this way, they train in the gateway to the nectar-like Dharma.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Subhūti.
“Only those who are untiring can study this; practicing such study constitutes studying the path for all people throughout the ten directions of the world.
A Bodhisattva who studies in this manner does not enter the hells, the realm of animals, or the realm of hungry ghosts;
a Bodhisattva who studies in this manner will never be born in a borderland.”
Training in this way, one will no longer be born among the ignorant or the impoverished;
training in this way, one will no longer be blind, deaf, mute, or diseased;
training in this way, one will not violate the ten precepts.
Training in this way, one does not follow divination or fortune-telling;
training in this way, one stays far away from those who do not uphold the precepts.
A bodhisattva training in this way does not aspire to be reborn among the Nirmāṇarati devas.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva possesses *upāyakauśalya*. What is this *upāyakauśalya* of the *prajñāpāramitā*? From within the *prajñāpāramitā*, *upāyakauśalya* emerges;
by means of this *upāyakauśalya*, one enters the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) while extinguishing the self, yet does not follow the dharmas of those absorptions.
“A Bodhisattva who trains in this way does so to attain the power of purity, to attain the power of fearlessness, and to attain the power of the purity of the Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since all dharmas possessed by the Buddha are fundamentally pure, what constitutes a Bodhisattva’s attainment of the purity of dharmas?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva trains in this way, he trains in the purity of non-apprehension and the purity of all dharmas.
It is thus, Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they feel neither regret nor weariness; this is what it means to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*. Those who have not yet attained the Way are deluded;

they do not understand this Dharma and do not perceive this reality. For the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva always exerts diligence, thinking: "When people see me, they too shall emulate my diligence. For this reason, the bodhisattva attains power, diligence, and fearlessness.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they fully know the thoughts and intentions of all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions; none can surpass them.
It is like the earth producing gold and silver.
Only a few emerge from their station.
Thus it is, Subhūti;
only a few people follow the teaching and training of the dharma of the prajñāpāramitā.
It is as if, Subhūti,
few people seek the position of a Cakravartin king, while many seek the position of a minor king.
In the same way, Subhūti, [few seek the path of the Bodhisattva].
Few people follow the teachings of the *prajñāpāramitā* dharma; yet from among them, many seek the state of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.
Among those bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], few follow the teachings of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and even among those who study the *prajñāpāramitā*, few attain the stage of *avaivartika*.
A bodhisattva should form this thought:
"I shall study with diligence so as to aspire to and reach the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression). Furthermore, Subhūti!

Practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not harbor thoughts of anger toward others, does not seek out the faults of others, has no stinginess or greed in the mind, no mind that violates precepts, no mind harboring resentment, no indolence, no confusion, and no delusion.
When the Bodhisattva studies the Prajñāpāramitā at that time, all the other pāramitās are fully encompassed by it.

Studying the Prajñāpāramitā is for the purpose of illuminating all the pāramitās, for the purpose of entering into all the pāramitās, and studying the Prajñāpāramitā is for the purpose of bringing the remaining pāramitās to fulfillment.
For example, it is as if someone were to say:
"This is my own domain; I shall externally establish twelve categories.
It is thus, Subhūti!
