The bodhisattva’s training in the perfection of wisdom is entirely subsumed within it.
For example, Subhūti,
when a person dies and their life-force is exhausted, all the faculties of the body cease.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva trains in the perfection of wisdom, they train in all the perfections, for all of them are subsumed therein.
A bodhisattva who wishes to train in crossing over all the perfections should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva wishes to study the prajñāpāramitā, they are studying the infinite.
Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the people within a single buddha-field many?
Subhūti replied to the Buddha,
“Very much.
The Buddha said:

"If there were a bodhisattva who made offerings to as many people as those within a single Buddha-field, and continued making such offerings until the end of their own life, would their merit not be great?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It would be very much so."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"It is not as good as a bodhisattva maintaining the prajñāpāramitā for even the duration of two fingers snapping together.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme; for this reason, one swiftly attains Buddhahood. Thus it is, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva who wishes to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become the sole Honored One among the people of the ten directions; who wishes to provide for and bestow gifts upon the poor, the destitute, and the solitary throughout the ten directions; who seeks the realm of the Buddha; who desires to obtain the wisdom that the Buddha delights in; who desires to obtain the solitary roar of a lion; who desires to attain the station of a Buddha—if they wish to obtain all these things, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.”
"A Bodhisattva who trains in the Prajñāpāramitā trains in all other dharmas as well.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Does a Bodhisattva also train in the dharma of an Arhat?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Even though one knows the dharmas of an arhat, if one does not delight in practicing them nor train in the meritorious deeds performed by an arhat, how could one ever attain it?"
The Bodhisattva fully knows all that is practiced by Arhats, yet he does not train in it, does not practice it, and does not dwell within it.

When a Bodhisattva trains in this manner, there is no one in the heavens above or the world below who can surpass him; he completely transcends the level of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, and thus draws near to Sarvajñā (omniscience).
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they are not far from the *prajñāpāramitā* and are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they neither increase nor decrease within the dharma of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and they remain apart from the paths of the arhat and the pratyekabuddha.
If a bodhisattva further forms this thought:

"By upholding this prajñāpāramitā, I shall attain sarvajñatā," they possess a limited conception and thus do not practice the prajñāpāramitā; nor does the prajñāpāramitā possess any such characteristic.
"One should maintain the attainment of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) without thought, without vision, and without conceptualization; this is called practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. Chapter 23:

On Guarding Practice (*Caryā-rakṣaṇa-parivarta*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-three: On Guarding Practice. At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra was seated in the great assembly and had this thought:
"Regarding the practice of a bodhisattva, there is no one in the world of the ten directions who can surpass it, let alone reaching the state of Buddhahood oneself."

In the ten directions, a human rebirth is difficult to obtain; having obtained it, a long life in peace and security is rare; and among those who have attained this, one who resolves their mind to practice the Buddha-way is difficult to find—how much more so is one who practices the Buddha-way with a sincere heart?
"One who wishes to act as a leader for all people throughout the ten directions is difficult to find.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra transformed himself into mandārava flowers, took them and scattered them over the Buddha; having scattered them, he spoke these words:
"Is it by practicing the bodhisattva path that one proceeds toward the Buddha-way?"

All their vows shall be fulfilled; they will be closely protected and fully guarded. Those who practice in this manner shall all attain Buddhahood, becoming fully endowed with the teachings of all sūtras, the teachings of the *Sarvajña* (Omniscience) sūtras, and the teachings of the *Tathāgata* sūtras; it is the same for the teachings of the *Avivartika* (Non-retrogression) sūtras as well.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"If a person seeks the Buddha with a sincere heart, then within this Dharma, even a single moment of reflection will not be far from it.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:

"I desire to cause people to increase their mindfulness within the Dharma and not grow weary of the suffering of birth and death; for all that is above and below heaven is suffering, yet for the sake of humanity, one must endure all diligent and arduous practices."
The mind forms this thought:

"All those who have not yet crossed over shall be caused to cross over; all those who have not yet been liberated shall be caused to be liberated; all those who are terrified shall be caused to find peace; and all those who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa shall be caused to attain parinirvāṇa."
Śakra Devānām Indra asked the Buddha:
“What merit does a bodhisattva who has newly resolved gain by exhorting others and rejoicing in their joy?
What merit does a bodhisattva who follows the successive stages gain by exhorting others and rejoicing in their joy?”

“Even up to those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and those who have reached the highest level of *avaivarta*, if one encourages them and assists them in their joy, what kind of merit will they obtain?
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:

“The weight of Mount Sumeru may still be known by its number of pounds; however, the merit from encouraging and assisting those who first resolve their minds toward awakening (*prathamacittotpādika-bodhisattva*) and sharing in their joy is immeasurable.”
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"One may still weigh and measure the extent of a single Buddha-field, but the merit of an A-jū (Aśubha) Bodhisattva who exhorts others and assists them in their joy has no limit."
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"If one were to take all the water in every ocean within the realm of a single Buddha, break a single hair into a hundred parts, and use one such part to draw out that ocean water until it was entirely exhausted, one might still be able to count the number of drops; yet the merit of an irreversible Bodhisattva who practices exhortation toward others and assists them in their joy is beyond counting."
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:

“One might still be able to measure the extent of the empty space contained within all the realms of incalculable buddha-fields—whether it be a bushel and a half, a peck and a half, or a pint and a half—and thus know its volume; yet the merit of an *anavivarta* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva who practices exhortation toward others and assists them in their joy is inexhaustible.”
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Those who are distracted by Māra will not rejoice upon hearing this; those belonging to Māra’s retinue who do not rejoice upon hearing this have descended from the heavens of Māra, having heard this and failing to rejoice."
Why is this? If there is one who seeks the Buddha with intention, it is for the purpose of destroying the realm of Māra;
if there is one who resolves to seek the Buddha, one should assist them in their joy, for this is the destruction of the realm of Māra.
"The mind shall not depart from the Buddha, nor from the Dharma, nor from the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; in this way, one should assist them in their joy.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"As Śakra Devānām Indra has spoken, those who assist others in their joy draw near to the Buddha. By virtue of this merit of assisting in joy, in every place where they are born throughout their lives, they will be desired by all people for offerings; they shall never hear an evil sound, they shall have no fear of falling into the three evil realms, they shall always be reborn in the heavens, and they shall always be honored throughout the ten directions."
Why is this? Such persons who assist the Bodhisattva in his joy act as universal givers and protectors for all people throughout the ten directions. Why is this?

"A bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment gradually increases [their merit] until they personally attain Buddhahood; having achieved Buddhahood, they shall deliver all people throughout the ten directions.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The mind is like an illusion; by what cause can one attain Buddhahood?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive an illusion?
Subhūti replied:
"No. Even the transformation-illusion is not seen.

If the illusory mind were separated from the transformation, and the transformation were separated from the illusory mind—even if these were separated, would one see a distinct dharma that could lead to the attainment of the Buddha-way?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Neither seeing nor departing from—wherein transformation and illusion are both departed from and illusion is not seen even by the mind—one shall attain Buddhahood. Yet there is no dharma and no seeing; what dharma, then, should be preached? Is there attainment or non-attainment?"

These dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, and even their remoteness is fundamentally non-existent. Whether one attains them or does not attain them, they are fundamentally unarisen; nor is there anyone who becomes a Buddha. Even if there were no dharmas, one still could not become a Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If that is so, the Prajñāpāramitā is originally devoid of opposition; dharmas are originally devoid [of self-nature], and thus there is no opposition, no realization, no guarding, no practice, and no dharma whatsoever that can be attained."
Why is this? Because apart from the Prajñāpāramitā there is fundamentally no form, and fundamentally no separation; for what reason, then, could one attain Buddhahood within the Prajñāpāramitā?
“The Buddha is detached from that which is fundamentally non-existent; what is there that is fundamentally non-existent which could attain Buddhahood?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“As Subhūti has spoken of detachment, so too this Prajñāpāramitā is non-existent, detached from that which is fundamentally non-existent, namely Sarvajñatā.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Although one is detached from the fundamental nature of the prajñāpāramitā, that fundamental nature itself has no place from which it arises. Subhūti!"
"One should contemplate in this way and enter deeply into guarding [the mind]; therefore, by being detached from what was originally non-existent, one attains Buddhahood.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Although one knows that detachment from the original nature means that the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent, this constitutes not guarding the *prajñāpāramitā*. One who does not fully practice the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot attain Buddhahood."
The Buddha said:

"As Subhūti has said, one does not become a Buddha by attaining the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor does one become a Buddha by being apart from it or not apart from it; yet one cannot become a Buddha apart from the *prajñāpāramitā*. One who does not attain the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot become a Buddha."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, it is exceedingly profound and difficult to fathom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"As for what you said:
'The bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound and difficult to reach.
The diligent and ascetic practices and the profound dharmas spoken of by the bodhisattva do not reside in the grasping of nirvāṇa."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the matters thus described, a bodhisattva does not engage in arduous practices. Why is this?"
There is no one who realizes [it], nor is there anyone who attains realization within the Prajñāpāramitā, nor is there any dharma of the sūtra that can be realized.
When a bodhisattva hears this and is neither afraid, nor indolent, nor discouraged, this is called practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.
Although one performs these practices, one does not perceive the performance of them; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Although one draws near to Buddhahood, one does not perceive it; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
To remain far removed from arhats and pratyekabuddhas, neither perceiving nor thinking of them—this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is like space, which has no thought of being either near or far.
Why is this? Because emptiness is fundamentally without form.
When practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, there is neither being far from the Buddha nor being near to the Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā has no form.
It is like a magician who creates an illusory person; that illusory person does not form such a thought:
"The Teacher is near to me; the person I observe is far from me.
Why is this? Because the manifested person has no physical form.
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this; it does not form such a thought as:
"The path of the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha is far from me, while the path of the Buddha is near to me."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā has no form.
It is like a reflection appearing in water, which does not form such a thought:
"For what reason does the reflection appear in the water?
If something is near, one does not think of it as near; if it is far, one likewise does not think of it as far. Why is this?
Because a shadow has no form, so it is with the Prajñāpāramitā; it likewise does not have this thought:
"Are the paths of the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha far?"
"Is the Buddha-way near?
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā has no form.

The Prajñāpāramitā has no object of affection and no object of aversion; that which belongs to the Tathāgata is without attachment and without arising, and the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise: it neither arises nor is it attached.
For example, it is as if a Tathāgata were to manifest a transformed person; that person would not form the thought,
"The path of the Arhat or Pratyekabuddha is far removed from me," nor would they say:
"The Buddha-way is near to me.
Why is this? Because the transformed person has no physical form.
The Prajñāpāramitā also does not form this thought:
"The path of the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha is far removed from me.
Nor does it think:
"The Buddha-way is near to me.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā has no form.

For example, suppose a skillful artisan carves a mechanical wooden figure, or perhaps a wooden figure in the form of various animals; it cannot move or act on its own, but moves only in response to external forces. This wooden figure does not think:
"I shall move, shake, bend, stretch, lower, or raise myself, so as to delight those who behold me."
Why is this? Because the wooden man originally has no thought.
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: according to what each person practices, they all individually obtain it; yet, although this is so, the Prajñāpāramitā is neither form nor thought.
It is, for example, like constructing a great ship upon the ocean; why is this?
It is because one intends to ferry merchants across.
Yet the ship itself does not form such a thought:
"I shall deliver sentient beings.
Why is this? Because the boat is fundamentally without thought.
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: according to what each person practices, they each attain it for themselves; likewise, the Prajñāpāramitā has neither form nor thought. It is just so.
For example, in a vast wilderness, all things—the myriad grains, hundredfold crops, grasses, and trees—all grow therein, yet the earth does not form this thought:
"I shall produce them," or "I shall not produce them."
The Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all dharmas of the sūtras, yet it does not even think:
"From this, there is arising or non-arising. Why is this?
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is fundamentally formless.

It is like a *maṇi* jewel from which all its treasures emerge; likewise, the *prajñāpāramitā* brings forth all the sūtras, dharmas, distinctions, and instructions. Even so, the *prajñāpāramitā* remains without thought.
For example, when the sun shines upon the four continents, its radiance does not think or say,
"I shall illuminate them all. Likewise,
although the Prajñāpāramitā illuminates all the teachings of the sūtras, the Prajñāpāramitā itself remains without thought.
For example, just as water reaches everywhere, yet the water does not form the thought,
"I shall go somewhere," so too the *prajñāpāramitā* reaches all sūtras and dharmas; nevertheless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without thought.
For example, just as there is nowhere that wind does not reach, yet the wind does not form the thought,
"I shall go somewhere," so too is it with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) which accomplishes all sūtras and dharmas; even so, the perfection of wisdom has no such thought.
For example, the summit of Mount Sumeru is adorned by the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, yet Mount Sumeru does not form this thought:
"I shall adorn the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven from above."
"The Prajñāpāramitā accomplishes sarvajñatā (all-knowledge); yet, even so, the Prajñāpāramitā is without thought.
It is like the great ocean from which all manner of rare and precious jewels emerge, yet the seawater does not form this thought:
'I shall produce these jewels from within.'"
In this same way, the Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all the teachings of the sūtras; yet, even so, the Prajñāpāramitā is without thought.

For example, just as the Buddha gives rise to all merits and completely covers all beings, bestowing an impartial mind upon the people of the ten directions, so too does the Prajñāpāramitā bring all the teachings of the sūtras to fulfillment.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
is it a sublime practice? Subhūti replied:
"What I have heard from the Buddha is that when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, it is not a practice of loftiness.
Thereupon, several hundreds of thousands of devas of the realm of desire had this thought:
"We should pay homage to those in the ten directions who have resolved their minds upon the path of the Bodhisattvas."
Why is this? Because when practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not enter *parinirvāṇa* midway.
In this way, the bodhisattva exerts himself in ascetic practices, yet does not fall into or realize [the fruit] within these dharmas.
Subhūti said to the devas:
"Although one does not fall midway or realize [nirvāṇa] prematurely, this is not considered arduous toil.

To don the armor of the Dharma for the sake of immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* beings throughout the ten directions, in order to deliver them and lead them to nirvāṇa—this indeed is the difficulty of arduous toil."
These people are fundamentally non-existent; since they are fundamentally non-existent, they cannot be sought or found.
Thus, the bodhisattva reflects:
"In order to deliver people, I deliver the people of the ten directions; in doing so, I deliver emptiness."

Why is this? Emptiness is neither distant nor near, and it possesses nothing at all. For this reason, the bodhisattva practices with diligent austerity, seeking that which is fundamentally non-existent in persons. Desiring to deliver beings, he delivers what is like empty space; he dons the armor of virtue. He dons the armor of virtue for the sake of persons, desiring to ferry them across; therefore, the bodhisattva dons the armor of virtue.
As the Buddha has taught, a person has no fundamental basis.
To clearly understand that the basis of a person is non-existent is what constitutes the deliverance of persons.
That a bodhisattva hears this and is neither afraid nor terrified is what constitutes the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Apart from persons, there is fundamentally no person; apart from form, there is fundamentally no form; apart from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is fundamentally no consciousness; apart from all dharmas, there is fundamentally no dharma.
“That a bodhisattva hears this and is neither afraid nor indolent—this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“For what reason is a bodhisattva neither afraid nor indolent?”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Because it is originally non-existent, there is no fear; because it is originally pure, there is no laxity. Why is this so?"
Seeking the root of indolence, one finds that it has no cause; indolence itself, likewise, does not exist.
When a bodhisattva hears this teaching on non-indolence and is neither afraid nor terrified, this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"When a Bodhisattva practices in this manner, all the devas pay him homage, and all the Brahmās pay him homage.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Not only do the devas and the Brahmās pay homage to the Bodhisattva; even up to the Akaniṣṭha devas—including the Abṛha, Atapa, and Sudṛśa heavens—all pay homage to the Bodhisattva who practices the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, the present Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as incalculable asaṃkhyeyas, all keep the Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā in mind and together protect him, knowing that this Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā is an avaivartika (non-retrogressive)."

Suppose all the people within as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were made into Māras, and each single Māra were transformed into as many followers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; even if such Māras, each with such a retinue of followers, were to attempt together to harm a Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, they could not destroy them midway, nor could they find an opportunity to prevail against them midway.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom through two dharmas, Māra cannot find an opportunity to interfere midway.
What are these two?
First, viewing all sūtras and dharmas as empty; second, not abandoning sentient beings of the ten directions but protecting them all.
These are the two matters.
There are two matters by which a bodhisattva cannot be moved by any māras.
What are these two matters?
First, not losing one's original vow; second, being protected and watched over by all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
These are the two matters.
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, the devas go to the bodhisattva’s dwelling to inquire about the profound teachings of the sutras, and the devas praise and commend them, saying:
"I shall soon become a Buddha.

One should establish oneself according to this Dharma teaching; having established oneself according to this Dharma teaching, all who suffer distress shall obtain protection, those who have not yet found refuge shall find a place of self-refuge, one shall act as a Dharma-shelter for the sake of humanity, and those who are sightless shall be granted clear vision.

For those who establish themselves according to this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the present Buddhas of the ten directions—countless and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* in number—all together protect and sustain those who practice the *prajñāpāramitā*. Each of these Buddhas, within the fourfold assemblies in their respective lands, speaks of the merits of these bodhisattvas and each praises them as excellent.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"It is as if I were now praising and speaking of the Buddha Rāṣṭrapāla.
The Buddha spoke again:

"Just as the Bodhisattvas in my own buddha-field practice the Prajñāpāramitā, so too do the Buddhas of the ten directions now likewise praise and speak of the Bodhisattvas who practice the Prajñāpāramitā."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Do all Buddhas praise bodhisattvas in this way?
The Buddha said:
"No praise is bestowed.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"There are those who practice the bodhisattva path but have not yet attained the stage of *avaivartika*; the Buddhas likewise praise them."
Subhūti asked the Buddha again:
"What kind of practice of the bodhisattva path is praised by the Buddha?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“There are bodhisattvas who follow the practices performed by the Buddha Akṣobhya when he was a bodhisattva in his previous lives, as well as the practices performed by the Buddha Roca when he was a bodhisattva in his previous lives; there are bodhisattvas who follow these teachings, and for this reason, the Buddhas of the ten directions praise these bodhisattvas.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the various sūtras and dharmas of the prajñāpāramitā, they have faith that all things are fundamentally non-arising. Although this bodhisattva has not yet attained the bliss of the dharma of non-arising, they establish their faith therein. They believe that all dharmas are fundamentally empty; although this bodhisattva has not yet attained the stage of *avaivartika*, they believe that all sūtras and dharmas are fundamentally non-existent like *nirvāṇa*. Although this bodhisattva has not yet entered the ground of *avaivartika*, by establishing themselves in accordance with these teachings of the Dharma, they will swiftly attain *avaivartika*."
Because there are those who should practice this Dharma, the Buddhas of the ten directions all together praise these bodhisattvas.
These bodhisattvas, for the sake of transcending the stage of the Arhat and the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, proceed toward the stage of the Buddha.

If there is a bodhisattva who practices in accordance with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are praised by all Buddhas; one should know that such a bodhisattva will before long be established in the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva hears the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they believe it without doubt.
The bodhisattva forms this thought:"
"It is exactly as the Buddha has taught; it is true and not otherwise.
This Bodhisattva shall, in the future, hear this Prajñāpāramitā from the presence of Akṣobhya Buddha, and what he hears from other Bodhisattvas shall likewise be so.
One who forms such faith in the *prajñāpāramitā* is considered to be established upon the stage of *avaivartika*.

If there are those who hear the *prajñāpāramitā* and believe in it, their merit is exceedingly great and not small; how much more so for a bodhisattva who stands in accordance with the teachings of the *prajñāpāramitā* dharma? One who stands in accordance with these teachings of the dharma will swiftly enter into *sarvajñatā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If, apart from the fundamental non-arising of all dharmas, no dharma can be attained, what dharma is there that becomes a Buddha?
What dharma is there that speaks or expounds the sūtras?"
The Buddha said: "As Subhūti has stated:
'If one is detached from the fundamental non-existence of dharmas and nothing can be attained, what dharma is there that becomes a Buddha?'"
"Furthermore, there is no dharma that can be called 'one who preaches the sūtra.

This fundamental non-existence (mūla-abhāva) is itself without basis; what could possibly exist within this fundamental non-existence to establish a 'non-existent one'? There is no fundamental non-existence that shall attain Buddhahood, nor is there any fundamental dharma that acts as a Buddha."
"Fundamentally there is no non-existence, and even the one who preaches the sutra cannot be apprehended.
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep; it is through the diligent and arduous practice of a bodhisattva that they personally attain Buddhahood."

Why is this? Because there is no dharma of words that can be apprehended, nor is there anyone established within primordial non-existence; furthermore, there is no dharma that shall become a Buddha, nor is there anyone who preaches the sutra.
"When a bodhisattva hears this, they do not fear, do not tremble, do not doubt,
and do not grow weary. Subhūti said to Śakra-devānām-indra, "Just as Śakra-devānām-indra has spoken,
when a bodhisattva diligently practices and hears the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they believe it without hesitation and do not grow weary."
Subhūti replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“Kauśika! Since all dharmas are empty, what is there to cause doubt or weariness?”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"As you have spoken, Subhūti, everything is explained as being empty; it is entirely without attachment."

"It is, for example, like shooting at empty space where there is nothing to which one can become attached; so too is the sutra spoken by Subhūti, for which there is likewise nothing to which one can become attached.
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Is what I have said in accordance with the teachings of the Buddha's Dharma?"
"Is there any increase or decrease?
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra: "Kauśika!
As the Buddha has taught, the Dharma teachings are all equal and without distinction; as Subhūti has spoken, he speaks only of the matter of emptiness.
Subhūti does not perceive the Prajñāpāramitā, nor does he perceive one who practices the Prajñāpāramitā, nor does he perceive one who attains Buddhahood;
he does not perceive Sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), nor does he perceive one who attains Sarvajñatā.
One does not perceive the Tathāgata, nor is there anyone who attains the state of a Tathāgata;
one does not perceive that which is unarisen, nor does one perceive anyone who realizes that which is unarisen;
one does not perceive the ten powers, nor is there anyone who seeks the ten powers.
One does not perceive the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), nor does one perceive one who seeks the four fearlessnesses.
The sūtra-dharma is fundamentally pure and is likewise unobtainable.

Subhūti stands according to this teaching of non-attainment; Subhūti, standing thus according to the teaching of non-attainment, is a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* to a degree a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and ten-thousandfold.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom sets aside the stage of the Buddha-way and the stages of the paths of the arhats and pratyekabuddhas; since these do not equal the stage of this bodhisattva, one who wishes to uphold the honor of all people in the worlds of the ten directions should establish themselves in such a way according to the teachings of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, many tens of millions of devas from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven took up transformed māndārava flowers and scattered them over the Buddha. Having scattered them, the devas spoke thus:
"We, too, shall establish ourselves in accordance with the teachings of the Dharma."

At that time, one hundred and sixty bhikṣus sitting in the assembly rose, adjusted their robes, and paid homage to the Buddha. Having paid homage, each held a transformed mandārava flower in his hand; they scattered these flowers over the Buddha, and having scattered them, they spoke thus:
"We, too, shall establish ourselves in accordance with the Dharma teaching."

At that time, the Buddha smiled, and from his mouth issued rays of various colors. Their brilliance reached the buddha-fields of the ten directions, illuminating them all; the light then returned, circled the Buddha three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt down, and asked the Buddha:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; since you have smiled, there must be a meaning behind it."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These one hundred and sixty bhikṣus and the various devas shall become buddhas during this Bhadra-kalpa; they shall all share the same name, Uccanāgomin."

When they become Buddhas, the number of their bhikṣu-saṃghas shall each be equal, and their lifespans shall likewise each be equal; each of those lifespans shall be one hundred thousand years. They shall become Buddhas one after another in succession, and when they become Buddhas, each shall remain for the full duration of that world, raining down flowers of five colors.
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Eight;
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter 25: On the Successive Teachings. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Five: On the Successive Teachings.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“One who establishes [the practice] in this manner cannot be surpassed.”

When a bodhisattva establishes themselves in this way, it is as if they were established as a Buddha; in so establishing themselves, there is no one acting as their teacher. This is the establishment of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Those who wish to establish themselves in this way should follow the teachings of the Prajñāpāramitā.

If there should be one who practices this Prajñāpāramitā, it should be known that such a person has come from among human beings, or has come from the Tuṣita heaven. Such a person has either heard the Prajñāpāramitā from among human beings or from the Tuṣita heaven; they have either practiced it among human beings or practiced it in the Tuṣita heaven.

Why is this? After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, if the Prajñāpāramitā is seen in the ten directions or seen in the Tuṣita Heaven, and if there are those who practice this Prajñāpāramitā or transcribe it, all the Buddhas will look upon them and protect them.

This bodhisattva further teaches and transforms others, encouraging them toward harmonious union; one knows that this bodhisattva has made offerings to so many Buddhas since the past, and has not cultivated merit within the ranks of the arhats or pratyekabuddhas; one knows that this bodhisattva has studied this *prajñāpāramitā* since making offerings to so many Buddhas, remaining neither afraid nor terrified.

If there are those who receive the Prajñāpāramitā, those who study it, those who uphold it, those who understand its meaning, or those who follow it, know that such bodhisattvas are no different from seeing the Buddha face-to-face.
This bodhisattva neither halts nor slanders the *prajñāpāramitā*; one should know that this bodhisattva has been making offerings to numerous Buddhas.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Even if there are people who perform meritorious deeds for a Buddha and, with them, seek the state of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha, they will ultimately attain Buddhahood without exception."
"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā, they should always remain far removed from the paths of the arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"I entrust this prajñāpāramitā to you; hold it fast."

Ānanda! Regarding the sūtras I have spoken for you, setting aside the Prajñāpāramitā and the mahopāyakauśalya and the various mahādhāraṇīs—if all the other sūtras I have spoken that you have received were to be entirely scattered and lost, even though that would happen, the fault would be slight.
"If you were to lose or forget the Prajñāpāramitā that you have received from the Buddha, the fault would be exceedingly great and not small.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"I further entrust this Prajñāpāramitā to you.
