The city was four hundred and eighty li in length and breadth, constructed entirely of the seven treasures. It had seven concentric walls, between which stood marvelous trees made of the seven treasures. Above the walls were canopies of fine gauze and silk brocade made of the seven treasures, covering the tops of the walls. Between these were lattice-work pavilions made of the seven treasures, from which tinkling bells hung down. Outside each of the four city gates were pleasure pavilions. Surrounding the city were seven tiers of moats, within which grew various kinds of lotuses: *utpala*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *saugandhika*, and *mahāsaugandhika* lotuses, all blooming amidst the waters of the moats.
On the land there are *campaka* flowers; such various flowers number in the hundreds and thousands.
Within the ponds there are many diverse and wondrous birds—ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and other species of marvelous birds—numbering in the hundreds and thousands.
Within the pond were boats made of the seven treasures, and people boarded these boats to enjoy themselves and play within the water.

Throughout the city, five-colored banners and streamers were arranged in rows; furthermore, five-colored banners and streamers were suspended, and there were also various multicolored flower-canopies set out, filling every street and alleyway within the city.
It is like the palace of Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where the sounds of suspended banners, streamers, and music of hundreds and thousands of kinds never cease day after day.
It is like the Nandana-vana grove in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where the sounds of music and unending joy prevail; the happiness of that city is likewise such as this.

Within that city there were no ordinary people; they were all bodhisattvas. Among them were some who had achieved realization and some who had merely resolved their minds toward enlightenment, all dwelling together therein in a happiness beyond description.
All the garments and ornaments therein were of such profound and brilliant preciousness that they could not be further calculated.

In that land there was a bodhisattva named Dharmodgata, who was the most exalted and honored among the assembly of bodhisattvas; he enjoyed himself with six million eight hundred thousand ladies and handmaidens.

The bodhisattvas throughout the kingdom of Gandhāra constantly paid their respects to Dharmodgata. For him, they erected a high seat in the center of the city, with seats arranged in descending order on either side. Among them were thrones of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; each seat was adorned with multicolored embroidered hangings and cushions. Between the seats, various kinds of fragrant flowers were scattered, and above each seat was spread a canopy of interlaced precious jewels. All around, both inside and out, famous incenses were being burned.

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata constantly sat upon a high seat to preach the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas; among them were some who listened, some who wrote it down, some who studied it, some who recited it, and some who upheld it.
From here, go to the land of Gandhāra to where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata resides; he himself shall explain the Prajñāpāramitā to you, and he shall act as your teacher and instruct you.
Why is this? For thousands of billions of eons in the past, I have constantly been your teacher; I was your teacher at the very moment you first resolved to attain enlightenment.

When you go to your teacher’s presence, whether you see him or hear of him, do not speak of his faults, nor dwell upon them. If you should see him, be careful not to doubt him and be careful not to be indolent toward him.
Why is this? You have not yet mastered *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); you must clearly discern the works of Māra.
O son of good family!
Be careful not to follow them; do not employ the teachings of Māra.
When the Teacher is in the inner palace, his noble instructions should be honored no differently than if he were a Buddha.

Because you must rely upon the Dharma of the sutras, do not harbor thoughts of wealth, profit, or greed. Whatever you possess should be given to the Teacher; you should take delight in showing him sincere respect and reverence.
"One who practices this conduct without deficiency will, before long, be able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, having heard these instructions from the emanation Buddha, was immediately filled with leaping joy and exultation. Because of that leaping joy and exultation, he immediately attained the samādhi of beholding all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"

When we were originally Bodhisattvas, by means of our diligent application, we heard the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attained the realization of sarvajñatā; furthermore, we shall also obtain the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four ways in which there is nothing to guard against, and the eighteen unique qualities.

At that time, we also attained this samādhi, and at that time, the Buddhas likewise praised us in this way: "Your practice shall also be like ours; by practicing in this manner, you shall fully attain all the merits possessed by a bodhisattva."
Then, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita arose from his samādhi and had this thought:
"From where do all Buddhas originally come?
To where do they go?"
Having reflected thus, he again raised his voice and wept bitterly, and further thought:
"The Buddhas have instructed me to go to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata resides."
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva then departed from there.
On the way, he reached a country named Mārakānta (The Land Delightful to Māra). Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva stayed overnight in a garden outside the city and thought to himself:
"The Buddha’s sutras are truly difficult to obtain; how much more so is it to even hear them!"
"I shall serve my teacher to the best of my ability.

Now, this body of mine is moreover impoverished; I have no rare or precious objects, nor flowers or incense with which to make offerings to my teacher. Since I possess nothing at all, I beg leave to sell my own body and use the proceeds to make offerings to my teacher."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the city streets and bazaars, crying out for sale:
"Who wishes to buy me?
At that time, Māra was playing outside the city, sporting with fifty thousand court ladies; seeing the Bodhisattva from afar and hearing the sound of his self-proclamation, Māra thought to himself:
"This Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita has sold himself in order to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, intending to seek Buddhahood.
This person shall emerge from my realm and deliver a great multitude of beings."
"Shall I now perish?
Let the men and women of this entire land neither see my form nor hear my voice!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, finding no buyer for his body, rolled upon the ground, weeping and crying out loudly:
"I wish to sell my own body to provide for my teacher, yet there is no one at all who will buy it.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, seeing from afar in the heavens how Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva was thus diligent, thought to himself:
"I shall go down and test him to see whether he seeks Buddhahood with ultimate sincerity, and not merely out of flattery."
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra descended and transformed himself into a brāhmaṇa, asking Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!
Why do you undergo such diligent toil?"
"For what reason are you weeping so bitterly? Sadāprarudita replied,
"There is no need to ask."
The mendicant brahmin asked this up to three times:
"Whatever you wish to command, please tell me; I desire to assist you.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied:
“If you, O practitioner of the Way, wish to know, it is because I wish to sell myself in order to make offerings to my teacher.
The brāhmaṇa said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
“It is because you wish to make offerings to your teacher.”
The brahmin said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita: "Good man!
Now I wish to perform a great sacrifice; I desire human blood, I desire human flesh, I desire human marrow, and I desire human hearts."
"If you are able to give it to me, I shall provide you with even more wealth.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied with great joy,
"I am willing to give it to you."
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva immediately took up a knife and pierced both his arms; blood flowed profusely, which he took and gave to him.
He further cut the flesh from the inner parts of both his thighs and took it to give to him;
he then broke his own bones and took the marrow to give to him.
Just as he was about to stab his own chest, a daughter of an elder on a multi-storied pavilion saw him from afar and felt pity and compassion for him.
At that time, the daughter of the elder, accompanied by five hundred female musicians and court ladies, came to where the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita was and asked:
"O son of good family!..."
"You are still so young and upright; for what reason do you cut your own body?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied to the woman:
"Because I wish to make an offering to my teacher, for this reason I am selling my blood, my flesh, and my marrow, intending to take them to offer to my teacher."
At that time, the daughter of the elder asked the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"If one makes offerings to a teacher, what kind of merit can be obtained?"
"What is the name of that teacher?
Where does he reside?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied to the woman:
"The Master resides in the eastern direction; his name is Dharmodgata. He shall preach the Prajñāpāramitā for me.

Having heard it, I shall practice and maintain it, and by so doing, I shall swiftly attain Buddhahood. I shall personally obtain the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the four bases of intrepidity, the four ways in which there is nothing to guard, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. I shall turn the Wheel of Dharma and deliver all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
At that time, the daughter of the elder said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"As the noble son has said, there is nothing in the heavens above or the earth below that can compare to it."
"Do not distress yourself so; I myself will give you gold, silver, precious treasures, and rare objects.
I shall go accompanied by five hundred court ladies, for I also wish to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and further desire to hear the sutra."
At that time, the brahmin said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
Such diligence is difficult to equal.
Do you wish to know me,
son of good family?
"I am Śakra Devānām Indra, King of the Gods; I have merely been testing you.
Whatever wish you seek to obtain, I shall grant it all to you.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied to Śakra, King of the Gods:
"If you would have compassion for me, restore my body to its former state.
The Bodhisattva’s body was immediately restored to its former state.
Śakra Devānām Indra then departed.
At that time, the daughter of the elder said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"Let us go together to my parents' home to request gold, silver, precious gems, and rare objects, and then depart with their permission."
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita immediately followed her to his parents' house.
When the girl returned, she related these matters in detail to her parents, who replied to her, saying:
"What you have said is most excellent; it is difficult to hear."
"I also wish to travel with you; however, reflecting upon my own old age, I am unable to go myself.
Tell me whatever it is that you desire to obtain. The girl replied, "I desire gold, silver, rare treasures, and exquisite objects."
Her parents said, "Daughter, take whatever you please.

Thereupon, the girl took for herself gold, silver, various jewels, rare treasures, and excellent objects; she filled [the carts] with much powdered sandalwood, famous incense, and other miscellaneous precious perfumes. She loaded five hundred wagons with these heavy loads and was accompanied by five hundred female attendants.
At that time, five hundred handmaidens all went to inform the parents of the noble daughter, saying,
"We wish to serve the noble lady and follow the Bodhisattva on his journey.
Having reported this, they immediately set out together with her.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with the group of five hundred women, gradually led the way and departed.

From afar he saw banners and streamers in the land of Gandhāra, like those suspended in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; from afar he heard the sounds of music in the land of Gandhāra; and again, from afar he saw that above the city walls of Gandhāra there were seven layers of canopies made of the seven treasures, and beneath them were seven layers of jeweled lattices, with bells hanging between each layer. Surrounding the city on all sides were seven layers of trees made of the seven treasures, and outside the city were pavilions for recreation where men and women played and enjoyed themselves—some riding in chariots as performers for their own amusement, others walking about as performers for their own amusement. Fragrant winds dispersed in all directions, spreading everywhere so that there was no one who did not smell them, just like celestial incense; for this reason, it is called the land of Gandhāra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women all saw this from afar.
Having seen it, they were all filled with great joy and leaped for gladness, thinking to themselves:
"It would be improper for us to ride in carriages; we should descend and enter the city on foot."
“Then the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women together entered through the western city gate.

Once the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had entered within the city gate, he saw from afar a high terrace, intricately carved and inlaid with gold and silver, painted in the five colors—black, yellow, red, white, and blue—which shone with brilliant radiance. On all four sides and corners of the terrace, the eaves were turned upward toward the sun; bells were suspended, and banners and streamers fluttered as musical instruments played in harmony.”
Having seen it from afar, he asked a person coming out of the city:
"What kind of terrace is this, adorned with seven-jeweled lattices so exquisitely beautiful?
That person replied to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"Do you not know, O worthy one?
Within this assembly there is a bodhisattva named Dharmodgata, the most supreme and honored among all people; there is no one who does not make offerings to him and pay him homage."

Because this bodhisattva employs the *prajñāpāramitā*, he constructs this dais; within it is a casket made of the seven precious jewels, with a base of purple-polished gold, upon which the *prajñāpāramitā* is written. Inside the casket are several hundred kinds of various famous incenses.

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata made offerings every day, taking various flowers and famous incenses, lighting lamps, hanging banners and pennants, using flower canopies and various jewels, and employing hundreds of kinds of music to offer them to the Prajñāpāramitā.
The other bodhisattvas’ offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā were likewise.
The devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven each thrice during the day and thrice during the night brought maṇḍārava flowers and mahāmaṇḍārava flowers to offer to the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner.

When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women heard this, they were filled with great joy and leaped for joy beyond measure. Together they went to the place where the Prajñāpāramitā dais was located. They took various flowers and various incenses and scattered them over the Prajñāpāramitā; they took various robes woven with golden threads, some of whom scattered the robes over it, some of whom folded the robes, some of whom spread the robes against the walls, and some of whom offered the robes as alms.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women, having made offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, proceeded to a place not far from the great assembly hall where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata’s high seat was located. From afar they saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata seated upon the high seat; he appeared youthful, with a handsome countenance, radiating a brilliant light as he preached the Prajñāpāramitā to several thousand billions of people.

When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, they were all filled with great joy and leaped for gladness. They took various kinds of flowers and incense and scattered them over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata; they further took many kinds of jewels and scattered them upon him. They also took hundreds of kinds of precious garments of diverse colors and offered them to the Bodhisattva, prostrating themselves before the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and circumambulating him eight hundred times.
Having done so, they spoke these words: "We, too, shall surely attain this honored sutra, and we shall likewise become as you are."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, holding the profound sutras and elegant words, addressed the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women, saying:
"Welcome; I hope you have not been fatigued."
"Whatever you are commanded by others to do, or whatever you desire to obtain, do not hesitate or find it difficult.
I am a teacher who delivers beings; I have nothing at all that I hold dear.
Then, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita said to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata:

"When I was originally seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, I wept aloud in a desolate mountain. In the sky above, there appeared a transformed Buddha, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks and possessing a purple-golden hue from which billions of radiant flames issued forth. At that time, the transformed Buddha sighed in praise and said to me:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
"One who seeks the Prajñāpāramitā should act in this manner.
He then said to me:

"Go east from here for more than twenty thousand *li*; there is a country named Gandhāra, four hundred and eighty *li* in breadth and length. Its precious jewels and ornamental decorations are like those of the palaces in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There is a Bodhisattva named Dharmodgata, the most honored among men, who constantly and repeatedly instructs others."

Go to that place, and you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā; for throughout thousands of billions of past eons, he has constantly been your teacher—he was the teacher at the time you first resolved to attain enlightenment.

At that time, hearing the name and reputation of the Teacher, he was filled with great joy and exultation, unable to contain himself; because of this joy and exultation, he immediately attained the samādhi of seeing all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, all the Buddhas praised me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
One who seeks the Prajñāpāramitā should do so in this manner."
When we originally sought the Buddha, we sought the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner; those who obtain the Prajñāpāramitā will themselves attain Buddhahood in this same manner.
After the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra for me, he disappeared from sight.
I thought to myself:
"From where did the Buddha come?"
"Where does he go?
I bring this matter before you, Master; I pray that you will explain it for me: from where does the Buddha come, and where does he go?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata replied,
"Virtuous one, listen well.
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita replied:
"Very well! Listen attentively.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata in reply.
"Emptiness originally comes from nowhere, and when it departs, it goes nowhere; the Buddha is also like this.
Non-conception originally comes from nowhere, and when it departs, it goes nowhere; the Buddha is also like this."
Having no location, they originally come from nowhere, and in departing, they go nowhere; the Buddha is also like this.
Having no place of birth, they originally come from nowhere, and in departing, they go nowhere; the Buddha is also like this.
The formless has originally no place from which it comes, and upon departing, it likewise has no place to which it goes; so too is it with the Buddha.
Illusion has originally no place from which it comes, and upon departing, it likewise has no place to which it goes; so too is it with the Buddha.
A wild horse has originally no place from which it comes, and upon departing, it likewise has no place to which it goes; the Buddha is also like this.
A person within a dream has originally no place from which they come, and upon departing, they likewise have no place to which they go; the Buddha is also like this.
Nirvana fundamentally comes from nowhere, and in departing, it goes nowhere; the Buddha is also like this.
Mental imagery fundamentally comes from nowhere, and in departing, it goes nowhere; the Buddha is also like this.

There is no arising; there is no duration, for originally there is nowhere from which it comes, and in departing, there is nowhere to which it goes. If one wishes to know the Buddha, it is also like this.
There is no destination, for originally there is nowhere from which he comes, and in departing, there is nowhere to which he goes. If one wishes to know the Buddha, it is also like this.
Space fundamentally comes from nowhere, and in departing it goes nowhere; if one wishes to know the Buddha, it is also like this.
The fruit of the sūtras fundamentally comes from nowhere, and in departing it goes nowhere; if one wishes to know the Buddha, it is also like this.
"The fundamental source has nowhere from which it comes, and its departure likewise has nowhere to which it goes; if you wish to know the Buddha, he is also like this.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita heard of the profound matters of the Dharma from the Buddha—matters such as these, which are incalculable, inconceivable, and immeasurable—and [he realized] that this Great Dharma is just so.
At that time, while still seated, he attained sixty thousand gates of samādhi.
What are these gates of samādhi? They are:
the samādhi of having no location, the samādhi of being without fear such that one's hair does not stand on end, and the liberation from all māras.
The Samādhi of Fearlessness; the Samādhi of Liberation from the Root of Craving; the Samādhi of Emerging from Battle and Departing from Affliction;
the Samādhi of Entering the Inconceivable Direction; the Samādhi of the Wisdom Entered by an Immeasurable Multitude, like the waters of the great ocean;
the Samādhi Adorned with Merits Like Mount Sumeru; and the Five Aggregates.
The samādhi of contemplating the formlessness of the six sense-bases; the samādhi of entering the realms of all Buddhas;
the samādhi of seeing all Buddhas in their entirety; the samādhi of the bodhisattva guarding the Way; the samādhi of explaining that all sūtras and dharmas are fundamentally formless;
the samādhi of precious adornments; the samādhi of learning to enter all precious things; and the samādhi of mindfulness of all Buddhas.
The Samādhi of Subtle Illumination; the Samādhi of the Bodhisattva’s Exalted Height; the Samādhi of True Non-retrogression and Turning the Wheel of Dharma;
the Samādhi of Adorning the Buddha’s Merits; the Samādhi of Being Without Defilement and Fully Purified;
the Samādhi of All Heard Matters Being Like the Great Ocean; the Samādhi of Having Nothing to Guard and No Faults; and the Samādhi of Delighting in the Sound of the Sūtras.
The Samādhi of Pervasive Sound; the Samādhi of the Manifest Banner of the Chapters of the Sūtra-Dharma;
the Samādhi of Entering the Formless Body of the Tathāgata; the Samādhi of Universally Beholding the Formlessness of All Sūtra-Dharmas;
the Samādhi of the Bodhisattva Seal; the Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Vision; and the Illumination of All Realms, wherein the aspirations of the Buddha-realm are fulfilled.
The Samādhi of the Feet; the Samādhi of Resolving the Difficulties of People in the Ten Directions; the Samādhi of the Adornment at the Approach to Buddhahood;
the Samādhi of Various Miscellaneous Flowers of Different Colors; the Samādhi of Abundant Precious Jewels; the Samādhi of the Constant Turning of the Dharma Wheel;
the Samādhi of All Sounds Heard Afar Entering the Essential; and the Samādhi of Entering the Fundamental Nature of People in the Ten Directions.
The Samādhi of Pervading All Three Realms, the Samādhi of Accomplishing All Meritorious Qualities, the Samādhi of Nothing Being Able to Surpass the Six Pāramitās,
the Samādhi of Destroying the Nets of Other Heretics When the Bodhisattva Sits Beneath the Tree,
and the Samādhi of the Tathāgata Manifesting Flight— these are adorned by an incalculable number of meritorious attainments.
The Samādhi of All Precious Jewels, Wisdom, and Merit; the Samādhi of the Stage of Sarvajñā (Omniscience); the Samādhi of Universal Purity;
the Samādhi of Universal Illumination; the Samādhi of Entering the Roots of Birth and Death of Beings Throughout the Ten Directions and Emerging from Wisdom;
and the Samādhi of the Complete Equality of the Past, Future, and Present.
In this manner,
the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita attained sixty thousand dharma-gates of samādhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata rose and entered the palace.
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Nine;
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-nine:

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita peacefully arose from his samādhi and, together with five hundred women, went to the gate of Dharmodgata’s palace. Standing outside the gate, he thought to himself: "I have come here for the sake of the Dharma;
since my teacher is inside, it would be improper for me to lie down or sit. I must wait until my teacher comes out, ascends the high seat, and preaches the Prajñāpāramitā, only then shall I sit."
The five hundred women also all followed the example of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and stood up.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata had finished instructing the women in the palace on the path of the sutras, he bathed and washed himself, put on new clothes, ascended the terrace of the Prajñāpāramitā, and sat there in contemplation, entering various samādhis; thus he remained for seven years, neither moving nor wavering.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women likewise practiced constant walking meditation for seven years, neither sitting nor lying down.
After those seven years had passed, a deity spoke from the sky above, saying:
'Seven days hence, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall arise from his samādhi.'"
At that time, when the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita heard the voice of the deva, he thought to himself:
"Now I shall provide a seat for my teacher and sweep and sprinkle it to make it pure."

The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women went together to the place where the sutra was being preached. Upon arrival, they specially prepared a high seat for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata; then, each of the five hundred women took the garment she was wearing and spread it upon the seat.
At that time, the evil Māra thought to himself:
"Never before has such a thing occurred; never before have I seen the like.

This Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita has prepared a high seat for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and, out of reverence, seeks the Buddha-way with diligent vigor and courage, without rest or weariness. One who attains the Way shall leave my realm, and those whom he delivers and liberates will be beyond calculation."
"Now I shall destroy them midway.

At that time, Māra the Evil One completely destroyed all the seats where the bodhisattvas were sitting, making them all crooked and warped, and rained down sand, gravel, stones, thorns, and dry bones.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women, seeing that the seat was crooked, sunken, and defiled with filth, thought to themselves:
"Now the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall sit upon this to preach the sutra, and all his disciples shall come to listen; we must now sweep it clean and arrange the seating once more."
Having together swept and arranged all the seats, he thought to himself:
"There is much dust on the ground now; I fear it will soil the Teacher and the various bodhisattvas. We should sprinkle it together."
He traveled everywhere searching for water but was unable to find any.
Why was this? It was the work of Māra, the Evil One.
He thought to himself:
"Now that we have searched for water and can find none at all, we must take our own blood and sprinkle it upon the ground.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women each took a knife and pierced their bodies in various places to draw out their blood, which they used to sprinkle on the ground, out of their compassionate devotion to the Dharma.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"Is there truly such a person in the world?
It is because he is diligent, respectful, compassionate, and filial toward his teacher of the sutras."
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra went to where the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita was and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Your worthy diligence is truly difficult to equal; because you have practiced such diligent devotion and filial piety toward your teacher, it will not be long before you now hear the Prajñāpāramitā."
"O Wise One!
Please convey our message regarding those whom others command: if there are such persons as these, we shall all protect them, and whatever they desire to obtain, we shall grant it all."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita said,
"That which I desire to obtain, Śakra Devānām Indra shall know of himself. Thereupon,
Śakra Devānām Indra immediately transformed the ground so that it became entirely of lapis lazuli, with golden sand upon it.
Śakra Devānām Indra caused the body of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women to be restored to their former state, healthy and whole.

He then manifested a pool of lapis lazuli water on the four sides of their seats; surrounding the pool were railings made of various jewels, as well as steps for the seven-jeweled pool. On both sides of the steps stood rows of jewel-trees of many hundreds of kinds, arranged in exquisite beauty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women were storing water for the bodhisattvas.
Celestial *mandārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers rained down in all varieties, totaling four thousand *shí*.
Śakra Devānām Indra took them and gave them to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying to him:

"Take these flowers to offer to the Prajñāpāramitā, and scatter them over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and the other bodhisattvas; and when five hundred celestial garments are spread upon the seat where Dharmodgata sits, take these and offer them as well."
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva immediately accepted them all and then offered a prayer of aspiration.

At that time, after seven years had passed, Dharmodgata Bodhisattva arose from his samādhi and ascended to the high seat; he sat together with forty trillion bodhisattvas, and those seated before him were exceedingly numerous.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women all scattered flowers together, and taking powdered sandalwood incense, honeyed incense, and various precious gems, they offered them all by scattering them over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and the other bodhisattvas. Having then placed their heads at his feet in prostration, they circumambulated him three times and withdrew to stand aside, gazing upon the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata with reverent minds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata presided over a great assembly within a square enclosure forty *li* on each side, which was filled with people.

Then, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata looked in the four directions at those gathered there—namely, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women—and because they sought to obtain the Dharma of the sutras, he spoke these words of the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!..."
Listen further:
all dharmas of the various sutras are entirely equal, and the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise entirely equal.
The original source of all dharmas of the various sutras is thus incalculable.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is without obstruction, and the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise without obstruction.
Just as a phantom person has no form, the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise without form.
It is so. All that belongs to a self (*ātmiya*) is utterly severed and fundamentally pure; likewise, the *prajñāpāramitā* is fundamentally non-existent.
For example, just as intercourse with a woman in a dream is fundamentally non-existent in its very appearance, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā* fundamentally non-existent.
That which is called "fundamentally non-existent" is such that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also fundamentally non-existent.
An arhat, nirvāṇa, and emptiness—which are without arising—are such that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also empty and without arising.
The *parinirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata is fundamentally equal and without distinction; likewise, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also fundamentally equal and without distinction.

For example, it is like lighting a fire: as soon as the fire is extinguished, it originally comes from nowhere, and when it goes out, it goes nowhere; in this same way, the *prajñāpāramitā* originally comes from nowhere, and when it departs, it goes nowhere.
For example, just as Mount Sumeru seen in a dream is fundamentally non-existent, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā* fundamentally non-existent.
For example, just as a Buddha manifests flying, so too does the *prajñāpāramitā* manifest as being nothing at all.
Just as one reflects upon the pleasures of desire and finds them to be non-existent, so too does one reflect upon the *prajñāpāramitā* and find it to be non-existent.

The person and their name are non-existent; even the *tathāgata* is non-existent. One who previously saw [the Buddha] perceives this through the causes of what was done; likewise, one who contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā* perceives that its fundamental nature is originally non-existent.
For example, just as a magician’s conjured elephant is fundamentally non-existent, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā* fundamentally non-existent.
For example, just as space has no place of abiding, so too the *prajñāpāramitā* has no place of abiding.
For example, just as there is nothing a master illusionist cannot achieve through his training, so too is it with the *prajñāpāramitā*; there is nothing it does not reach.
The past, future, and present cannot be combined into one; one should understand that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise free from past, present, or future.
Names have no form and characters have no shape; likewise, the Prajñāpāramitā reaches nowhere and enters nowhere, yet it neither arrives anywhere nor enters anywhere.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is empty and possesses nothing.
It is like space, which reaches nowhere and enters nowhere, yet neither reaches nor enters anything.
Why is this? Emptiness is fundamentally without form; such is the Prajñāpāramitā.
Such is the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Prajñāpāramitā enters into earth, enters into water, enters into fire, enters into wind,
and enters into space; it enters into that, enters into this,
and enters into form, enters into sensation, enters into perception, and [enters into volitional formations...]
They enter into birth-and-death, and they also enter into consciousness; they enter into the person, and they also enter into the life-span;
they enter into birth, and they also enter into the virtuous and the non-virtuous;
they enter into desire and the absence of desire; they enter into existence and non-existence. Furthermore—
They enter into perception and also enter into non-perception; they enter into aspiration and also enter into non-aspiration;
they enter into non-arising and also enter into non-production;
they enter into the sun and moon, and also enter into the constellations; they enter into the asuras and also enter into the nāgas.
...they also enter among the ghosts and spirits; they also enter among the gandharvas, the kinnaras, the mahoragas, the rākṣasas, and the garuḍas;
they also enter among the preta and the birds and beasts.
They enter into the hells; they also enter among those that fly, those that crawl, those that walk, and those that breathe;
they also enter into poverty and low status, as well as wealth and high status;
they also enter among the wise, the sages, and the stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*).
They also enter into the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, they also enter into the stage of Anāgāmin, they also enter into the stage of Arhat,
they also enter into the stage of Pratyekabuddha, they also enter into the stage of Bodhisattva, they also enter into the stage of Buddha, they also enter into Nirvāṇa,
and they also enter into the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa).
They enter into the five faculties, and they also enter into the five powers;
they enter into the seven factors of enlightenment, and they also enter into the eightfold path; they enter into wisdom, and they also enter into non-wisdom;
they enter into the ten powers, and they also enter into the four fearlessnesses; they enter into the Buddhist sūtras, and they also enter into...
The worldly scriptures also enter into the practice of sorcery and incantation, as well as that which is not sorcery;
they enter into the knowledge of past lives, as well as into the sphere of conduct;
they enter into the cycle of successive births and deaths, as well as into diligent exertion and lack of exertion; and they enter into sovereignty, as well as into...
Lacking self-mastery, they enter both liberation and non-liberation;
they enter both the agreeable and the disagreeable; they enter both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
they enter both the intelligent and the unintelligent; and they enter into clarity.
The middle also enters into ignorance; it enters into the past, enters into the future, and enters into the present;
it enters into the visible and enters into the invisible;
it enters into the teaching and enters into the Dharma; it enters into existence and enters into non-existence.
"Everything, moreover, enters into all that is with form and enters into all that is without form.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In this manner, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata explained to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita the locus where the Prajñāpāramitā enters, speaking in this way for seven days and nights."
At that time, the people listening to the sutra perceived it as being only the duration of a meal.
Why was this? It was due to the power and grace of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita heard the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, he was filled with great joy and leaped for gladness; together with the five hundred women, he offered celestial robes and eight hundred measures of various jewels as an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
Śakra Devānām Indra took celestial mahāmāndārava flowers and scattered them over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, as well as over all the other bodhisattvas, using them to augment their merit.

At that time, all the trees within the realm of a single Buddha—the medicinal trees, the fruit trees, and the various jewel trees—all bent their trunks and bowed down in prostration before the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

Heavenly rain fell of honey-scented flowers, the fragrance of which was heard throughout an entire Buddha-field. When all the people smelled the scent of these flowers, each of them saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata from afar preaching the sutra upon his high seat, and they also saw the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita along with the five hundred women. The hearts of all the people became gentle and joyful; they all paid homage from afar to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, and the entire kingdom trembled.
At that time, many thousands of billions of people all attained immeasurable sutras and dharmas, and incalculable bodhisattvas all attained the stage of *avaivartika*.
The daughter of the elder and five hundred women said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:

"We wish to become your maidservants; we vow to offer our bodies and lives in refuge to you, and we wish to serve as your attendants. We shall together take these five hundred chariots filled with precious treasures and offer them all to you, our teacher."
For what reason?
Now our Teacher has undergone great hardship for our sake; we hold our Teacher to be no different from the Buddha.
We have received this great grace, having been able to hear the sublime words of the Honored One’s sutra.
Having heard this sutra, we no longer harbor any doubts as large as a hair.

Now, even if we were to serve our teacher with our very bodies for thousands of billions of koṭis of kalpas, we would still be unable to repay even a moment’s worth of his kindness, solely because we have been granted the opportunity to hear this honored scripture.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita accepted all five hundred women as well as the five hundred chariots and precious jewels. Having accepted them for the sake of the Way and its virtue, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita wished to offer them to his teacher and addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying:

"I pray that you will accept my own person, these five hundred women, and these five hundred chariots and precious jewels to be presented to the Great Master. Have compassion for us and please accept them, so that we may obtain merit."

At that time, because the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata wished to cause the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to fulfill his merit, he accepted all five hundred women as well as the five hundred chariots and precious treasures.
Having accepted them, he in turn gave them back to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Take these five hundred women to serve as your attendants, along with the five hundred carts of precious jewels."
At that time, the devas and humans of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven each exclaimed in praise:
"Excellent, excellent!
That the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita gives away everything he possesses to his teacher—such a resolve is difficult to attain."
At that time, several thousand billions of devas and humans came together to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was to listen to the sutra.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita was filled with great joy and exultation, and he immediately attained sixty thousand gates of samādhi while sitting upon his seat.
What are the gateways to samādhi?

They are: the samādhi of aspiration and joy, the samādhi of majestic deportment, the samādhi of exhorting virtue, the samādhi of the full moon, the samādhi of the blazing radiance of the sun, the samādhi of the conduct of the Tathāgata, and the samādhi of mindfulness of all Buddhas.
The samādhis produced by the Bodhisattva are: the samādhi of delighting in wisdom, the samādhi of firm abiding in liberation,
the samādhi of non-abiding amidst all objective realms, the samādhi of entering the various adornments of buddha-lands,
the samādhi of entering the marks and marklessness of the Tathāgata, and the samādhi of the seal of formlessness upon the people of the ten directions.
The Tathāgata emerged from the Samādhi of Sitting, the Samādhi of Joy in Fearlessness, the Samādhi of Discarding Precious Jewels,
the Samādhi of Adorning the Power of the Tathāgata, the Samādhi of Joy in Clearly Illuminating All Dharmas of the Sūtras,
the Samādhi of Explaining the Understanding that Nothing Comes from Anywhere, and the Samādhi of Purity Like a Brahmā.
They all equally enter the samādhi of the past, future, and present; the samādhi of the fundamental beginning and the future end having no abode;
the samādhi of adorning the Buddha-treasury; and the samādhi in which the resonance of the Buddha’s voice is fully perfected.
"By means of this samādhi, sixty thousand gateways were attained.
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita emerged from samādhi, acquired the power of wisdom, and entered entirely into the sūtras and dharmas of all bodhisattvas."
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita said to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata:
"Master, I pray that you will explain the voice of the Buddha; how should one know it?
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"Listen attentively, O Wise One!

For example, a lute is not accomplished by a single factor; it requires wood, a frame, strings, and a person who moves their hand to play it. Only then does its sound become harmonious and free, allowing one to perform whatever melody one desires."
Wise ones who wish to understand the Buddha’s voice should do so in this same way.

A bodhisattva has an original aspiration from the beginning; through successive lifetimes they cultivate merit, provide instruction, and inquire about the Buddha’s deeds. It is through the convergence of these matters that the Buddha-body is perfected, and the Buddha’s voice is likewise so.

These dharmas all arise from causes and conditions; they cannot be attained through the practices of a bodhisattva, nor can they be attained apart from the practices of a bodhisattva; they cannot be attained through the body of a Buddha, nor can they be attained apart from the body of a Buddha.
Worthy one, if you wish to know the body and voice of the Buddha, it is only by combining these factors that you can hear the Buddha.

Furthermore, worthy one, it is like a skilled master of the long flute whose tone is harmonious and blends perfectly with song; though the flute itself is made of bamboo, it is only when there is a skilled player and all these elements are combined that its sound becomes mournful.

The attainment of the body of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not accomplished by a single matter, nor by two matters; it is accomplished through hundreds of thousands of matters. It results from the merit accumulated life after life and the power of original vows, as well as from teaching others life after life. For these reasons, the marks and secondary characteristics of the Buddha-body are fully realized and seen in this way.

It is like this: suppose after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, someone were to create an image of the Buddha. When people see this image of the Buddha, there are none who do not kneel, prostrate, and make offerings to it.

That image is upright, beautiful, and exquisite, no different from the Buddha himself; seeing it, there are none who do not praise it, and none who do not offer flowers, incense, and silken fabrics as worship.
"The worthy ones call upon the Buddha; does the spirit reside within the image?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied, "It does not reside within."
The reason for creating images of the Buddha is simply to enable people to obtain merit.

An image of the Buddha is not made by means of a single thing, nor is it made by means of two things; there must be gold and a craftsman. Furthermore, if there were people who had seen the Buddha during his lifetime, or if there are those who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they therefore create images so that people of the world may make offerings and thereby obtain merit.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied to his teacher, saying,
"It is for the sake of making images after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.
Dharmodgata Bodhisattva replied:
"As the worthy one has said, the attainment of the Buddha-body is likewise: it does not rely on a single thing, nor does it rely on two things; it relies upon many tens of millions of things."

There is the practice of a bodhisattva, which fundamentally seeks Buddhahood. If, at that time, people constantly see the Buddha performing meritorious deeds, by virtue of this they achieve the Buddha-body, with its wisdom-transformations, flight, and the accomplishment of all the primary and secondary marks.
The attainment of Buddhahood is likewise.
"Worthy one, listen further!

For example, a drum is not produced by a single factor, nor is it produced by two factors; there must be a master, there must be leather, there must be a mallet, and there must be a person who strikes it, for its sound then to emerge."
If a wise person wishes to know the Buddha, it is not accomplished by means of one or two matters, but rather through many thousands of various matters.

There is the initial aspiration for enlightenment, there is the practice of the six *pāramitās*, and the clear realization that all things are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*). Since this fundamental non-existence is a state from which nothing arises, he sat beneath the tree and subdued Māra. He thoroughly understood that all the teachings of the sūtras are like illusions and no different from them; it is by these means that he attained the body of a Buddha.
“Wise one, listen further!

For example, it is like a painter who has a wall, pigments, a master craftsman, and a brush; when these factors are combined, a painted figure is produced. If you wish to know the Buddha-body, it is not accomplished by a single factor, but by hundreds of thousands of factors.”

The Bodhisattva has fundamental practices of giving, observes the precepts without transgressing the ten matters, constantly follows virtuous teachers, and always maintains an impartial mind toward the people of the ten directions such that none can destroy it. Life after life he sees the Buddhas, hears of the deeds of the Bodhisattvas, and upholds them firmly without forgetting. In every lifetime he is free from flattery and always acts with utmost sincerity. Worthy one, if you wish to know how the body of a Buddha is attained, it is like this.
“Wise one, listen further!

For example, consider the palaces of the devas and humans in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, which illuminate everything with their radiance and are exquisitely beautiful. Just like these celestial mansions, they were not made by themselves, nor were they brought from elsewhere; they have no creator, they originally come from nowhere, and when they pass away, they go nowhere—they are born of causes and conditions.”

It is because that celestial being originally performed meritorious deeds and practiced giving in this world that he was able to be born above, dwelling at ease within a palace; for this reason, that person obtains a palatial mansion.

The wise who wish to know the Buddha-body as born of causes and conditions do so because they desire to see the Buddha; such persons have possessed merit in previous lives, have been reborn far removed from the eight unfavorable states, and are sagacious and full of faith in the Buddha.

If the wise wish to know the body of a Buddha, they should understand that it originally comes from nowhere and departs to nowhere; there is no creator, nor is there anyone who brings it forth. It is fundamentally formless and without attachment, like a palace in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
The reason the Buddha manifests his body is that he wishes to deliver and liberate the people of the world.
"Worthy one, listen further!

For example, an echo in the mountains cannot be produced by a single factor, nor can it be produced by two factors; there must be the mountain, the person, the calling, and the ear that hears. It is through the convergence of these conditions that the echo is formed."

If the wise wish to know the body of a Buddha, it is thus without form and without attachment; it is born of causes and conditions. Life after life one understands emptiness and practices emptiness; all birth and death have no birth or death as their cause and condition. The Buddha’s wisdom fully understands that fundamentally there is no birth or death, and fundamentally there is also no one who enters *parinirvāṇa*.
The Buddha manifested this in the world and spoke thus: "Virtuous one, you should know that the Buddha’s body is like this.
"Virtuous one, listen further!
It is as if a master illusionist were to conjure a person who is upright and beautiful, no different from a Cakravartin king."
Whatever he spoke, there was no one among the multitude who did not rejoice upon hearing it.
If anyone came to him seeking gold, silver, or precious jewels, he gave them all of it.
If anyone sought his cherished garments and robes, he gave them all of those as well.

When the King sat, rose, or walked among the multitude, he was always composed and serene; there was no one who saw him who did not pay him homage with reverence. This illusion is not accomplished by means of a single or two things;

there is the illusory incantation and the assembly of people, and according to what each person prefers, various manifestations appear. Among them, those who are wise recognize that these are created by an illusionist; they know that these manifested forms come from nowhere and go nowhere, understanding that they are fundamentally empty and produced by transformation. Thus, the wise pay their respects with reverence, yet remain unattached.

The wise who wish to know how the body of a Buddha is formed should understand it as follows: it is produced through causes and conditions, brought into being by hundreds of thousands of factors; it possesses the conduct of a bodhisattva, merit, and the virtue of exhortation and assistance, bringing peace and security to the people of the ten directions for those who have fulfilled the bodhisattva vows—thus should one who wishes to know the body of a Buddha understand it.

Because the wise desire to know whether the Buddha is a human being, they distribute countless sutras and transmit them to others, causing each person to practice dhyāna-samādhi and engage in contemplative discernment, and teaching the sutras to others so that each may learn.
When the gods and people heard this, there were none who did not rejoice. Among them, some were conceited; some lacked a sense of shame; some were lewd and disorderly; some were stingy and greedy;

some were violent and arrogant; some were self-opinionated; some delighted in strife; some would not accept admonition; some were shrouded by lust, anger, and delusion; and some committed incalculable evils. Yet the Buddha stood in the midst of the great multitude, upright and magnificent; his sitting, rising, and walking were serene and composed. The Buddha’s manifold evils were already exhausted, and he possessed only virtues. The Buddha causes all people to attain peace and security, and he himself performs the work of a Buddha. By nature, the Buddha is originally empty and unattached, like the creations of a magician.

The Bodhisattva manifests a body so upright, handsome, and beautiful that, though they see it, they do not become attached to it, nor do they harbor any conceptual thoughts regarding it; though they know it is non-existent, they pay homage with reverence and perform boundless offerings.
The wise who wish to know that all Buddhas of the past, future, and present arise from causes and conditions, each based upon tens of millions of distinct factors.
“A Bodhisattva should form this thought, should practice this, and should maintain this; by practicing in this way, a Bodhisattva quickly attains Buddhahood.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata spoke of the Buddha-body, forty-eight thousand Bodhisattvas immediately attained the practice of complete faith, and ten billion Bodhisattvas all attained the dhāraṇī-dharmas;
two hundred billion Bodhisattvas attained unimpededness, such that they were able to answer all questions posed to them.
Four hundred billion bodhisattvas all attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression);
eighty trillion bodhisattvas all attained the dharma of abiding in the *asaṃbhavakāra* (unborn) practice.
At that time, *maṇḍārava* flowers and *mahāmaṇḍārava* flowers rained down upon the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and the other bodhisattvas.

By the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, all musical instruments throughout the entire Buddha-field spontaneously produced sounds. Countless tens of millions of devas scattered celestial garments from the air, raining them down upon the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata and the other bodhisattvas. The devas played music in the sky, together rejoicing in the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata. The celestial garments were arranged in rows, covering the entire Buddha-field; the incense of the devas, such as *mṛdvīka* (honey-scented) incense, reached everywhere, and its diffusion likewise pervaded the whole. The earth within the Buddha-field trembled, and all the bodhisattvas beheld the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, all the Buddhas praised the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata from afar, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the Buddhas bestowed their instructions upon the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
"When you attain Buddhahood, in a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Kamakathipālaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"When you attain Buddhahood, your title shall indeed be such as this.
Furthermore, these five hundred women shall, after some time, all likewise become Buddhas.
At that time, the five hundred women were immediately transformed into men; thereafter, in every successive birth, they were never separated from the lands of the Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and his five hundred followers have always possessed superior talent throughout their successive lives, and they shall constantly teach all people in the world.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“If there are bodhisattvas engaged in practice who wish to attain Buddhahood—whether they see a present Buddha or seek the Prajñāpāramitā after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa—they must always be diligent and always show reverence toward the Prajñāpāramitā, just as the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita did.”

Chapter 30: Entrustment. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Practice of the Path*, Chapter Thirty, the Entrustment: The Buddha stroked Ānanda’s shoulder with his hand three times and said to him, “I entrust this *prajñāpāramitā* to you;
hold it fast and keep it in mind with careful attention.”

Ānanda! This Prajñāpāramitā is entrusted to you by its very characteristics; always maintain it with clear understanding. Grasp the characters with clear understanding, and when reciting or writing them, do not allow anything to be omitted. Examine the writing attentively without looking left or right, for there may be all manner of obstacles. Be mindful of this sutra and ensure that no character is missing.
I entrust this Prajñāpāramitā to you, Ānanda. Why is this?
Because, Ānanda, this sutra—

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses an inexhaustible treasury of sūtras throughout the past, future, and present; this sūtra governs all dharmas, for everything that exists emerges from within it.

Ānanda! Whatever sūtras the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught for the sake of sentient beings in the past, future, and present—those innumerable volumes of sūtras, the various forms of wisdom, the diverse collections of scriptures, the different inclinations of those he encountered, and the teachings on the paths and wisdoms according to the respective practices of sentient beings—all that has been spoken in the past, future, and present has emerged entirely from this treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā. All dharmas contained within these sūtras have issued forth from it.

Ānanda! Whatever kinds of perceived signs there are, whatever various modes of conduct, whatever kinds of faculties, whatever kinds of cleverness, whatever kinds of folly, and whatever kinds of wisdom—whatever the people seek and the wisdom they seek for those ends—the Tathāgata knows them all completely.
Ānanda! All emerge from within the Prajñāpāramitā; all are fully understood in this way. Ānanda!

The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is the illumination of all wisdom, it is my own body, for all things emerge from within it and are born from within it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If you revere my words, revere my Dharma, and if you revere, love, and serve me—if you revere yourself as being toward the Buddha, if you have loving-kindness for the Buddha, and if you have filial piety for the Buddha—then, with all such reverence toward the Buddha, you should maintain this loving-kindness, filial piety, and reverence within the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
You have shown reverence therein, having made offerings to all the Buddhas; I entrust this to you, Ānanda!

That which you ought to have done has all been accomplished; your body possesses loving-kindness, your speech possesses loving-kindness, and your mind possesses loving-kindness. You are filial toward the Buddha, and it cannot be said that you lack filiality;
you always encounter the Buddha when the time is right, and it cannot be said that you do not encounter him at the proper time;
you always act in accordance with the Dharma, and it cannot be said that you do not act in accordance with the Dharma.
Your mind is always pure and free from blemish; though you have seen the Buddha, you do not say that you have seen him. By being thus, you have fully repaid the Buddha’s kindness.
I tell you this, Ānanda!

If even a single word of this Prajñāpāramitā were lost from within it, and you were to abandon it, intending not to write it down, you would be acting in vain; for you lack compassion and filiality toward the Buddha, and thus you shall no longer see me.
Ānanda! You no longer show reverence toward the Buddha. Ānanda!
Ānanda, you no longer follow the Buddha’s teaching; Ānanda,
you no longer serve and employ it.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

All the reverence you have shown the Buddha until now does not constitute a complete offering to the Buddha. If, from this Prajñāpāramitā, you were to lose even a single phrase or a single word, it would be considered a betrayal of the Buddha’s kindness.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“Receive this Prajñāpāramitā with careful attention and mindful recollection. Out of filial devotion to the Buddha and in order to uphold his teachings, know that this is entirely the instruction bestowed by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. To employ it as an offering constitutes the ultimate great compassion for all sentient beings (*sattva*). All Bodhisattvas should regard it as seeing the Buddha and should revere it as the Dharma of all Buddhas.”
As you draw near to and uphold the treasury of the Buddha, reflect thus with earnest attention:
"Regarding this Prajñāpāramitā, one should grasp it with careful precision; do not lose even a single word."

"After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, you should protect this sutra so that it does not diminish, and you should uphold it and transmit it to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as the treasury of the scriptures of all Buddhas."
Ānanda! I entrust this to you; you should hold it and transmit it to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who maintain it. Ānanda!

The merit performed by the Bodhisattva shatters the prison of the toil of birth and death; those who are ignorant and bound by attachments are all delivered and liberated; none among the hosts of Māras are not subdued; all dharmas of desire are entirely eliminated; he ascends to the seat of the Buddha and realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thereby attaining the Way of the Buddha, so that all people who are sightless and deluded may be opened to understanding.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“The foremost, singular Great Way has no duality; this is the wisdom of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and it is the definitive resolution of the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“After my parinirvāṇa, all the people within the entire trichiliocosm, you shall teach them all to enter the Dharma of the sūtras and cause them all to achieve the path of arhatship. Teaching such numbers of people every day, for one kalpa or even a hundred kalpas, you shall preach the sūtras to them all so that they may attain parinirvāṇa.”

Even so, you have not constantly and fully served me; it would be better for you to take up even a single verse from this Prajñāpāramitā and teach it to a bodhisattva. By doing so, you will have fully served the Buddha and fully made offerings to him.
The Buddha said:
"I now praise you for this and entrust to you the Prajñāpāramitā; even in one kalpa or a hundred kalpas, I could not finish [this task], so I have merely given a rough exposition here."
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I shall now question you; you should answer.

The Buddha extended his golden arm from within his kāṣāya, raised his right hand and placed it upon Ānanda’s head, stroking Ānanda’s head, and resting his hand upon Ānanda’s shoulder, he spoke to Ānanda:
“What do you think, Ānanda?
Do you not feel loving-kindness toward the Buddha?
Ānanda replied:
“The Buddha, the God among Gods, shall know this himself.
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha then asked Ānanda again:
“What do you think, Ānanda?
Are you filial toward the Buddha?
He asked this three times.
Ānanda said, "The Buddha,
the God among Gods, will surely know for himself.
The Buddha said:
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
You have loving-kindness for the Buddha; this is how you repay the Buddha's kindness. Ānanda!"

You should pay the utmost honor and profound respect to the Prajñāpāramitā; cherish these words and the words you contemplate, ensuring that what your mind contemplates is clear and distinct. Abandon everything else, and let your entire mind be centered within this.

When copying this scripture, one must ensure the characters are correct from beginning to end. While holding it or studying it, one should carefully transmit it to a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, providing him with a fine, long roll of plain silk. One should skillfully transcribe it so that the preceding and following lines of the scripture correspond perfectly. When writing, one should use a fine brush upon high-quality silk. One should take refuge in it, serve it, prostrate before it, and make offerings—using fine incense, powdered incense, blended fragrant oils, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags, all like the incenses found in the heavens. Having placed these among purified sesame seeds and prepared fine lamp wicks from clean sesame oil, one should take refuge with head bowed to the ground, then light the lamps and pay homage with increased reverence, serving it with devotion.
When the Buddha was preaching this Prajñāpāramitā, he was at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha, seated in the midst of his assembly of disciples.
The Buddha attained Buddhahood at the age of thirty; on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, after the midday meal, he preached this sutra.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the disciples, bodhisattvas, devas, asuras, nāgas, spirits, and human beings were filled with great joy; they paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Sutra on the Practice of the Way of Wisdom, Scroll Ten.
